News.title: Former mayor, 68, collapses and dies during row at meeting of Britain’s ‘craziest’ council
News.content:
'LASTING LEGACY' Former mayor, 68, collapses and dies during row at meeting of Britain’s ‘craziest’ council







Next

A FORMER mayor collapsed and died after a row erupted during a meeting at Britain’s “craziest council”.

Peter Neal, 68, died after suffering a “serious medical emergency” at an Attleborough Town Council meeting in Norfolk on Monday evening.



An air ambulance was scrambled to the scene but despite the best efforts of paramedics, he was sadly pronounced dead.

Members of the council administered CPR and used a defibrillator as they desperately tried to save Mr Neal’s life.



Daniel Piddington, the council’s deputy mayor, offered his “heartfelt condolences” to his Neal’s family and friends.

The local authority is flying its flag at half mast as “a mark of respect” as tributes flood in for the former mayor.

Mr Neal tragically passed away in the town hall after pleading to end years of turmoil at a council dubbed “battleborough” or “Britain’s craziest council”.

According to EDP, he pleaded: “Please, please can we find a way forward?”

But just moments later, Mr Neal collapsed.

The 68-year-old was mayor of Attleborough Town Council between 2002 and 2003 and has been vocal in urging the authority to resolve its differences.



The council said in a statement on Wednesday: “Attleborough Town Council is deeply saddened to confirm that a member of the public suffered a serious medical emergency during last night’s Council meeting and subsequently passed away.

“The Council extends its sincere condolences to their family and friends at this incredibly difficult time.”

Cllr Jacob Allen, who helped provide CPR in the council chamber said: “Peter Neal was an exceptional member of our community.

“His contributions to public life, both as a councillor and as mayor, have left a lasting legacy in our town.

“His contributions to public life, both as a councillor and as mayor, have left a lasting legacy in our town.”



Jeremy Burton, who worked alongside Neal on the council, said he was a “dedicated family man” and “his huge personality and sharp wit will never be forgotten”.

An East of England Ambulance Service spokesman said: “We were called on Monday evening just after 8.40pm to a medical emergency at Queen’s Square, Attleborough.

“Two ambulances, an ambulance officer vehicle and the East Anglian Air Ambulance were sent to the scene.

“Sadly, despite the best efforts of everyone involved, the patient died at the scene.”

News.title: Cops who pepper-sprayed & Tasered amputee, 92, ‘could have contributed to his death’ three weeks later, coroner told
News.content:
Next

TWO cops who pepper-sprayed, batoned and Tasered a 92-year-old amputee who had dementia may have contributed to his death, a coroner was told.

Donald Burgess was sitting in his wheelchair when officers were called to his care home after he refused to let go of a specially adapted butter knife.



The officers had been called to Park Beck in St Leonards-on-Sea on June 21, 2022 after Donald poked a worker in the stomach with the butter knife.

Chilling bodycam footage showed the pensioner screaming in pain as PC Stephen Smith sprayed him before repeatedly striking him with his baton.



Within seconds, PC Rachel Comotto then joined in by Tasering the elderly man when he was still clutching the knife.

The entire incident lasted less than 90 seconds.



The elderly man’s family are now asking for the inquest into his death to be reopened, after the two cops were cleared of assault at Southwark Crown Court last year.

At a pre-inquest hearing in Lewes, their barrister Jesse Nicholls said there was a clear need to investigate whether the use of force contributed to Donald’s death 22 days later.



He said: “This is a case where an elderly and very vulnerable man was subjected to significant force by police and later died in circumstances he would not have been in.”

Mr Nicholls claimed the actions of the two officers may have caused “physiological stress” that may have had a “causative” effect on the care home resident’s death.

Donald, who had one leg, was a wheelchair user with dementia and a history of serious health problems including diabetes and carotid artery disease.

The family’s solicitor said officers made no effort to assess the situation before using significant force within one minute and 14 seconds.

He said: “They’re shouting, screaming threats against him while he is sitting unmoving in a wheelchair.”



When Donald was asked how he was, he replied: “I’m dying.”

The officers then handcuffed him and removed him from the care home.

The solicitor also highlighted comments allegedly made by PC Comotto as they left, saying: “You can hear PC Comotto laughing and saying, ‘Is there any Pava left in the can.'”



He said PC Comotto told care home staff she was unaware what type of home Park Beck was.

The solictor added: “They might have checked that before using spray, baton and Taser.”

Donald was taken to Conquest Hospital, where he was treated for a urinary infection.

He was not allowed to return to the care home after being discharged on June 28 and remained in hospital.

He later tested positive for Covid on July 9 and died 22 days after police were called to the home.



A post-mortem gave his cause of death as heart disease with bronchopneumonia.

Lawyers representing the officers and Sussex Police argued there was no evidence the use of force brought about his death any sooner.

Tom Day, representing Sussex Police, said: “There is no evidence the actions of the officers brought about his death any sooner than it would have been.”

Despite Donald only having one leg, PC Smith claimed he did not realise he was disabled.

PC Comotto denied being “trigger-happy”.



Both officers were cleared of assault occasioning actual bodily harm at Southwark Crown Court in May last year.

Following the verdict, Donald’s family said they were “disappointed and saddened” after an “incredibly distressing” three years.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Assistant Coroner Michael Spencer said he would give his decision on whether to reopen the inquest at a later date.

PCs Smith and Comotto are also due to face a police disciplinary tribunal next week.

News.title: Why putting welfare bill at top of agenda is both a smart political and economic move for Kemi
News.content:
POLITICS FIX Why putting welfare bill at top of agenda is both a smart political and economic move for Kemi







Next

BRITAIN’S enormous benefits bill has once again been thrust to the top of the political news agenda.

Tory leader Kemi Badenoch is today pledging to stop welfare claimants using their money to buy cigarettes and booze, instead limiting them to just the essentials.



It could prove to be both a smart political move from the Conservative chief who is seeking to tap into frustration from workers that people on benefits splash out on luxuries.

But it might also make economic sense if, as the Tories claim, this would help reduce the eye-watering amount of money the government is currently spending on welfare.



This year the country is set to splurge around £150billion on benefits – dwarfing the defence, education and prisons budget combined.

Such gargantuan spending levels have forced successive governments to push taxes to peacetime records – with Andy Burnham likely to hike them yet again in next month’s Budget.

The PM did however acknowledge this week that the last two Budgets had whacked up taxes enormously, and that he needed to “get the balance right”.

He could find it tricky though to cut spending if his notoriously reluctant Labour MPs oppose any meaningful spending restraint.

At least he has some good news to trumpet today though, having signalled he will lift the ban on drinking alcohol at football matches.

For 40 years booze has been prohibited during games to avoid fuelling drunken disorder – something the PM branded “unfair”.



While fans have welcomed the plan, police chiefs are already lining up to criticise it on the grounds it will lead to hooliganism and stretch their already thin resources.

News.title: At least 9 dead after huge fire breaks out on bus as terrified passengers forced to jump out windows to escape blaze
News.content:
DEADLY INFERNO At least 9 dead after huge fire breaks out on bus as terrified passengers forced to jump out windows to escape blaze







Next

AT LEAST nine people have died after a huge fire broke out on a moving bus and trapped dozens of terrified passengers inside.

Choking black smoke quickly filled up the packed double-decker after a blaze broke out near the driver’s seat with several travellers forced to smash the windows and jump out to escape the flames.



One woman and eight men were confirmed to be among the victims with around 35 people crammed onto the bus at the time of the fire.

The driver and conductor of the bus have both been arrested.



Passengers told police they reported a concerning burning smell coming from the front of the bus as it headed down the Yamuna Expressway near Jewar, India late on Wednesday night.

Several people repeatedly asked to pull over as the smell worsened on board but the driver and conductor said there was no issue, witnesses claimed.

A few minutes later, the front of the bus became engulfed in flames as it came to a dramatic halt in the middle of the highway.

Most passengers were said to be asleep when the fire took hold at around 11.30pm.

Fleeing passengers became trapped as smoke filled up the burning wreckage and blocked off the exits.

People were forced to smash the windows and leap out onto the road before rushing back to try and rescue others.



Emergency crews rushed to the scene and said they managed to pull 20 passengers from the bus.

The bus was travelling from Kashmiri Gate in New Delhi towards Mahoba.

The cause of the fire is yet to be confirmed.

President Droupadi Murmu called the tragedy ” extremely heartbreaking”.

As Prime Minister Narendra Modi expressed grief over the bus fire tragedy, saying: “Distressed to hear about the loss of lives due to a fire tragedy on a bus in Greater Noida, Uttar Pradesh.



“Condolences to those who have lost their loved ones. Praying for the swift recovery of the injured.”

An investigation into the fire is ongoing.

News.title: Labour could be forced into ‘rainbow alliance’ to stay in power after next election, shock poll reveals
News.content:
Next

LABOUR could be forced to rely on a “rainbow” alliance of Lib Dems and nationalist MPs to stay in power after the next election, a bombshell mega-poll suggests.

Andy Burnham‘s party would emerge as the largest in a hung Parliament with 241 seats but fall a whopping 85 short of an outright Commons majority, according to the YouGov MRP survey.



Kemi Badenoch’s Tories would come second on 130 seats, pushing Nigel Farage’s Reform into third on 123 in a stunning reversal of fortunes.

Just a year ago, YouGov’s last MRP put Reform on a staggering 311 seats — just 15 shy of an outright majority and on course to dominate the Commons.



The latest projection would see Mr Farage’s party lose 188 of those predicted seats and tumble from first place to third.

It also marks a remarkable recovery for the Tories, who were projected to be virtually wiped out with just 45 MPs in the same poll last September.



The projected result would still leave no party with an easy route to power and could trigger frantic horse-trading after polling day.

Even if the Conservatives and Reform joined forces, they would muster only 253 MPs — 73 short of the official 326 winning line.

But Labour would also struggle to govern alone and could need the backing of several opposition parties to keep Mr Burnham in No10.

Sir Ed Davey’s Lib Dems are projected to win 71 seats, taking the two parties to 312 between them.



That would leave them 14 MPs short of the official majority threshold.

Labour could therefore be forced to turn to the nationalists or other smaller parties to get legislation through the Commons.

Plaid Cymru is projected to win 15 seats, meaning a Labour-Lib Dem-Plaid alliance would scrape over the line on 327.

The SNP, meanwhile, is forecast to surge to 40 seats, opening up another possible route to a Commons majority.

The Greens are projected to win nine seats.



The result raises the prospect of a sprawling multi-party deal, whether through a formal coalition or looser agreements to prop up a Labour government.

Head of elections at YouGov Patrick English said the poll showed that the fragmented state of Britain’s politics impacted the right harder than the left.

He said: “YouGov’s latest projections put Labour clearly ahead of both Reform and the Conservatives in terms of seats, while being only a fraction ahead of each on vote share.

“While Labour alone remain well short of a majority, there are a wide range of possible ‘coalition of the left’ options open to them to build a majority in a way where there just simply isn’t for Reform and the Conservatives on the right.

“While the British political left is more fragmented than the right in terms of the number of different parties, their collective vote share is bigger and translates efficiently into seat wins.”



The poll would also deliver a string of humiliating personal defeats.

Reform defectors Robert Jenrick and Suella Braverman are both projected to lose their seats to their former party.

Mr Jenrick quit the Conservatives for Reform earlier this year, while Ms Braverman also crossed the floor to Mr Farage’s party.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Labour would suffer casualties too, with Health Secretary Yvette Cooper projected to lose her Pontefract, Castleford and Knottingley seat to Reform.

News.title: Rowdy Brit stag and hen dos set to be slapped with £2,500 fines in Spanish city as penis straws & blowup dolls banned
News.content:
PARTY POOPER Rowdy Brit stag and hen dos set to be slapped with £2,500 fines in Spanish city as penis straws & blowup dolls banned







Next

BRITS hoping to let loose on rowdy hen and stag dos at a Spanish holiday city could soon be hit with giant fines under new proposed laws.

Whether you are Team Bride or a Lad on Tour you may want to rethink the penis straws and blowup dolls as Valencia threatens fines of up to £2,500 for its raucous revellers.



The city has proposed regulations to curb the rowdier Brit traditions with the plans put the city on track to become the first area to explicitly target pre-wedding celebrations.

Maximum fines of £2,500 will be reserved for punters who commit the most serious offences, such as refusing to cooperate with the council or engaging in disrespectful behaviour.



But even simply wearing a mankini or sipping from a penis straw could leave a bad taste in the mouths of pre-nuptial partygoers as they risk being slapped with fines.

Carrying explicit adult novelties or wearing clothing depicting human genitalia in public areas could carry huge fines of up to £644.

Boisterous gatherings would be classed as an offence if they take place on the streets between 10pm and 8am from Sunday to Friday.

Anyone caught partying between these times could face the whopping fines unless the event has been officially organised by the council.

Mockery or deliberate harassment towards vulnerable people such as elderly residents, children and people with disabilities, would be met with penalties.

Fines could be upped if the behaviour is carried out by groups or involves filming victims.



The draft legislation also proposes fines of up to £1,299 for drinking alcohol on the street with the fines potentially doubled if the offence takes place in or near a protected building.

The law is still at the drafting stage and will have to be reviewed by officials before it can be formally adopted.

In 2023, a similar ban was threatened in the Costa del Sol with authorities hoping to thwart the wild antics of tourists.

Other fines have been introduced across Spain to help curb poor behaviour, including in Vigo, Galicia.

A rule was introduced in Marbella in 2024, where urinating in the sea was banned on 25 beaches in the area.



In Barcelona and Majorca, wearing swimming costumes or being topless in restaurants and shops could land you with a fine of up to £258.

In May 2024, a wedding party erupted into a violent brawl on a Majorcan beach.

Eight men were arrested at Balneario Illetas beach club, located between Palma and Magaluf, just days before attending a wedding on the holiday island.

News.title: Andy Burnham admits Britain can’t afford more damaging hikes in Budget and Labour must get ‘balance’ right
News.content:
Next

ANDY Burnham has signalled Britain can’t afford another tax-raising Budget.

He said Labour has to be “conscious” of more damaging hikes and must get the “balance” right.



It came after the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development said UK growth will slow next year.

The PM was quizzed on whether the balance between taxing wealth and taxing income is right and whether it will be addressed at the October Budget.



Burnham said: “We have two budgets in 2024 and 2025 and we have to be conscious of the extent to which we have raised revenue. And we have to make sure we get the balance right.”

Ex-Chancellor Rachel Reeves raised taxes including a national insurance raid on employers and a three-year freeze on income tax thresholds.

Meanwhile, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development report comes just weeks before Chancellor John Healey delivers his Budget where he may need to find £15 billion.

Fresh forecasts show growth of just 1 per cent next year which is a slowdown from the 1.1 per cent predicted in June.

But UK growth for this year has nudged up 0.2 per cent to 1.1 per cent.

They are now expecting inflation to slow down to 2.6 per cent but this is higher than the 2.4 per cent predicted earlier in the summer. The Bank of England target is 2 per cent.



They also say that the Bank of England may be forced to cut interest rates to boost growth.

The OECD latest outlook pointed to “increasingly important risk” to the world economy if debt and deficit levels weren’t brought down.

Separately, IMF boss Kristalina Georgieva said economic shocks had been “pushing debt levels up like a staircase not to heaven”.

She added that governments had taken “no action to contain that service cost”.

Treasury minister Emma Reynolds said: “Despite unprecedented pressures and conflict in both the Middle East and in Europe, the UK economy is showing strong resilience.”



Shadow Chancellor Andrew Griffith said: “The OECD have downgraded the UK’s growth for 2027 to just a third of the average growth rate of the G20.

“We can and should aspire to do much better.”

News.title: Fears of Brexit betrayal after Sir Tony Blair demands Burnham plots a return to EU within a decade
News.content:
Next

SIR Tony Blair has demanded Andy Burnham plots a return to the EU within a decade – declaring “everything” should be on the table.

The intervention has sparked fears of a Brexit betrayal as it comes days after Mr Burnham did not rule out pledging to rejoin the bloc in a future manifesto.



Sir Tony called for a pledge to rejoin a reformed Europe to be put at the heart of the Government’s ten-year plan.

The former PM claimed Brits would vote differently if the 2016 Brexit referendum was held again today and that the promised benefits of leaving the EU had “not materialised”.



The comments are contained in the foreword to a major new report by the Tony Blair Institute setting out a new blueprint for Britain’s relationship with Brussels.

The TBI argued the Prime Minister should work towards rejoining a “significantly reformed” EU over the next decade and drop Labour’s red lines.

Free movement, payments to Brussels, the Single Market and customs union should all be considered again, it said.

Sir Tony wrote: “Britain should signal an intention if the terms are right to enter into a structured formal relationship with Europe and initiate a process of negotiation where everything is on the table, but nothing agreed until everything is agreed.”

The report said ending free movement “deserves to be examined again” and argued it could help Britain secure much deeper access to the Single Market.

Britain should also be willing to follow common EU rules and make financial contributions where ministers decide the benefits are worth it, the report added..



But Sir Tony made clear his proposed EU comeback is conditional on Brussels changing too.

He said he wanted a Europe on a “credible path to reform” on its economy, defence, immigration and the way it operates.

Sir Tony wrote: “We should be clear that we want back into a formal relationship with the EU. But it must be a Europe on a credible path to reform, a Europe of nation states, a Europe capable of being a genuine global power.”

The Tories last night insisted Labour “should stop trying to turn back the clock and instead focus on setting out serious proposals for the future”.

Shadow Cabinet Office Minister Mike Wood blasted: “Andy Burnham has left the door open to rejoining the EU and now Tony Blair is piling the pressure on him to drag us back into the bloc.”



A Reform UK spokesman also said: “Tony Blair needs to accept he lost this battle long ago. And he should know better than anyone that Brussels has never reformed and never will.

“Britain voted to leave the European Union, and we should get on with making Brexit work rather than endlessly discussing how to reverse it.”

News.title: Blood tests find high level of cancer-causing forever chemical in residents near factory
News.content:
Blood tests have found "really high levels" of a cancer-causing forever chemical in dozens of people living near a major chemical factory in the UK.

The residents, from Thornton-Cleveleys, Lancashire, have been told they could be at elevated risk of serious health conditions from the substance, known as PFOA.

The village has been under investigation for years by the Environment Agency over contamination of soils and locally grown food from the substance, which is a type of forever chemical - so-called because they do not easily break down.

That investigation said high levels likely came from the nearby AGC Chemicals factory, which used it to manufacture coating for frying pans until 2012.

Sam and her husband, both from the village, have been told they were at increased risk of health impacts from PFOA. However, she told the BBC was more shocked by her son's result.

"When we opened the results...it was like, my God, that is ridiculously off the scale.

"I feel guilty because I've introduced [my children] to that way of life. I know it isn't my fault, but the guilt is horrific. Knowing that I've offloaded what levels I probably had over the years into those children when I breastfed them - that's heartbreaking," she said.

News.title: Watch: Trump greets China's Xi beside plane in rare presidential welcome for foreign leader
News.content:
Donald Trump has welcomed Xi Jinping at the Joint Base Andrews with a red carpet and military flyover to kick off a historic three-day US visit.

During the welcome, which included a red carpet, two B-1 bombers flew overhead to celebrate Xi's arrival.

The supersonic aircraft are a key part of the US's combat arsenal, and produce a notoriously loud roar when they pass by.

The BBC's Bernd Debusmann was at Joint Base Andrews and unpacks the pomp and pageantry behind Xi's welcome to America.

News.title: Teenagers to be offered new vocational GCSE subjects in school
News.content:
New vocational GCSEs will be introduced from 2029 for 14-year-olds alongside existing core academic subjects in England.

The new subjects could include building and construction, business management and finance, and child development.

A new national target for employers to help create 200,000 work experience opportunities for under 16s is also being set by Prime Minister Andy Burnham, as part of reforms to shake-up the education system to better prepare young people for the world of work.

Education unions said the ideas were welcome but a clear strategy was needed to make them happen. The Conservatives said the plans risked "throwing away" progress made in recent years.

Standards for the new qualifications will be set nationally by the regulator Ofqual to ensure grades are in line with other GCSEs, and will gradually replace other qualifications at this level such as BTec tech awards.

The vocational GCSEs will be designed to allow teenagers to progress at 16 to studying similar courses at college, including the new V-levels, which colleges are teaching from autumn 2027, and T-levels.

The idea is to create a clear pathway for teenagers into different types of work through a ladder of qualifications.

News.title: Judge temporarily overturns Trump's White House media ban
News.content:
A judge has ordered the Trump administration to immediately reinstate access to the White House for three news organisations barred from the building last week by the president.

A District of Columbia court issued a temporary restraining order against the ban, meaning CNN, MS NOW and Politico must have their access restored for 14 days, after ruling the move "likely violated their constitutional due process rights".

The three outlets launched a legal challenge after their reporters had their passes for the White House confiscated and were denied access.

The Trump administration defended the move in court, accusing the outlets of publishing false information and threatening national security - an argument the court rejected.

The White House is yet to comment on the ruling, and lawyers acting for the president may take further legal action.

Judge Timothy Kelly ruled, external CNN, Politico and MS NOW were "likely to succeed" in showing the White House had not exercised "adequate due process" in implementing the ban.

He also cast doubt on the Trump administration's arguments that the bans were motivated by national security concerns, pointing out the president made no mention of that in his initial announcement.

The ruling continued: "The record lacks factual support for Defendants' contention that the revocation of Plaintiffs' hard passes will in fact protect national security or that national security will be endangered if the Court orders their passes reinstated while this litigation proceeds."

In its defence of the ban, the Trump administration cited a number of articles published by the outlets, including some about construction at the White House, including work on a new ballroom.

The judge said that "in most cases" the stories the White House took issue with were written by journalists who "did not even hold card passes" - and in the remaining cases, the Trump administration did not demonstrate "reason to believe that the reporter's possession of the hard pass was integral to the stories identified".

In its original filing, the Trump administration cited declarations from defence department officials supporting the ban - but the judge said they had "no direct knowledge of how reporters operate in the White House, or about any of the facts at issue here".

Ted Boutrous, the lawyer representing the news outlets, told CNN, external: "This is a strong ruling vindicating freedom of the press, due process and the rule of law."

On Monday, major US TV networks pulled out of White House pool duties in protest at the ban. The arrangement sees media organisations share material with each other to save on costs and space when broadcasting presidential events to the American public.

Forty-nine media organisations - including CBS News, The New York Times and Fox News - also filed a legal brief in support of CNN, MS NOW and Politico's lawsuit.

Trump frequently criticises news organisations, and his administration has launched legal action against a series of outlets, including the New York Times, the Wall Street Journal and the BBC.

Some of the lawsuits have resulted in media organisations agreeing to pay multi-million-dollar settlements. Trump's lawsuit against the BBC is ongoing.

News.title: What we know after video shows moment of RAF training jet crash
News.content:
A video of the crash shared on social media appears to show the two pilots ejecting from the aircraft before it nosedives, crashes and bursts into flames.

The footage shows a plume of smoke and fire erupting as the aircraft hits the ground, appearing to narrowly miss residential properties.

Kay - who hosts the BBC's Security Brief - described footage of the pilots ejecting being caught on camera as "quite remarkable" and said the pilots' ejection seat was "one of the big lifesavers in this whole story".

He said there are two options for ejection that can be taken in a T2 jet - which usually involves an experienced pilot trainer and a student.

One option involves both pilots ejecting individually by pulling a black and yellow ring placed between their legs on the jet, the second option is called "command ejection" where one pilot ejects both seats, with whoever sitting at the back going first.

According to Kay, once the pilot decides to eject the seats, it sets off a miniature detonation cord (MDC), a thin explosive line that is used to shatter the canopy of a jet in the event of an emergency.

"The aircraft seat is designed for the pilot to be able to eject at zero speed and zero height, and that will allow enough time for the parachute to inflate, and then the pilots hit the ground," he added.

"As far as I'm aware this is the first known case of this variant, the T2, ejecting pilots out of it," he said, adding that the safety record for these jets is "obviously very good".

News.title: Mother of teen who died ‘deeply hurt’ that NHS staff may have accessed son’s records inappropriately
News.content:
The mother of a teenage boy who died in hospital has said she is "deeply concerned and hurt" after learning his medical records may have been accessed inappropriately for years after his death.

Paula McGowan, whose 18-year-old autistic son Oliver died in 2016, was told that at least five members of staff at Bristol Foundation NHS Trust may have accessed his records without permission as recently as this year.

Three nursing staff are under formal investigation, while a doctor who no longer works for the trust has self-referred to the General Medical Council. Another member of staff is having their case reviewed separately.

The trust said it was "deeply sorry" for any stress and anxiety caused.

It said it had voluntarily referred itself to the Information Commissioner's Office.

It is the latest case involving concerns that NHS staff may have accessed patient records without a legitimate professional reason. In July the head of NHS England, Sir Jim Mackey, issued a "stark warning" that staff could face the sack or even prison for doing so.

Recent high-profile examples include the victims of the Nottingham and Southport attacks and a child who was injured in a crocodile enclosure in Cambridgeshire.

This month an investigation for the Health Services Journal found that at least 214 NHS staff have lost their jobs and around 2,000 been sanctioned for snooping on sensitive patient data over the past five years.

Oliver, who had a mild learning disability and epilepsy, died in 2016 at Southmead Hospital in Bristol after being given anti-psychotic medication that his family had repeatedly warned he should not receive.

After requesting information about his medical records, his mother was told that 38 people had accessed the data since his death, with 637 items viewed and 67 printed off.

News.title: Prison staff told not to use inadequate cells as overcrowding worsens
News.content:
Prison governors in England and Wales have been warned against using unsafe cells to cope with overcrowding, according to documents leaked to the BBC.

The six-page letter from the Prison Governors' Association (PGA) has been sent to members urging them to abide by the law when using cells, ensuring they meet health and safety requirements and are suitable for the number of inmates they are holding.

Prison staff told the BBC they were increasingly having to put two inmates in single occupancy cells, as overcrowding across the adult male estate worsens.

"Keeping two prisoners in cells built for one isn't ideal, but the pressure is on to maintain operational capacity.

"We don't have the space. Some cells have problems with heating or plumbing and they [prisoners] shouldn't really be in there to be honest," one governor said.

"The infrastructure is failing, especially in the older establishments, and cramming people into cells isn't going to help - especially when the toilet or sink isn't working."

A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said: "Cells are only doubled up where it is safe to do so."

News.title: Burnham describes ban on alcohol in football stands as 'discrimination'
News.content:
Andy Burnham has branded a ban on fans being allowed to drink alcohol in the stands during men's football matches as "discrimination".

The prime minister told reporters that "I don't think it's fair for football fans to be singled out", as he suggested a change could be trialled.

Laws are in place which prevent drinking in view of the pitch at stadiums for clubs in the top five tiers of men's football in England. Other sports do not face such a restriction.

The Football Supporters' Association (FSA) said the "outdated" legislation should be reviewed, but police chiefs have warned against relaxing the law and would like to meet the PM to "explain the challenges".

The legislation was introduced in 1985 by Margaret Thatcher's government for English and Welsh football grounds. At the time, then-Home Secretary Leon Brittan said that alcohol was a "major contributory factor in violent and disorderly behaviour" in football grounds.

Burnham is a keen football fan and a season-ticket holder at Premier League team Everton.

Shortly before he became prime minister, he criticised the restriction on football fans as he attended a rugby league game at Everton's Hill Dickinson Stadium where it was possible for supporters to have a drink in the stands.

Speaking to reporters on his trip to the United Nations in New York, Burnham was asked if it was still his view now he is in Downing Street.

Burnham replied: "I think that legislation dates to an era where football was very different.

"And I do believe there is a case to remove that discrimination. There are different ways it could be done. It could happen on a trial basis.

"But I'm not going to back away from what's been a long held view of mine. I don't see how it can be fair that some supporters of one sport can be treated differently."

Government sources have stressed that Burnham was restating an opinion that he has long held, rather than making any sort of policy announcement.

The prime minister's comments are not being seen inside government as an indication that he is looking to change the law in the area.

A trial or pilot scheme to look at whether a change would be possible is not being ruled out but any wider move would require extensive consultation involving football clubs, fans and the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport - none of which is currently planned.

News.title: Tories would prevent long-term jobless spending benefits on alcohol and cigarettes
News.content:
The Tories estimate the proposed changes would move about 350,000 claimants onto the lower rate of Universal Credit, saving around Â£538m a year.

Under the proposals, anyone fit to work would get six months on full benefits to find a job.

Every two years a claimant has previously worked would buy an extra year on the full rate of Universal Credit - but those who have not contributed enough would drop to a new "Subsistence Allowance", worth 70% of the full rate.

The party said this would protect "those with a strong employment record".

For example, a 58-year-old who has worked since leaving school but has been made redundant would keep the full allowance up to state pension age.

Claimants who are sick, disabled or already in work would also be exempt, with only those judged capable of work affected.

The Tories said loading the "Subsistence Allowance" onto a pre-paid card, with restrictions on what the money can be spent on, would ensure taxpayers' money supports claimants with essentials like food.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the current system "where someone who can work chooses not to, and earns more benefits than someone in a job" was "unfair".

"The best welfare is a well-paid job. So, we will be tough on those who exploit the system because the current system is unfair to workers, taxpayers and those who truly need support," she said.

"Welfare must be a safety net for those who genuinely need it, not a lifestyle choice for those who can't be bothered."

However, Helen Barnard, director of policy and research at the anti-poverty charity Trussell, said the proposals were "deeply misguided".

"Universal Credit already falls well short of what people need to afford the essentials like food and heating, forcing people across the UK to the doors of food banks," she said.

"We see people's health being damaged and their ability to find and maintain work undermined by the severe hardship so many are facing."

Reform UK's economy spokesman, Robert Jenrick, said the Tories had left record numbers on long-term benefits and the proposals "won't even put a dent" in the welfare bill.

The Conservatives have already pledged to scrap Personal Independence Payment, the main disability benefit in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, for "low-level" mental health conditions to help cut the welfare bill.

The party also wants to make it harder to claim sickness benefits, which it said would mean more people are required to look for work.

Spending on benefits has ballooned in recent years and is forecast to rise to Â£408.6bn in 2030/31, according to figures from the Department for Work and Pensions.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has insisted he will get the welfare bill down, for example by tackling but number of young people not in education, employment or training, but not through "crude cuts".

News.title: Harry Potter play producer says cost of living made two-part show 'impossible'
News.content:
A Harry Potter And The Cursed Child producer has said the rising cost of living made it "literally impossible" to retain the play's original format in two parts.

The production has been cut down to a single three-hour show and is set to re-open in the West End next month.

"The cost of living has gone up 30-40% since the pandemic, including running shows," producer Sonia Friedman said in comments reported by media at a launch event. "The only way we could continue to run it as a two-parter would be by charging an amount for the tickets that would be unaffordable and inaccessible."

The two-part play, a sequel to JK Rowling's books, premiered in the West End in 2016 and closed on 20 September.

The changes to the West End production follow the 2021 relaunch of the play as a single show on Broadway in New York City.

"The pandemic, the cost of living and the wars going on around the world accelerated that decision in New York, and that's where we are now with London," Friedman said.

"Of course we'll miss it but it was absolutely the right call and we've got a beautiful alternate version that we're very proud of."

Director John Tiffany said at the launch event that he and writer Jack Thorne - who also wrote acclaimed Netflix series Adolescence - had to be "dragged, kicking and screaming to make the one-parter" due to the success of their original script, the Times reported.

However, Tiffany said the new version meant "more people are going to get to see this show and not have to pay a fortune for it", according to The Stage.

The play takes place 19 years after the final book and follows Harry's son Albus Severus as he arrives at Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry.

The production has been seen by more than 14 million people around the world, including over 2.5 million in London.

The reimagined one-part production will retain some of its original cast, including David Ricardo-Pearce as Harry Potter, Thomas Aldridge as Ron Weasley and Naana Agyei Ampadu as Hermione Granger.

New actors have been cast in the roles of Albus Potter, Ginny Potter, Rose Granger-Weasley, Draco Malfoy and Scorpius Malfoy.

News.title: Corrie Mckeague's mum: 'We did all we could to find him'
News.content:
"We definitely did all we could and I can honestly sleep at night knowing there was nothing I physically could have done any different."

It is 10 years since Nicola Urquhart's son, Corrie Mckeague, disappeared on 24 September 2016 after a night out in Bury St Edmunds, Suffolk. For the months and years that followed, she embodied a mother's love and determination to find the truth: to never give up.

The RAF gunner's body has never been found but he was officially declared dead in 2022, when an inquest ruled he had died after climbing into a commercial waste bin before it was tipped into a waste lorry.

Nicola is composed and reflective as she recalls when her son went missing. He had just turned 23 and within months would become a dad.

She says her son would be forever in her thoughts, but adds: "I've given myself closure; my son is dead."

She spoke to the BBC after what would have been Corrie's 33rd birthday and ahead of the 10th anniversary of his disappearance.

She says she last saw her son when she went for a birthday meal with him at Cheers in Bury St Edmunds, adding he was a "social hand grenade" who "really did live every moment at a hundred miles an hour".

A decade on, she says there is "never an end" to losing somebody but it is about "managing each day".

News.title: UK military jamming other nations' satellites to defend itself, BBC told
News.content:
The British military has been jamming or blocking satellites from other countries in order to defend itself from hostile threats, the BBC has been told.

The RAF has been using a ground-based system for the past year, which a defence source said had already been used "to deter our adversaries".

It is understood the system could be used to prevent a hostile nation's satellites from tracking the movement of the UK's nuclear armed submarines or other sensitive military operations, such as those involving special forces.

It comes as the head of the RAF said the UK faced "unprecedented threats" from adversaries in space, coinciding with the creation of a new RAF unit set up to defend Britain's satellites.

The Ministry of Defence (MoD) said the new Space Effects Squadron will be focused on "disrupting, degrading and denying hostile threats in space".

The squadron will protect British satellites used to warn of incoming missile attacks, provide communications and help guide ships, the MoD said.

In a speech on Wednesday, Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said daily lives depend on satellites that power everyday technologies like mobile phones and banking apps, adding the loss of GPS would cost the UK economy Â£1.4bn a day.

"Our dependency on space is precisely why it is increasingly under threat from our adversaries." he said.

"We depend on them for everything from weather forecasts, energy supplies, and financial transactions to sat-navs, mobile phone connections, and Amazon deliveries," said Streeting, adding that the loss of "everyday conveniences would undermine our daily freedoms, and trust in our institutions."

Speaking at the UK Space Conference, Streeting said the threat from Britain's adversaries was growing in "scale, speed and sophistication", adding that the "challenges in space increasingly mirror the geopolitics on Earth".

A number of nations are believed to have similar ground-based systems against satellites. Last year the then head of the UK's Space Command said Russia was trying to jam UK satellites with ground based systems "every week".

The defence source described the UK's terrestrial electronic warfare capability as "world leading, and more".

Last week US confirmed for the first time that it had also deployed an unspecified "weapon" in space to defend its own satellites.

Both China and Russia condemned the move - warning of an arms race in space.

However, Washington has already accused both Russia and China of developing their own space weapons - ranging from electronic jammers, lasers to blind other satellites and even projectiles that can be fired from satellites in orbit.

News.title: 'I knew something was wrong when my baby's head was too big'
News.content:
Not long after Bethany Hardy's daughter was born, she felt something was wrong with her new baby.

Nancy's head was a strange shape and much larger than her body, and she struggled to lift it.

By the time she was nine months, her parents, from Leeds, were seriously worried about their child.

Nancy was a year old when she was eventually diagnosed with sagittal craniosynostosis, a rare condition where the skull does not grow properly - but the delay meant she had to undergo more invasive surgery.

She had six operations, including blood transfusions and a skin graft, and spent a month in hospital - but Bethany believes if she had been diagnosed sooner, the treatment would have been less traumatic.

Recalling the first few months after Nancy's birth, Bethany says: "She really struggled lifting her head, tummy time, that kind of stuff, because her head was a lot larger than her body.

"By nine months her head was on the 98th percentile but her body was on the 24th, which straight away kind of rings alarm bells because they should all be in line."

Nancy was referred for an X-ray, but her parents instead decided to book a private consultation at Great Ormond Street Hospital in London.

Specialists were able to identify Nancy's condition, which is caused by parts of the skull fusing together before birth, merely by visual observation and she was then offered reconstructive surgery on the NHS.

News.title: Home secretary says undetected migrant landings 'unacceptable'
News.content:
The Home Secretary has said migrant landings on UK beaches are "not acceptable", as she ordered an urgent review after two boats reached Kent without being intercepted.

Shabana Mahmood told Border Security Command to carry out the review after vessels came ashore at Samphire Hoe, between Dover and Folkestone, on Tuesday, and near Folkestone on Monday.

Twenty-one people were detained on Tuesday after the arrival at Samphire Hoe.

Five people were also detained on Monday after the uncontrolled landing near Folkestone, the first undetected landing for a year. The Home Office has not said whether more people are being sought.

News.title: Will.i.am backs campaign for Sir Tom Jones to return to The Voice
News.content:
Will.i.am has endorsed a petition to have Sir Tom Jones reinstated on ITV's The Voice.

Sir Tom told his social media followers earlier this month that the broadcaster had "fired" him as a judge on the show.

The 86-year-old singer from Treforest, Rhondda Cynon Taf, has appeared as an on-off coach on the singing competition since it premiered in 2012.

Superfan Aaron Howlett, 50, from Kingston-upon-Hull, started the petition which has received more than 63,000 signatures from around the world.

ITV thanked Sir Tom for all of his years on The Voice and the "countless incredible and unforgettable moments" he gave the show.

Speaking on BBC Radio Wales Breakfast on Wednesday, Howlett said he had been a fan of Sir Tom for four decades.

"Sir Tom is one of the last living legends," he said. "His voice resonates with so many people, young and old."

News.title: Watch: The arms race in space and how the UK is defending itself
News.content:
The head of Britain's Royal Air Force has warned that we we now face an unprecedented threat in space, which could have a devastating effect on the satellites we rely on for communication, internet, bank transfers and satnav.

A defence source has told BBC defence correspondent Jonathon Beale, that Britain has already used a ground based system to jam or block the satellite communications of a hostile state.

Beale explains there is now a new arms race going on in space.

More on this story.

Anthony Gordon admits he was surprised to come off during England’s World Cup semi-final and says he will never get over the heartbreaking defeat to Argentina.

Gordon put his country on the cusp of a first final since 1966 when he scored in the 55th minute in Atlanta, but his withdrawal 11 minutes later changed the course of the game.

Boss Tuchel replaced him with defender Ezri Konsa and England barely got out of their own half again as Argentina scored two late goals to advance.

“I was (surprised), being totally honest,” he said of his substitution. “Only because I’d just scored, so I’m the type of player that, I’ve said before, I’m really good when I play off adrenaline.

“When I score, I normally don’t have many bad games because I get into an untouchable mode of confidence.

“It makes me feel on top of the world. Especially in that moment, on that stage, I felt really good.”

Asked whether he will ever get over the disappointment of losing, he said: “No, I don’t think so.

“Being totally honest, I think any time you lose anything of value in life – whether it be a person or something like a match or anything you really want to have or win or anything of large value – you’ll never be the same person. It leaves a scar, but that scar doesn’t always have to be a negative one.

“You can be a better person for it. You can learn different things about the world, about yourself.”

Much of the post-mortem of the defeat was around England’s inability to keep the ball, with Tuchel suggesting it was not in the country’s “DNA”.

Gordon, who has made a flying start to life at Barcelona, also believes players in this country cannot keep the ball in a way that world champions Spain, who visit Wembley on Saturday for the Nations League opener, can.

“I think culturally, it’s not just that tournament or that game where we couldn’t control a game,” he said. “England as a nation, we don’t have that strength like the Spanish, where we control games like they do. It’s not in us.

open image in gallery ( Getty )

“I’m not sure it’s something that can be taught because now I think playing in Spain, I can speak with an educated view on the way they keep the ball is different.

“It’s very different from what I’ve ever experienced playing in this country.

“It’s not in the English DNA and it’s probably something I’ve only realised to that extent from playing in Spain now.

“Because I think we, as English players, are educated the same way as the Spanish players.

“We know how to keep possession, but it’s the decision-making of certain players in Spain, which it’s just not a natural thing. I even look at some of the decisions they take on the ball sometimes and think, ‘I’m not sure how you’ve seen that’.

“It’s the way they’re built. I don’t know what it is, something that maybe we can’t ever put a name to, but they’re definitely built different.

“So I’m not sure we can ever get that, but we can definitely get better, or maybe go the other way and really play to our strengths, which is to play physical, play direct football, and on the counter-attack.”

Jobless benefits claimants could be banned from spending their welfare payments on alcohol, cigarettes and gambling under a Conservative plan to slash the UK’s welfare bill.

An estimated 350,000 benefits claimants would face receiving their payments on a pre-loaded card, which it would be impossible to use for cash withdrawals, betting, or buying cigarettes or alcohol.

Under the Tory scheme, anyone who claims Universal credit (UC) when they are looking for work would get six months of full benefits – but after that, anyone who has not consistently contributed to the welfare system over years would have their payments slashed.

The full rate would be available only to people who have contributed to the welfare system through their taxes for a sustained period.

Under the plans, every two years a UC claimant has worked would buy them an extra year on the full rate of the benefit.

But jobseekers who do not have a record of working and contributing would have their UC standard rate cut by a third to a new “subsistence allowance”.

And that payment would be loaded onto a “back-to-work” pre-payment card that came with the restrictions on spending.

The card could be used for food and other everyday essentials, and to pay for bills.

People who are off sick or disabled, or who are claiming UC while in work, would be exempt.

The Conservatives estimate the shake-up could save taxpayers £538m a year.

Party leader Kemi Badenoch claimed the current system was unfair to workers.

“Some will say this is unfair on people claiming benefits. What is unfair is a system where someone who can work chooses not to and earns more from benefits than someone in a job,” she said.

“Helping people into work is not punishment. The best welfare is a well-paid job. So we will be tough on those who exploit the system because the current system is unfair to workers, taxpayers and those who truly need support.”

open image in gallery Long-term jobless people face curbs under the Tory plans ( PA Wire )

She said the UK should not “be borrowing from our children and grandchildren to support people who simply refuse to work”.

Helen Whately, the shadow work and pensions secretary, said: “We cannot go on like this – with millions of people living on benefits instead of in work. Britain can’t afford it.”

Further plans for welfare reform are likely to be revealed at the Conservative conference this month.

Prime minister Andy Burnham has indicated that reforms to the benefits system will be revisited under his government.

A Labour Party spokesperson said: “The Conservatives had 14 years to fix our welfare system but they completely failed to make meaningful reforms.

“Now they are proposing an unworkable new card scheme, which does nothing to tackle the numbers of people their system left signed off and written off.

“While the bill for the taxpayer rose by £33 billion in their last year in government, this Labour government is introducing effective and sustainable welfare reform alongside a £3.5 billion employment support package to help people stay in or return to work, and the national rollout of the jobs guarantee for young people who have been on Universal Credit.”

Organisations representing the hospitality and betting industries and human rights in the UK declined to comment.

Anthony Albanese has revealed that an autonomous artificial intelligence agent developed by OpenAI hacked a government website containing health data of Australians, in what could be the ​first known breach of its kind.

Speaking to reporters in New York on Wednesday, the Australian prime minister said the AI agent was carrying out a research task on health and medical statistics when it accessed both public and non-public data on the Medicare portal run by Services Australia in June.

Australia's deputy prime minister, Richard Marles, told ABC radio that the agent had approached three other Australian websites in the course of its research and interacted with them "in a way that a member of the public might", acting in an authorised way.

But he said that when it sought information from the Medicare portal and was refused, "it effectively hacked into that medical portal and got that information anyway".

"It's that unauthorised access which we are very concerned about," Mr Marles said. "The impact is relatively minor, but the incident is very serious."

Mr Albanese said OpenAI did not alert the Australian government to the breach until months later on 10 September, when it sent an email to a generic public mailbox.

"Today I spoke with the CEO of OpenAI, Sam Altman, to express Australia's extreme concern about this incident," Mr Albanese said, adding that he had also told Mr Altman he was disappointed it had taken the company "way too long" to inform the government of what had happened.

OpenAI said it was still investigating the incident but had found no evidence that patient records had been accessed.

The company said its review had identified activity involving several Australian government websites and services as its "models attempted to look up answers".

open image in gallery Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese at a press conference during the United Nations General Assembly, revealing that an AI agent developed by OpenAI infiltrated an Australian government website in June, in New York ( Reuters )

Mr Albanese said there was no evidence of a wider compromise of the government's services network and that no personal information was believed to have been accessed, though investigations were continuing.

The disclosure came less than a day after Mr Albanese co-signed a joint statement with 21 other countries, including Canada, Spain and Germany, calling for "urgent global guardrails" on frontier AI models, on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York.

At a UN Security Council meeting on Wednesday, tech leaders warned of the dangers of unregulated AI development. Yoshua Bengio, a Canadian researcher dubbed one of the "godfathers of AI" and co-chair of the Independent International Scientific Panel on AI, spoke of an "unprecedented threat" and dangers he described as "real and imminent".

China's UN ambassador, Fu Cong, told the meeting that Beijing believed continuous improvement of regulatory frameworks, emergency response and cross-border cooperation on AI was needed, while prime minister Andy Burnham said the UK was ready to lead an international effort to establish AI standards.

"We've all heard the warnings which we must heed… so we have to rise to this moment," Mr Burnham said.

open image in gallery OpenAI CEO Sam Altman listens to a speaker at the United Nations Security Council during a session on Artificial Intelligence during the 81st United Nations General Assembly, at UN Headquarters in New York City ( Reuters )

French president Emmanuel Macron warned against allowing the US and China to dominate global decision-making on AI in his address to the assembly.

US president Donald Trump struck a different tone, telling the UN General Assembly on Tuesday that he opposed new regulation of AI and that US law enforcement would step in if needed.

"We're going to watch it closely through the Department of Justice," Mr Trump said.

He has dismissed recent warnings about AI's dangers as a "hoax", saying: "I'm not going to stifle growth of something that will be bigger than the Industrial Revolution.”

He also said US government documents would use the term "super intelligence" instead of artificial intelligence going forward.

The White House's science and technology adviser, Michael Kratsios, echoed the US president in his remarks to the Security Council.

"You cannot govern technology you do not understand. This body and others like it should focus on sharing best practices to build domestic capacity, not establishing a global regulatory scheme."

When Dolly Parton died, it was her nephew Bryan Seaver who broke the news to the world.

The Queen of Country had long trusted Seaver, the son of her sister Cassie Parton, as her head of security and handpicked him to make the announcement in a widely-shared video.

However, in the weeks since her August 25 death, a series of troubling allegations have led to Seaver being fired from his security role by Parton’s estate.

Danny Nozell, Parton’s longtime manager, filed a restraining order Tuesday against Seaver in a Tennessee court on behalf of She's Alive LLC, the company that now manages Parton’s business empire. The filing claimed that Seaver’s “terrorizing conduct made their continued retention untenable.”

As Variety reported, the filing went on to allege that Seaver threatened Nozell and various other employees in an attempt to extort money, calling himself a “killer” and “literally an international arms dealer and mercenary.” He allegedly added: “All I do is warfare.”

open image in gallery Dolly Parton's nephew Bryan Seaver has reportedly been fired as head of security ( Getty Images/Dolly Parton )

In a statement to TMZ, Seaver denied the allegation that he was attempting to extort money from the estate, but maintained other claims were simply taken out of context.

“I am a career soldier and military contractor and do conduct arms deals for foreign governments,” Seaver told the publication. “I am a security professional and I am a killer.”

He continued: “However, nothing in this lawsuit were threats and most of the comments I stand by. I was talking frankly in a private way with Danny who I thought was my friend and he fancies himself a gangster. A lot of these messages are two guys having rage talk and crying on the phone together while we were grieving.”

Seaver spent more than two decades as Parton’s head of security, succeeding his father Larry Seaver in the role. He runs Squadron Augmented Protection Services (SAPS), LLC, which describes itself as “the premier provider of critical security services in Nashville.”

As a child, Seaver often found himself on tour with Parton. Her 1993 song “Romeo” was reportedly written as a warning to the then-16-year-old Seaver about the dangers of getting his heart broken.

In Nozell’s legal filing, it is alleged that Seaver began a campaign of intimidation in the weeks leading up to Parton’s death in an attempt to obtain significant sums of money.

open image in gallery Dolly Parton died with a net worth of over $450 million, according to estimates ( Alamy/PA )

The documents contain reproductions of text messages allegedly sent by Seaver to Nozell, including one that threatens: “I’m going to destroy the entire brand if you don’t get these [Dollywood business partners] out of our bit. . . . I’m going to go to Billboard Magazine with my s***. Just like you. I’m going to ratf*** every [Dollywood business partner] entity I can possibly conjure.”

Another allegedly stated: “I’m not an entertainment person. I’m a killer. I sold 27 million $ worth of ammunition and arms to the Haitian Police on day Dolly died. Entertainment is not my game. I have spent my career breaking things and spying on African and Arab leaders. And protecting Dolly.”

A third was claimed to say: “I’m going to set up a podcast dedicated to ruining Dolly’s brand partnerships and telling the violations these people have done on us. It’s going to be great. Or f***ing pay me.”

Another reportedly claimed: “I am vengeance for my people for the next 50 years. I have no debt. I only own swords and guns. My children have 3 houses to live in forever. My wife owns everything. All I have is animosity and memory. But I’m going to spend the next times I have on earth ratf***ing anyone that has ever betrayed my family.”

In a separate statement to ABC News, Seaver described the restraining order against him as “spurious and simply a publicity stunt.”

He again suggested his words had been misconstrued, saying: “Dolly called me her killer. It was a joke we used around her camp. I was her ‘baby boy ninja’ and Danny Nozell took that text out of context to somehow imagine that I was threatening him. He’s always called me The Killer. I’ve never threatened anyone ... They are my friends and my brothers and colleagues.”

Seaver added: “I was fired. After the estate negotiated with me and my company for services in perpetuity and agreed to that service provision from my company. A week later they fired me for these contrived ‘threats.’”

SAPS had been responsible for security at various Parton properties, but footage from last week obtained by TMZ showed replacement guards taking over posts at Parton’s home in Nashville, as well as her museum and warehouse.

Parton died with a net worth of over $450 million, according to estimates.

Housebuilder Vistry has warned over more job cuts as it looks to save another £50 million after slumping to a half-year loss of over £660 million and warning over full-year profits.

The group’s new boss Adam Daniels announced sweeping changes to turn around the troubled builder’s fortunes, including cutting its regional operations from 25 to 12 and leaving the private home sales market in the South East.

The overhaul will lead to further job losses among its workforce of around 4,150 as well as site closures, but the firm is not revealing how many will be affected.

open image in gallery Vistry said it will become much smaller but more focused, slashing its new homes target to around 12,000 completions a year (PA) ( PA Archive )

Around 350 workers have already left the group since the summer including some departures under a recent voluntary redundancy programme, which delivered savings of £25 million earlier this year.

The latest cost-cutting efforts come as Vistry reported pre-tax losses of £661.3 million for the six months to June 30, against profits of £40.9 million a year earlier after taking a £475 million write-down and another £73.2 million provision for building safety on high rise properties in the wake of the Grenfell Tower tragedy.

On an underlying basis, it reported pre-tax losses of £83.3 million against profits of £80.6 million a year earlier.

Vistry gave an alert over its full-year outlook, cutting its guidance to around £165 million from a previous forecast of £200 million, but this is excluding a £40 million hit from delayed deals and some £470 million in write-downs expected at the full-year stage.

The group looked to reassure that it did not expect to need to launch an investor cash-call and has the support of lenders, who have waived certain banking covenants due to the swingeing overhaul announced.

Mr Daniels said the actions will see the business become much smaller but more focused, slashing its new homes target to around 12,000 completions a year.

A hospital has launched a probe into NHS staff after it emerged that the medical records of an 18-year-old were accessed years after his death.

Oliver McGowan, who was autistic and had epilepsy, died in November 2016 after doctors at Southmead hospital, Bristol, gave him an antipsychotic medication, despite medical records showing he had an intolerance to antipsychotic drugs.

Shortly after, he had a rare reaction, developed severe brain swelling and died weeks later. An inquest into his death found the medication was appropriately prescribed but a 2020 independent review commissioned by the NHS found his death was “potentially avoidable”.

After years of campaigning by Oliver’s parents, Paula and Tom, new legislation was introduced in November 2022 to ensure all NHS staff have mandatory training for caring for patients with autism and learning disabilities in hospital.

Now, a decade after his death, his parents have revealed that Oliver’s medical records have been accessed hundreds of times by staff and, on at least one occasion, inappropriately by a doctor earlier this year.

open image in gallery Oliver McGowan, who was autistic and had epilepsy, died in November 2016

More than a dozen NHS workers are now being investigated by Bristol NHS Foundation Trust, which runs the hospital, including 16 who are not employed by the trust and four who are, according to emails seen by The Independent.

One doctor, who is no longer an employee of the trust, accessed his records in March 2026 without a legitimate reason and referred themselves to the General Medical Council.

Speaking to The Independent, Ms McGowan described the revelations as a “violation”.

“Oliver was failed horrifically. The treatment he received led to his death,” she said.

“I think people have forgotten that he's a person. He was a young teenager, and he was treated like dirt, as if he's a commodity, as if people have the right to just access and delve and nose.

“It calls into question how these people value Oliver as a person, his privacy. Does Oliver not matter? Do they not care? It's a violation of his privacy.”

The NHS has been at the centre of several recent incidents where staff have been found to have snooped on patients’ records inappropriately, most recently in the cases of the victims of the Southport and Nottingham Killings and the three-year-old from Cambridge who fell into the crocodile pit.

A former healthcare worker also received a caution from the Information Commissioner’s Office for attempting to obtain and sell the medical records belonging to the Princess of Wales.

open image in gallery Oliver McGowan’s death in 2016 was ‘potentially avoidable’, a review found ( PA Media )

In July, NHS England chief executive Sir Jim Mackey said any unauthorised staff member who views patient medical records would face dismissal after he described the action as a "disgraceful breach of patient trust and against the law".

Bristol NHS Foundation Trust launched a probe after a subject access request from Mr and Mrs McGowan revealed 38 staff and former staff had accessed Oliver’s records over the past decade.

So far, the trust’s probe has found that a doctor who does not work at the trust had accessed Oliver’s records without a legitimate reason as recently as March this year. Four staff members still working at the trust remain under investigation.

Of 22 staff members still working at the trust, 15 have been found to have had legitimate reasons for accessing his records, for example, as they cared for him or were involved in subsequent investigations.

In an email from Professor Steven Hams, the trust’s chief nursing and improvement officer, to the McGowans this week, seen by The Independent, it said: “At present, three current employees remain under formal investigation because the Trust has not yet established a legitimate clinical or operational reason for their access to Oliver’s records. These investigations have not concluded, and no final determination has been made...

“Of these three individuals, two are registered with the Nursing and Midwifery Council, and one is a student undertaking nurse training.

“A fourth individual remains under separate review with the Chief Medical Officer. No determination has yet been made in relation to that access.

“In relation to former employees, I have written to those for whom contact details are available and requested responses by 2 October 2026. Those enquiries remain ongoing.

“As previously advised, one former employee has already been identified as having accessed Oliver’s records without an established legitimate reason and has self-referred to the General Medical Council. The final number of inappropriate accesses, and the total number involving professionally registered individuals, cannot therefore be confirmed until the outstanding investigations and enquiries have concluded.”

Another email from Professor Hams to the McGowans in August, seen by The Independent, confirmed an audit showed 653 instances of Oliver’s records being viewed or printed.

Mr McGowan told The Independent: “The investigation is still ongoing, but we do know there was no appropriate reason to go in and access the information. Whether there's malice involved, I don't know. But what we do know is that Jim Mackey has said that this won't be tolerated. What we call out for is for him to actually take action. We know this isn't isolated to Oliver's case.”

The trust has made a precautionary notification to the Information Commissioner’s Office over the potential breaches.

open image in gallery One NHS doctor has been found to have accessed Oliver’s records inappropriately ( PA Archive )

Professor Hams said in a statement to The Independent: "We are deeply sorry for the additional distress and anxiety that this situation may have caused Oliver’s parents at what has already been an incredibly difficult time for their family.

“Every patient and family has the right to expect that their personal information will be treated with care, respect and confidentiality. Any concern that records may have been accessed without a legitimate reason is something we take extremely seriously.

“As soon as these potential issues were identified, we took immediate action, including self-referring the matter to the Information Commissioner's Office and undertaking a thorough investigation.

“Most of the accesses reviewed have been linked to legitimate clinical or operational activity. A very small number of instances remain under investigation, and it would be inappropriate to reach conclusions before those enquiries are complete.

“We remain committed to being open and transparent about our findings. Should any inappropriate access or misconduct be identified, appropriate action will be taken through the relevant processes.

“We have remained in close contact with Oliver’s parents throughout this investigation and will continue to keep them informed as our enquiries progress."
