Sports.title: Antonelli has “perfect driving style” for 2026 cars – Russell | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Andrea Kimi Antonelli is enjoying an extraordinarily successful second season in Formula 1 because his driving style works perfectly with the current generation of cars, says his team mate.

George Russell is Antonelli’s closest rival at the top of the championship standings, but the second-year driver is 81 points ahead. This is a sharp contrast to last year, when Russell out-scored Antonelli by 319 points to 150.

While Russell said Antonelli’s ability was clear before this season, he believes the reduction in aerodynamic downforce and grip this year has played to his team mate’s strengths.

“Of course Kimi is extremely talented,” said Russell. “He’s an incredible driver and has been fast in his whole career.

“I think his driving style is very similar to what he had last year and I think with just how things have fallen this year, it’s kind of the perfect driving style for these cars.”

Russell believes the same is true of other drivers, including Lando Norris, who is the only driver to have won more than one round this season.

“If you look last year, there are definitely trends,” said Russell. “If you look at Brazil last year, Kimi had a really strong race and Lando won in Brazil, and they’re two drivers who are always very strong on the low grip tracks and they’re two drivers who are arguably the best-performing drivers of this season.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

“He’s an amazing driver and he was of course doing extremely well last year as well. Let’s see next year if it changes or not, but certainly his natural driving style suits very well for this regulation.”

Charles Leclerc echoed Russell’s view that Antonelli’s potential was clear despite his patchy rookie campaign last year.

“I wish I knew, but clearly he’s doing something that works very well,” said Leclerc. “But to be honest, it’s not that it comes as a complete surprise.

“If I look at Kimi going through the junior ranks, I think it was quite clear for everybody that he had something very special. If you look obviously at his first year in Formula 1, I think he probably faced challenges – it is not up to me to go into detail, I don’t know, but surely he had some struggles in the first year – but this year has been extremely impressive. I mean, from the first race to now, he’s been perfect and driving at a very high level against a driver that I rate extremely high as well, which is George. So he’s doing an incredible job.”

However Leclerc said there is only so much he can tell about Antonelli’s qualities from outside the Mercedes team.

“To [tell] you exactly why he’s so fast, and why he is outstandingly fast this year compared to last year, is very difficult for me. We are all here analysing the data of everybody but we can only go up to a certain amount of detail, then you really need the data of the actual car to dig into more detail.

“So it’s difficult. But his laps look a lot on the limit but somehow he manages to do the lap when it counts and that’s been very impressive to watch.”

Sports.title: Hadjar says injured wrist is “still going to be painful for a while” after comeback | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Isack Hadjar says he is still in pain from his injured wrist as he returns to racing this weekend.

The Red Bull driver, who has missed the last three rounds, said his wrist is “good enough to drive, so that’s all I need.”

He said no surgery was required on the injury and a pre-event simulator session indicated it is now strong enough for him to be able to drive.

“I have a small fracture on the outside of the wrist and it’s just quite a long process,” said Hadjar. “I didn’t need any surgery so it’s all natural and it takes some time.

“It’s still going to be painful for a while. It’s going to be six weeks.

“It says that it’s strong enough at the moment to resist the tensions. I had a test on the sim, it went well. I think it’s a similar environment as the cockpit. It’s actually, if anything, nearly identical. So if it’s fine on the sim, with the adrenaline on track and everything, I think I should be okay.

“It’s just been the training sessions have not been fun because I’ve been doing basically nothing with the left limb, so it’s been a bit boring.”

Hadjar confirmed he spoke to multiple Moto GP champion Marc Marquez, who has broken many bones during his career, notably in 2020 when he made an early return from one injury only to sustain another. Hadjar said Marquez told him: “Not to race.”

Red Bull confirmed today Hadjar will continue to drive for them next season. Hadjar said the news is “good, it is nice, but it is natural.”

“I’m not here to be hopeful,” he explained. “I’m here to show what I do on track and naturally, the rest comes, so it’s normal in a way.”

Sports.title: Excessive focus on battle between Ferrari drivers is “not fair” – Leclerc | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Charles Leclerc says too much attention has been paid to the on-track battle between him and his team mate, particularly since their clash at Monza.

The Ferrari driver has already admitted he went too far in his first-lap battle with Lewis Hamilton when he forced his team mate wide at turn two.

“Turn two in Monza is something that I’ve said repeatedly is not something that we want to see ever happen again,” said Leclerc. “And that [was] going too far on my side.

“But I’ve been through it already. I think it’s pretty clear that we don’t necessarily have to write [rules of engagement for] those things, I think it’s clear enough.

“But again, I feel like it’s being over-discussed and over-analysed when it’s about the red cars, and that’s not really fair.”

He alluded to incidents between the McLaren and Mercedes drivers during the final laps of the same race. “In Monza, if you look at the four top teams, three of them had fights like this with a car finishing in the grass, and at the end of the day, the only thing we are speaking about still now is the red car, which I don’t think is fair.”

Leclerc said both drivers have exceeded the limits of what is acceptable at times but he is happy with how they race wheel-to-wheel.

Sports.title: “Money fears” delay F1’s decision on whether Middle East races will happen – report | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Formula One Management is delaying its decision over whether to cancel the final two rounds of the season due to concerns over money, according to a report in The Times.

F1 will not receive its huge fees from the Qatar and Abu Dhabi grand prix promoters if it calls off the races. If the promoters make the decision to cancel, they will bear the costs.

But the longer F1 leaves the decision, the harder it may be to organise a replacement for either race. Cancelling a race would reduce the number of points available and could affect the championship situation, potentially even deciding it. Andrea Kimi Antonelli leads the championship by 81 points with 233 available.

Domenicali has indicated F1 has a plan to replace the Abu Dhabi finale if that cannot go ahead. This is believed to be a race at Imola in Italy.

F1 has already cancelled the Bahrain and Saudi Arabian grands prix as a result of the war. A replacement for the former, titled the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, will take place next week at the Sepang International Circuit.

Earlier this month FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem said the governing body will be guided by local promoters on whether the events could go ahead.

“Being from that part of the world, we can’t jump the gun and just say, that’s it, we are cancelling and then cancel,” he said.

“Are we going to allow our people, our staff, the drivers or the teams to go at risk? No, of course not. We will not. But we’ll have to also listen to the governments and to the local promoter there.”

Sports.title: Red Bull confirms Hadjar will remain as Verstappen’s team mate in 2027 | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Red Bull has given a vote of confidence to Isack Hadjar, extending his contract to drive for the team again next year.

Hadjar made his debut in Formula 1 last year with Red Bull’s second team, Racing Bulls, before being promoted to their leading squad this year.

“Since joining us at the start of the year, he has been superb on and off track,” said team principal Laurent Mekies, “especially considering this is only his second Formula 1 season, which made extending his contract an easy decision.”

Although Hadjar did not compete in the last three rounds due to injury, Hadjar made an impressive start to life at Red Bull, taking a podium finish in his sixth appearance in Monaco. Before being forced out due to injury he had scored 71 points to Verstappen’s 109.

Red Bull has struggled to find an effective team mate to pair Verstappen with. The team handed Sergio Perez a two-year contract extension during 2024 but dropped him at the end of the year for Liam Lawson. Perez’s replacement lasted just two rounds at the start of last year before Red Bull dropped him. Yuki Tsunoda, who replaced Lawson, ended the season with the largest points deficit to a team mate ever seen in F1, leading Red Bull to make another change.

Mekies said Hadjar performed well from the outset after moving up to Red Bull. He will race for the team this weekend in Baku for the first time since the Hungarian Grand Prix in July.

“You could see from that first weekend in Melbourne that he handled the step up with remarkable composure and had earned his place in this seat,” said Mekies. “The period since his injury has been a difficult one for Isack, but this extension is a testament to how much we believe in him and we can’t wait to see him back out on track.”

Hadjar said he is “really excited” by his new deal. “From the moment I signed, I set out to dedicate myself to the team, and with the support of Laurent and everyone in Milton Keynes, I’ve been able to justify the faith they’ve had in me,” he said. “I’m constantly looking to listen, learn and push myself further every single day, which only makes me more excited about what lies ahead.”

Sports.title: Shakur Stevenson Picks Leonard, But Ray Robinson Set The Harder Standard
Sports.content:
Shakur Stevenson prefers Sugar Ray Leonard to Sugar Ray Robinson. It is easy to see why. Leonard’s speed, movement, and command of distance resemble the qualities Shakur prizes in his own boxing. But Leonard’s finest wins also required him to fight through danger, and Robinson did that across a schedule neither man came close to matching.

“I like SRL better then I like SRR, This might make my people mad but SRL was one hellavu fighter to me his level was extremely high!!” said Shakur on X.

Stevenson posted that on X on September 22. He had previously called Robinson “buns,” then conceded Robinson was a great fighter and said he had been talking trash. His preference for Leonard is consistent with that view.

Leonard was no fighter who simply ran from trouble. He lost a hard 15 rounds to Roberto Durán, came back to beat him, and stopped Thomas Hearns late in their first fight. His footwork gave him choices; when those fights demanded more, he had offense and resolve to draw upon.

Robinson’s record makes the comparison tougher for Shakur. At age 29, Robinson was 108-1-2 with 72 knockouts. Shakur Stevenson (25-0, 11 KOs) has fought 25 times at the same age. Leonard had fought 34. Different eras produced different schedules, but Robinson’s total still speaks to his ability to win, recover, and do it again.

Shakur’s defense is exceptional. What remains unproven is how he would respond if his legs slowed and an opponent forced him to fight for long stretches at close range. Leonard showed he had answers when movement was insufficient. Robinson showed them more than a hundred times before his 29th birthday, backed by power Shakur has yet to display.

Shakur can like Leonard better. If he is judging the full range of what a fighter had to survive and deliver, Robinson deserves a closer look.

Nobody from modern eras, Leonard included, touches what Robinson accomplished by 29.

Robinson was 128-1-2 with 84 knockouts by the time he hit his 30th birthday, and that lone defeat to Jake LaMotta was avenged multiple times over. He was fighting every few weeks, traveling by car or train, taking on rugged contenders in 15-round fights with small gloves and no modern sports science. If Leonard had tried to keep that exact pace against that level of weekly attrition, his body would have broken down even sooner. Leonard had brittle hands and a detached retina by fight 28. Robinson had a jaw made of granite, brutal endurance, and lethal power in both hands.

Shakur picking Leonard makes sense purely through the lens of modern comfort. Leonard represents the blueprint Shakur relates to: the flashy television superstar, the Olympic gold medalist, the master of lateral movement, hand speed, and distance management. Leonard showed that a fighter could dictate terms, generate huge paydays, and maintain an aura without having to fight forty times a year in smoke-filled arenas.

Where Shakur’s comparison falls completely flat is what Leonard actually did when boxing finesse failed. When Leonard got pulled into absolute hell against Roberto Duran in Montreal, he stood flat-footed and fought. When he was fading and behind on the cards against Thomas Hearns, he unleashed a vicious, predatory assault to close the show. Leonard had a ruthless finishing instinct.

Shakur takes the defensive, perimeter-oriented parts of Leonard’s style and strips away the violent bite. Robinson was a destructive puncher who could knock an opponent out going backward or forward. Shakur is a pure points collector who treats contact like a disaster.

Shakur looking at Robinson and favoring Leonard sounds like modern revisionism. It is a fighter who relies on safety and low output, trying to validate his own approach, overlooking the fact that both Sugar Rays had an appetite for destruction that Shakur has never shown inside a ring.

Sports.title: Jaime Munguia May Vacate Rather Than Fight Bektemir Melikuziev
Sports.content:
Jaime Munguia may give up his WBA super middleweight title rather than defend it against Bektemir Melikuziev. Rick Glaser says Munguia’s team is considering that option. If his information is right, the decision would fit a career that has generally been managed with care. I expected Munguia’s team to have little appetite for Bek once the mandatory fight was ordered.

Glaser says Munguia’s camp is taking a “deep dive into the idea of giving up the title.” He has not said Munguia has vacated. The WBA has given the two sides until October 21 to make a deal and may call a purse bid if they fail to agree.

The Golden Boy connection makes this especially revealing. Melikuziev has fought under its banner since turning professional, and the company knows what its own fighter would bring against Munguia. Bek is a powerful southpaw with a damaging body attack. Munguia’s willingness to take punches while pressing forward would give him chances to land, but it would also give Bek chances to hurt him.

Munguia (46-2, 35 KOs) accepted the Canelo Alvarez fight for a huge payday and lost. Bruno Surace then knocked him out in a matchup Munguia was favored to win. Sergiy Derevyanchenko gave Munguia a hard fight, so his record is not free of risk. Melikuziev presents a different calculation: considerable danger with nowhere near Canelo’s commercial reward.

The WBA belt helped Munguia regain world champion status when he beat José Armando Reséndiz in May. Defending it is another matter. A purse bid could also take the choice of date, venue, and broadcaster out of his team’s hands. Vacating would leave Munguia free to pursue a bigger name at 168, though that freedom would come at Bek’s expense.

Melikuziev (17-1, 11 KOs) beat Darius Fulghum in a WBA eliminator in May 2025, then watched Munguia get the fight with Reséndiz. Bek told The Ring he had been assured he would get the next shot. If Munguia vacates, Bek may still get a chance to win the belt. He would lose the chance to win it from Munguia, a victory that would mean far more for his career.

We’re seeing the new age of belt-holders. Champions giving up their belts exposes the entire modern hustle around world titles. Fighters treat sanctioning body belts like disposable leverage tools rather than something to defend against legitimate threats. They want the belt purely to slap “world champion” on a poster, collect the promotional bump, and leverage it into an in-house payday.

The second a dangerous, low-profile puncher gets ordered as a mandatory, they drop the trinket in the trash and run. Look at the pattern playing out right now. Hamzah Sheeraz walked away from his belt rather than get in the ring with Janibek Alimkhanuly. Teofimo Lopez is on the verge of playing the same game,

Now Jaime Munguia’s camp looks ready to dump the WBA strap because Bektemir Melikuziev offers pure risk with zero casual crossover appeal. Bektemir is a nightmare matchup for a flawed fighter like Munguia. Bek is a heavy-handed, compact southpaw who specializes in cracking the ribs and punishing guys who march forward without defense.

Against Bektemir, Munguia risks getting stopped on regular DAZN for modest money, completely torpedoing his marketability for another mega-fight. Dumping the title completely strips away the pretense of championship prestige. Decades ago, winning a belt meant you took on whoever climbed the ladder, regardless of style or reward. What we’re seeing now is champions treating mandatory defenses like bad business propositions.

If Munguia vacates, Bektemir Melikuziev should get the first chance at the vacant WBA title, but the WBA would still have to choose his opponent. Its current rankings put Canelo Alvarez at No. 2 and José Armando Reséndiz at No. 3. A Canelo fight would be the biggest prize for Bek, though there is no indication Canelo wants it.

Reséndiz looks like the more realistic choice: he lost the belt to Munguia in May and would have a chance to win it back. That would give Bek a title opportunity, but it would deny him the higher-profile victory over Munguia that he has spent more than a year pursuing.

Sports.title: Cuban Boxing Greatness Crossed a Dividing Line
Sports.content:
Cuba produced professional stars before it became an Olympic boxing power. That history makes any list of its greatest fighters difficult to rank. Kid Chocolate and Kid Gavilan built their names in long professional careers; Teófilo Stevenson and Félix Savón never fought professionally. The dividing line was a political decision in 1962 that changed what a Cuban boxer could do with his talent.

Chocolate was a major New York attraction in the 1930s, admired for his speed and two-handed punching. Gavilan later won the welterweight title and made the bolo punch his signature. Luis Rodriguez added another championship to Cuba’s professional history when he beat Emile Griffith for the welterweight title in 1963. These men built their reputations in fights against the leading professionals of their day.

After Cuba banned professional boxing, a fighter who wanted that career had to pursue it abroad. José Nápoles became a welterweight champion after making his home in Mexico. José Legrá won the featherweight title while based in Spain. Later fighters such as Erislandy Lara left Cuba to compete for professional titles. Their success carried a personal cost that a list of wins and belts cannot show.

Cuba also built an amateur program under coach Alcides Sagarra that produced generations of Olympic champions. Stevenson won heavyweight gold in 1972, 1976 and 1980. Savón won the same prize in 1992, 1996 and 2000. Their medals need no imagined professional careers to give them value. But the absence of professional fights leaves one question open: how would the system’s best have performed against established champions over twelve rounds?

Guillermo Rigondeaux gave that question a partial answer. He won Olympic gold in 2000 and 2004, then left Cuba and became a professional champion. In 2013, he beat Nonito Donaire in a super bantamweight title fight, controlling distance and making a dangerous puncher miss repeatedly. Donaire was a proven champion, and Rigondeaux’s amateur schooling held up against him. One fight cannot settle how Stevenson or Savón would have fared as professionals, but it gives this comparison something firmer than speculation.

Lara’s December 2025 defense of the WBA middleweight title shows that Cuban fighters still succeed on the professional side of that divide. The strongest case for Cuba’s boxing greatness comes from looking at both sides: champions who proved themselves over long professional careers, Olympic greats whose careers took another course, and Rigondeaux, who crossed between them and beat one of the best.

Sports.title: Ben Whittaker Faces Conor Wallace With Little Buzz
Sports.content:
Matchroom’s countdown poster for the October 3 fight puts Ben Whittaker front and center in gold gloves, treating Conor Wallace like an afterthought tucked near the bottom. That tells you everything about how this IBF final eliminator is being sold. Matchroom wants the spectacle, yet they are hiding the very man brought in to provide a test at Birmingham’s Utilita Arena on DAZN.

The sanctioning body slapped a number two ranking on Wallace, dangling a mandatory shot at Dmitry Bivol for the victor. Matchroom calls this Whittaker’s most demanding fight to date, yet their own promotional material treats Wallace like a ghost.

Wallace is a heavy-handed southpaw who thrives on forward pressure, precisely the style that gave Whittaker fits against Liam Cameron. Cameron refused to play along with the showboating, got right in Whittaker’s chest, took away his operating room, and forced a difficult inside brawl that ended in a bizarre technical draw. That fight exposed the cracks in Whittaker’s viral persona.

Whittaker loves dropping his hands, leaning back, and relying on pure reflexes against timid opposition. A southpaw stepping outside the lead foot and drilling straight left hands down the pipe shatters that rhythm instantly. If Wallace gets past the jab, cuts off the ring, and forces Whittaker into the ropes, the fancy footwork disappears, leaving a grueling night of trench warfare.

Wallace built that top ranking touring the regional Australian circuit, highlighted by a narrow split decision win over Jerome Pampellone. Whittaker, despite his Olympic silver medal pedigree, spent his recent dates clowning against Richard Rivera, Braian Nahuel Suarez, and Benjamin Gavazi. Both fighters avoided the domestic shark tank of Joshua Buatsi, Willy Hutchinson, or Anthony Yarde to land in this position.

Taking an open sanctioning door is standard boxing business, but Dmitry Bivol waits on the other side. Bivol dismantles loose showmen with relentless robotic fundamentals, punishing anyone who drops their hands. Wallace is the final chance to discover if Whittaker has actual substance when an opponent fires back with bad intentions, and Matchroom is foolish to hide the danger.

Eddie Hearn labels Ben Whittaker a generational talent, but Matchroom matches him like an unpolished novice they are terrified of getting touched. If a promoter genuinely believes an Olympic silver medalist is that caliber of fighter, you do not keep him in bubble wrap for four years. Look at genuine generational fighters or top-tier Olympians: Vasiliy Lomachenko was fighting for a world title in his second professional bout. Sugar Ray Leonard, Floyd Mayweather Jr., and Andre Ward were dismantling legitimate, battle-tested contenders by their thirteenth fight.

Whittaker is 29 years old. He is not a 20-year-old kid who needs physical maturation or time to grow into his man strength. At his age, an elite fighter should be in his prime, yet Matchroom is treating this October 3 date with Conor Wallace like a massive hurdle rather than what it actually is: an exercise in matchmaking self-preservation.

Wallace is an eight-year pro whose record looks manufactured in a lab. He racked up wins on the Australian circuit against obscure opposition, barely edged Jerome Pampellone by split decision, and somehow landed the IBF number two ranking because the sanctioning bodies operate on regional belt accumulation rather than quality. S

erious boxing fans know Wallace is not a top ten light heavyweight in the world. He is a convenient mark with an inflated ranking.The fact that Matchroom selected Wallace for an IBF final eliminator instead of testing Whittaker against domestic threats tells the whole story. Why hasn’t Whittaker been matched against Joshua Buatsi, Anthony Yarde, Willy Hutchinson, or Dan Azeez? Those are the domestic names that would force Whittaker to prove he belongs.

Matchroom deliberately avoided that gauntlet because they know what happens when someone refuses to buy into the showmanship. The Liam Cameron fight gave away the game. When Cameron got inside, roughed Whittaker up, and took away his operating space, the flashy reflex defense fell apart. Whittaker looked ordinary, rattled, and completely out of ideas before that bizarre ring fall ended things in a technical draw. That reveals what Hearn and his team likely see behind closed doors in sparring. If a fighter looks unbeatable in the gym against world-class work, a promoter moves him fast to cash in.

When a promoter slow walks a 29-year-old Olympic medalist against handpicked opposition, it means the gym reports are raising red flags: leaks in the defensive fundamentals, getting clipped when trading on the inside, or an engine that cannot handle a relentless twelve-round pace.

It appears that Matchroom is trying to sneak Whittaker through an open back door to a massive payday against Dmitry Bivol without having him run a real gauntlet. Wallace was brought in to provide the illusion of a world-level eliminator without the actual danger. If Whittaker were the transcendent force Hearn claims, the training wheels would have come off years ago.

Sports.title: Gerrie Coetzee’s Bionic Hand Ends Michael Dokes’s Reign
Sports.content:
Michael Dokes had the faster hands and a title defense close to home on September 23, 1983. Gerrie Coetzee had two failed title bids and a reputation for fading late. Ten rounds later, Dokes was on the canvas, and Coetzee was the WBA heavyweight champion.

Don King billed the fight at Richfield Coliseum as “The Buckeye Homecoming,” though the crowd was about 7,000 in an arena that held 22,000. Dokes (26-0-2, 15 KOs), from nearby Akron, was a 5-1 favorite over Coetzee (28-3-1, 17 KOs). His title reign had begun with a disputed first-round stoppage of Mike Weaver, followed by a draw in their rematch.

Coetzee knew how a strong start could go wrong. John Tate had outlasted him over 15 rounds, and Weaver had stopped him in the 13th. Dokes showed his speed early and cut the challenger near the right eye in round two. Coetzee took the punches and kept coming.

His rebuilt right hand had earned him the nickname “The Bionic Hand,” and it remained one of his best weapons. Dokes had another punch to consider that night, though: Coetzee used his left hook more often than he had in earlier title bids. The hook made his attack less predictable while he pressed the quicker champion.

In the fifth, a short left-right combination put Dokes down on one knee. He rose quickly and fought back, but the knockdown changed the terms of the fight. Coetzee did not slow down as he had against Tate and Weaver. He stayed close enough to make Dokes work and reached the tenth ahead on all three official cards. Dokes still had good moments, particularly in the eighth; this was no uncontested march to the finish.

Coetzee landed two heavy rights past the midpoint of the tenth and followed Dokes into a corner. Dokes tied him up, but after referee Tony Perez separated them, Coetzee attacked again. A left-right combination sent Dokes down. The bell rang during the count, and Perez counted him out at the official time of 3:08.

The right hand helped Coetzee win the title on his third attempt. It also broke again, requiring surgery and keeping him out of the ring for more than a year. He lost the belt to Greg Page in his first defense. Dokes later admitted that cocaine and Jack Daniel’s had been part of his preparation, but that admission does not account for Coetzee’s work over ten rounds. On a night built to celebrate Dokes, the fighter everyone thought would fade was still throwing with force at the end.

Sports.title: Richardson Hitchins Accepts Keyshawn Davis Fight
Sports.content:
Richardson Hitchins agreeing to face Keyshawn Davis at welterweight exposes a massive tactical gamble that could backfire on both men. Hitchins cannot survive by running all night, while Keyshawn faces an agonizing dilemma: turn into a relentless pressure fighter or get picked apart from long range for twelve miserable rounds.

Keith Connolly admitted the cold truth to his man: this is a coin flip, yet the financial payout justifies the danger.

“We’ve accepted the fight. We’re waiting for a couple of commercial things to come through, so to speak, a date to be set. I told Hitchins, it’s a 50-50 fight. But I said, ‘This is the type of fight that if you take it, it’s worth the risk because of the money we’d be receiving, but also the opportunity of two guys fighting in their prime,’” Connolly said to Brian Custer.

Gustavo Lemos already provided the blueprint to rip Hitchins apart by refusing to let him settle into a rhythm. Keyshawn brings sharper reflexes and slicker counterpunches than Lemos, yet patience will ruin him here. Hitchins wants a slow, sleepy track meet where he can flick out light jabs and steal rounds without getting hit.

Keyshawn must trap Hitchins on the ropes, rip shots to the ribs, and fight through the inevitable clinches. Stepping into that pocket comes with severe danger. Hitchins excels at leaning on opponents, tying up arms, and forcing resets that drain an attacker’s stamina. Keyshawn cannot afford to reset every time Hitchins grabs him.

The jump to 147 pounds favors Hitchins physically. Keyshawn built his career down at lightweight, while Hitchins carries natural length and leverage that will look massive inside the ring. Keyshawn will not overpower Hitchins with size. He has to take punches to land his own, risking exhaustion against a rangy spoiler who knows how to make opponents miss.

Placing this fight on a massive Tyson Fury vs. Anthony Joshua stadium event or a David Benavidez vs. Michal Cieslak bill is the only way promoters can afford both purses. Neither man draws enough single ticket buyers to headline on their own. Once the money is guaranteed, Keyshawn must decide if he truly has the engine to chase Hitchins down.

Sports.title: Ade Oladipo’s Hamzah Sheeraz Defense Ignores Canelo
Sports.content:
Ade Oladipo says Hamzah Sheeraz gave up his WBO super middleweight title on principle rather than fight Janibek Alimkhanuly after Janibek’s positive test for meldonium. That is a defensible objection to the WBO’s decision. It becomes harder to accept as the whole explanation when Sheeraz’s route to the belt, his last defense, and his interest in Canelo Alvarez are put beside it.

“Hamzah Sheeraz has done the right thing. If Hamzah Sheeraz is being forced to fight a guy coming off a ban for taking drugs, the sport’s in a crazy place. If Janibek has served his time, then fine. Okay, you’ve served your time. You will now want to fight at 168 pounds. Work your way up. Work your way up. How are you, having cheated in your last fight, now getting the opportunity to fight the champion?” said Oladipo on his channel.

Oladipo made that argument in his video defending Sheeraz’s decision to vacate.

Canelo tested positive for clenbuterol in 2018 and served a six-month suspension. Janibek’s case is much more recent, a distinction Oladipo can fairly make. But if Sheeraz will not fight an opponent with a positive test in his history, why does a lucrative Canelo fight remain desirable? The answer may be that Sheeraz objects specifically to Janibek receiving a title shot so soon after his suspension. That is a narrower argument than ruling him out on principle.

Then there is Oladipo’s demand that Janibek work his way up at 168. Sheeraz got a vacant WBO title shot after one fight at the weight, a stoppage of Edgar Berlanga. His previous fight was a disputed draw with Carlos Adames at middleweight. He did not have to beat Osleys Iglesias or Lester Martinez before facing Alem Begic for the belt. Janibek, whatever one thinks of his test result, had already held unified titles at 160.

Begic looked out of his depth, and Sheeraz stopped him in two rounds. Sheeraz’s first defense offered a sterner test than anticipated: Simon Zachenhuber took him 12 rounds in Jeddah, where Sheeraz won a majority decision by scores of 116–112, 115–113 and 114–114. That performance gave reason to question how Sheeraz would handle Janibek’s southpaw counters. It does not prove how their fight would have ended.

The money adds another question. Queensberry won the Janibek purse bid at just over $1 million, leaving Sheeraz with roughly $750,000 under the proposed split. Sheeraz relinquished the title after his promoter had won the right to stage the fight. That sequence does not reveal his private reasoning, but it makes the risk and reward impossible to ignore.

The WBO approved the Begic title fight and then named Janibek as mandatory. Oladipo is right to question the organization’s handling of Janibek. He should apply the same scrutiny to how Sheeraz obtained the belt. A champion who won it against Begic, struggled with Zachenhuber, and vacated when Janibek came due leaves more to discuss than a simple stand for clean boxing.

Sheeraz has openly confirmed he has only one fight left on his Queensberry agreement, meaning he is standing on the doorstep of open free agency. Losing a fight against Janibek right now would have been a corporate disaster for his market value. If Sheeraz enters the ring against an avoided, southpaw like Janibek and gets knocked out or beaten by decision, his leverage vanishes overnight. Matchroom, Zuffa Boxing, and Queensberry would immediately slash their bidding numbers. A fighter coming off a devastating loss does not command eight-figure signing terms or dictate rights for major stadium headliners.

Walking into the open market without a belt looks weak, but walking in with a shattered chin and an exposed defense is fatal. Sheeraz and his team calculated that boxing purists and casual fans have short memories. They can absorb a temporary storm of criticism for dropping the WBO strap, dress it up with Oladipo’s peddled moral outrage about clean sport, and keep the zero on his loss column fully intact.

Once he finishes that final contracted appearance against a safe, beatable name, he presents himself to Eddie Hearn, Dana White, and Frank Warren as an undefeated, towering British commodity ready for stadium paydays or a cash out against Canelo. Oladipo’s defense is getting drowned out because the boxing public sees right through the ethical smoke screen: this is cold business asset protection designed to keep a fragile stock price high before hitting the auction block.

Sports.title: Shakur Stevenson Stalls Zuffa Boxing As Layoff Drags On
Sports.content:
Shakur Stevenson says a fight announcement is coming. Nearly eight months after he beat Teofimo Lopez, the opponent matters more than the tease.

“Even my haters begging for a fight announcement 😂 I love yall it’s coming lol,” Shakur posted on X.

The Lopez win gave Shakur the strongest moment of his career. He controlled a major fight at Madison Square Garden and had the crowd’s attention afterward, when he brought Conor Benn into the ring and called him “food.” That confrontation made a Benn fight look like an immediate possibility. It went nowhere.

Shakur then spent months discussing a fight with WBO welterweight champion Devin Haney at 144 pounds. Haney’s side said it accepted the proposed weight, but no fight followed. Shakur holds a WBO title at 140, yet he sought a welterweight champion three pounds below that division’s limit while his own challengers waited. Fans are entitled to ask which division he actually intends to fight in.

Zuffa Boxing signed Shakur during the layoff. Dana White paid for a fighter whose win over Teofimo had made him more valuable, but Zuffa has yet to put him in one of its rings. Jose “Rayo” Valenzuela, another Zuffa fighter, called for the fight. Shakur rejected it.

The WBO has already indicated that a mandatory defense is due. It should follow through with a formal order and a clear timetable if Shakur’s next fight does not satisfy that obligation. A champion’s search for a bigger payday cannot leave the rest of the 140-pound division waiting indefinitely.

The Zuffa brass thought they were purchasing the premier American pound-for-pound star right after his masterclass against Teofimo Lopez. Instead, they bought eight months of dead air, endless social media bickering, and an asset that bleeds public interest by the week.

A luxury car loses thousands the minute you roll it off the dealer lot; Shakur Stevenson has been parked in the driveway collecting dust, losing resale value with every single tweet.

What must drive Dana White mad behind closed doors is the refusal to cooperate with company business. In the UFC model, in-house matchups are the lifeblood of the company. Jose Valenzuela stepped up to hand Zuffa a ready-made fight featuring a dangerous, aggressive puncher against their prized technician. Shakur turned him down. Turning down internal company fights while angling for safety catches against Devin Haney at 144 pounds shows an athlete trying to run matchmaking from his couch.

White and the executive room would be entirely justified in pulling the plug, swallowing their pride, and sending Shakur right back out to free agency to waste somebody else’s time and money.

Handing Shakur an ultimatum list is the exact kind of hardball Dana White needs to play. If Zuffa lets him dictate terms, negotiate catchweights, and cherry pick soft touches after an eight-month vacation, they surrender control of their own promotional venture. Giving him three names with a take-one-or-walk clause would instantly test his nerve.

Ernesto “Tito” Mercado belongs right at the top of that sheet. Mercado is a wrecking ball with legitimate dynamite in both hands, stopping 18 of his 19 opponents. He attacks the body with nasty intent, walks through fire, and possesses the kind of brute physical strength that makes safety-first technicians sweat through twelve rounds. The light welterweight division has become a ghost town filled with inactive beltholders and sparring partners, making Mercado the only genuine killer at 140 with the punch to crack Shakur’s defensive shell.

Shakur wants no part of a heavy-handed pressure fighter who will force him to run for his life. Dragging elite sharks up from 135 would apply maximum heat. Andy Cruz is pure agony for Shakur. Cruz boasts Olympic gold credentials, textbook Cuban ring craft, and the punch placement to neutralize Shakur’s potshotting style. Cruz represents the one fighter who can beat Shakur at his own game, outboxing him from the outside while forcing the pace.

Floyd Schofield brings the explosive athletic threat Shakur previously avoided when their scheduled Riyadh bout dissolved. Schofield possesses blazing hand speed, sharp combinations, and the hunger of a young lion with nothing to lose.

Forcing Shakur to sign against Mercado, Cruz, or Schofield would strip away the diva behavior in seconds. If he refuses all three, White can rip up the contract, write off the sunk cost, and show the boxing world that Zuffa refuses to be held hostage by fighters who prefer typing to throwing punches.

Ghana News.title: Fund Accra-Kumasi Expressway with private capital, not state funds – Alan Kyerematen
Ghana News.content:
Former Trade and Industry Minister and United Party (UP) leader Alan Kwadwo Kyerematen is advocating private-sector financing for the proposed US$4 billion Accra-Kumasi Expressway, arguing that government resources could be freed up for other infrastructure needs.

Mr Kyerematen said commercially viable infrastructure projects such as the expressway should be structured to attract private capital, particularly where investors can recover their investment through toll revenues.

Speaking at a public lecture at the British Council in Accra on the theme, “Transformation of the Ghanaian Economy: From Stability to Prosperity,” he questioned the decision to use public funds to finance the entire project.

“You are using four billion dollars to finance a commercial road, which currently can be financed by the private sector. What happens in every country? Once the toll road is constructed, you don’t use government resources to fund it. It can pay for itself,” he said.

He argued that the government could instead allow private investors to finance, construct and operate the road under an arrangement that would enable them to recover their investment over an agreed period.

“We need to commend the government for at least thinking about public-private partnerships between our two actors, because it doesn’t make sense that for over 60 years we continue to rely on government resources to finance everything,” he said.

Mr Kyerematen said the principle should extend beyond the expressway to other infrastructure projects capable of generating revenue.

“Once the road is constructed, you don’t use government resources to fund it if it can pay for itself. Let the private sector manage that. Can you imagine what we can do with our public resources if we free them up?” he asked.

He said such an approach could release government resources for other pressing infrastructure needs, including roads within communities across the country.

The proposal comes as the government prepares to commence construction of the 175.6-kilometre expressway after the clearing of its right-of-way.

President John Dramani Mahama announced on September 14 that US$2 billion had been secured for the project and placed in a dedicated account at the Bank of Ghana. He said the money was sourced from taxpayers and that the project would not be financed through borrowing.

Finance Minister Dr Cassiel Ato Forson had earlier said US$1.7 billion had been secured and that the government expected the full funding requirement to be available by the end of 2026, also without borrowing.

The government's current model also envisages the expressway generating revenue after completion.

The Chief Executive Officer of Accra-Kumasi Expressway Limited, Francis Ahlidza, has said the road will be operated as a commercial asset to enable government to recover the taxpayers’ investment within the concession period.

He said the government established Accra-Kumasi Expressway Limited as a special-purpose company to oversee the development, construction and maintenance of the road.

Mr Ahlidza has also said economic analysis is being undertaken with the expectation that the investment could be recovered over a 50-year period, while generating additional revenue for expansion of the road network.

Mr Kyerematen’s proposal therefore centres on whether that commercial potential should be used to attract private capital from the outset rather than requiring the state to provide the initial financing.

He said greater use of private capital should form part of a broader economic transformation strategy in which government creates the policy and regulatory environment while commercially viable projects attract private investment.

Ghana News.title: Climate finance bureaucracy hurting vulnerable countries – Sierra Leone Minority Leader
Ghana News.content:
Sierra Leone’s Minority Leader has criticised what he describes as excessive bureaucracy in global climate-finance systems, arguing that countries bearing the worst impacts of climate change are struggling to access funding when they need it most.

Speaking to JoyNews’ Stephen Mensah during the Extraordinary Session of the ECOWAS Parliament in Accra, the legislator said complex administrative processes were slowing access to resources needed to respond to climate-related challenges across West Africa.

“The bureaucracy is too much,” he said, stressing that countries facing immediate climate threats must be able to secure financial support more quickly.

He argued that nations most vulnerable to floods, droughts, coastal erosion and other climate impacts are not benefiting sufficiently from existing climate-finance arrangements, despite global commitments under the Paris Agreement.

According to him, countries with high greenhouse gas emissions have a responsibility to support nations disproportionately affected by climate change through accessible and timely funding mechanisms.

The Minority Leader urged the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) to establish dedicated mechanisms to help member states navigate the administrative processes associated with climate funding.

He said regional support structures could help countries overcome delays and improve access to financing for adaptation, disaster preparedness and environmental protection projects.

The legislator also called for stronger accountability in the management of climate funds, insisting that the ECOWAS Commission should regularly brief parliamentarians on how resources are being used.

“We want the Commission to report to us as Members of Parliament as to how these funds are being spent, the projects they are undertaking and the impact of those projects,” he said.

His remarks come as ECOWAS leaders and parliamentarians intensify discussions on climate financing and regional resilience.

At the same gathering, Ghana’s Vice President, Professor Jane Naana Opoku-Agyemang, called for a stronger and more coordinated West African voice in global climate negotiations to secure funding for resilient agriculture, water management, coastal protection and clean energy initiatives.

Climate financing remains a major issue for many African countries, which contribute relatively little to global emissions but face some of the most severe consequences of climate change.

The Sierra Leonean legislator said reducing barriers to climate finance and improving transparency in the use of funds would be essential if the region is to build resilience and protect vulnerable communities from the growing effects of climate change.

Ghana News.title: Ghana–Yorkshire Trade & Investment Summit brings enterprise, culture and community together in Bradford
Ghana News.content:
For two remarkable days in September, the University of Bradford became a meeting place between Ghana and Yorkshire, bringing together business, academia, government, traditional leadership, entrepreneurship, culture and creativity under one roof.

Held on 11 and 12 September 2026, the Ghana–Yorkshire Trade & Investment Summit was convened by Mrs Nana A. O. Hagan, Founder and CEO of SHOFT CIC (Shaping Our Futures Together), whose ability to bring people together was evident in both the calibre and remarkable diversity of those who attended.

Equally remarkable was the partnership between the University of Bradford’s School of Management and the Ghana Scholarly Society (GSS). They were magnificently central to the success of the summit; together, they embraced the event and carried it with the same care, commitment and generosity one would extend when welcoming an honoured guest.

The summit was ambitious in scope. Its central focus was strengthening trade and investment between Ghana and Yorkshire, driven by innovation and sustainable growth. Yet what emerged over the two days was about more than economics. It was also about relationships, creating connections between people who might otherwise never have found themselves in the same room.

Among the special guests were the Lord Mayor of Bradford, Cllr Chris Herd; former Lord Mayor of Leeds, Cllr Abigail Marshall Katung; Bradford Council Leader, Cllr Stephen Anthony Place; and Dr Manoj Joshi MBE, DL, representing the Lord Lieutenant, Professor Adeeba Malik CBE, Personal Representative of HM The King in West Yorkshire.

They were joined by Professor Uduak Archibong MBE, Pro-Vice-Chancellor for Equality, Diversity and Inclusion at the University of Bradford; Ghana’s Deputy High Commissioner, Hon. Aquinas Quansah; and Nana Afua Apiatewa III, Nguabasin Atta Kuma Atta Henmaa of the Gomoa Assin Traditional Council, Ghana, and Konte Henmaa Nanakom of Greater Manchester, UK.

The calibre of the keynote speakers further reflected the summit’s commitment to meaningful discussion around finance, investment, international relations and economic development.

Speakers included Hon. Dr Stephen Amoah, Member of Parliament in Ghana, Deputy Ranking Member of Parliament’s Finance Committee and former Deputy Minister for Finance; Hon. Isaac Adongo, Member of Parliament, Chairperson of Parliament’s Finance Committee and Non-Executive Director on the Bank of Ghana Board; and Hon. Daniel Nana Addo Kenneth, Member of Parliament and member of Parliament’s Foreign Affairs and Regional Integration Committee, as well as Deputy Ranking Member for Private Member’s Bills and Motions.

They were joined by Mr Emmanuel Mensah Thompson Esq., Deputy Director-General of Ghana’s Securities and Exchange Commission.

The University of Bradford’s School of Management also brought its academic expertise to the gathering through Dr Kweku Adams, Associate Professor in International Business and Management; Dr Samuel Kusi, Assistant Professor of Marketing and Brand Consultant; Dr Boakye Boampong, Lecturer in International Business; Professor Richard Nyuur, Head of International Business, Marketing and Strategy; and Professor Yvonne Moogan, Director of the School of Management.

Together, this gathering of political, civic, diplomatic, financial and academic expertise provided a strong foundation for conversations about how Ghana and Yorkshire might build partnerships capable of creating lasting economic and social value.

The People Behind the Summit

Yet behind the dignitaries, presentations, exhibitions and conversations was another group without whom the occasion could not have run so smoothly: the volunteers.

Their contribution was exceptional. Watching them work was rather like watching a choreographed dance. Quietly and efficiently, they seemed to know where they needed to be and what needed to happen next.

Guests were welcomed, people were directed, practicalities were dealt with and the programme continued to flow.

At a large international gathering, it is often the people working behind the scenes who make everything happening in front of the audience appear effortless. The summit’s volunteers did precisely that.

Royal Tradition Meets Contemporary Enterprise

Adding colour, ceremony and a powerful connection with Ghanaian tradition was Nana Afua Apiatewa III, Nguabasin Atta Kuma Atta Henmaa of the Gomoa Assin Traditional Council, Ghana, and Konte Henmaa Nanakom of Greater Manchester, UK.

She graced the summit with her royal presence, accompanied by her linguist, royal umbrella bearer and an Adowa dancer.

It was a striking reminder that international relationships need not require people to leave their cultural identities at the door. Ghana’s traditions and contemporary ambitions could instead occupy the same space, each enriching the other.

Rather than treating culture as something separate from business, the summit allowed the two to speak to each other. That was particularly apparent in the presence of makers and creative entrepreneurs.

One such guest was Mrs Alice BazaaNaa, who travelled all the way from Wa in Ghana, West Africa. A weaver extraordinaire, she brought with her not simply a skill but a living repository of knowledge.

To watch her weave was almost to watch thought itself take physical form, individual threads crossing, separating and coming together until something far greater than the individual strands emerged.

Or, as I found myself thinking while watching her work: to watch her weave is to sit in your soul and interpret the intricacies of life.

There could hardly be a better metaphor for a summit concerned with creating connections.

Enterprise Has No Minimum Age

Perhaps one of the most delightful reminders of the summit’s breadth came from someone considerably younger.

Among the entrepreneurs present was 10-year-old Verity Ofori-Kuragu, an author and young entrepreneur.

Her inclusion mattered. Amid discussions involving parliamentarians, diplomats, academics, international markets, investment and economic opportunity was a child already experiencing what it means to turn imagination into something tangible.

It broadened the meaning of the word investment.

Investment is, of course, about capital and commerce. But it is also about investing in people, ideas and potential. Giving a young person the confidence to regard herself as an author or entrepreneur may produce returns that cannot yet be entered on a balance sheet.

Threads of Identity and Red Mother Earth

Towards the latter part of the summit, I had the privilege of contributing two interactive workshops and exhibitions of my own.

The first, Threads of Identity, explored the language and stories carried in African wax prints.

These fabrics are far more than beautiful arrangements of colour and pattern. Prints can have names and meanings, carrying messages about relationships, character, aspiration, social standing and everyday life.

Understanding those meanings can be particularly important when choosing fabric as a gift. A piece of cloth selected simply because it is beautiful might communicate something altogether unintended, enough, as I joked with participants, to start “World War 10,000!”

The workshop encouraged participants to look beyond the surface of the cloth and recognise fabric as a form of communication: something capable of carrying history, humour, identity and social commentary from one person and generation to another.

The second workshop, Red Mother Earth, turned attention from the language of cloth to the extraordinary resources provided by the earth itself.

The exhibition introduced some of the many natural materials traditionally used in African everyday life. These included Crescentia cujete, the calabash, transformed into storage vessels, household utensils and musical instruments, alongside natural loofah sponges and traditional chewing sticks.

Central to the display were also miniature examples of traditional cooking equipment fashioned from red clay: earthenware cooking pots, coal pots, a mukyea, a traditional hearth used for cooking, and a clay oven.

These small objects told a much larger story.

Long before terms such as sustainability, biodegradability and the circular economy became part of contemporary environmental discourse, communities were making practical use of what the natural world provided.

Earth became the material from which people cooked and sustained their families; plants became vessels, cleaning materials and implements for everyday life.

When many of these objects eventually reached the end of their usefulness, they could return to the earth from which they had come.

That simple cycle lay at the heart of Red Mother Earth: an invitation to recognise that some of the ideas now presented as solutions for a more sustainable future can also be found by looking carefully at knowledge and practices inherited from the past.

The Bridges That Remain

By bringing all these elements together, the Ghana–Yorkshire Trade & Investment Summit demonstrated something important about what international trade and investment can look like.

There were parliamentarians, civic leaders, diplomats and decision-makers. There were academics, financial experts, established businesses and emerging entrepreneurs. There were artists and makers. There was traditional authority and youthful ambition.

And there were conversations about economic development taking place alongside conversations conducted through cloth, craft, movement and heritage.

Holding those many threads together was the vision of Mrs Nana A. O. Hagan.

Creating an event is one thing. Creating an environment in which such different people can meet one another, recognise something of value in one another and begin conversations that may continue long after the chairs have been put away is something else entirely.

The Ghana–Yorkshire Trade & Investment Summit was therefore not simply about what happened at the University of Bradford on 11 and 12 September.

Its real measure will be what happens next.

Which introductions become collaborations? Which conversations become businesses? Which ideas cross borders? Which young entrepreneur is inspired by somebody she met? Which tradition finds a new audience? Which investment creates an opportunity?

The summit’s message was: “Building Bridges, Creating Value, Delivering Prosperity.”

For two days in Bradford, those bridges were not merely discussed.

They were being built.

Ghana News.title: ECOWAS must move beyond climate talk to concrete action – Sierra Leone Minority Leader
Ghana News.content:
Sierra Leone’s Minority Leader has urged the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) to move beyond climate conferences and discussions and implement concrete measures to protect communities from floods, mudslides and environmental degradation.

He said West African countries must translate climate commitments into enforceable laws and practical interventions that can be implemented across member states.

“Our actions should not be just limited to conferences, you know, to just talk shop. There should be proactive measures,” he said.

The Sierra Leonean legislator was speaking to JoyNews’ Stephen Mensah during the Second Extraordinary Session of the ECOWAS Parliament in Accra.

He called for common regional laws that member states could domesticate and enforce nationally, particularly in areas involving forest protection and activities contributing to environmental degradation.

According to him, overgrazing, deforestation and the destruction of forest reserves are worsening the effects of climate-related events, including flooding.

“If forests were not depleted, the effects of climate change would be minimal,” he said.

The Minority Leader said ECOWAS should strengthen regional cooperation to address activities that contribute to the degradation of natural ecosystems.

He argued that protecting forests should form part of a broader regional climate strategy because environmental damage in one country can have consequences beyond national borders.

He therefore wants member states to translate regional agreements into domestic laws and enforcement mechanisms capable of producing measurable results.

His call also extends to disaster preparedness, with the legislator advocating stronger systems to enable countries to respond quickly when floods, mudslides and other climate-related emergencies occur.

He said governments should invest in preparedness before disasters strike rather than waiting to mobilise resources after communities have already suffered losses.

The call comes against the backdrop of discussions within the ECOWAS Parliament on the region’s response to climate change and environmental challenges.

At the parliamentary seminar, Speaker Hadja Mémounatou Ibrahima urged lawmakers to look beyond climate statistics and consider the human consequences of environmental disruption.

The discussions have focused on the need for stronger environmental legislation, climate financing, early-warning systems and measures to build resilience across West African countries.

The Sierra Leonean legislator said the next step should be to translate such discussions into laws, funding commitments and programmes whose implementation can be measured.

He maintained that regional climate action should ultimately be judged by its ability to protect lives, livelihoods and communities from the growing risks associated with environmental degradation and climate-related disasters.

Ghana News.title: ECOWAS must adopt common disaster-preparedness laws – Sierra Leone Minority Leader
Ghana News.content:
Sierra Leone’s Minority Leader has called on the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) to establish common laws and institutions for disaster preparedness, arguing that several countries in the region remain inadequately equipped to respond to climate-related emergencies.

He said the absence of effective emergency-response systems was leaving communities vulnerable to the consequences of floods, mudslides and other disasters.

Speaking to JoyNews’ Stephen Mensah, the legislator said ECOWAS should develop a regional disaster-preparedness framework that member states can adopt and enforce.

According to him, the focus should shift from mobilising resources after disasters occur to putting systems in place that enable countries to anticipate and respond before lives and property are lost.

He cited Sierra Leone’s experience with a deadly mudslide as an example of the consequences of inadequate preparedness.

The Minority Leader said the disaster claimed more than 1,000 lives, with homes buried and some bodies never recovered.

He argued that the scale of such disasters demonstrates the need for West African countries to develop coordinated emergency-response mechanisms rather than relying primarily on individual national systems.

He said regional cooperation should include stronger early-warning mechanisms capable of providing timely information to communities at risk.

He also called for investment in resilient infrastructure and institutions with the capacity to respond rapidly when emergencies occur.

“Early warning” and “early action” have featured in the ECOWAS Parliament’s discussions on climate resilience. The regional parliament has also highlighted the need for stronger environmental policies and programmes aimed at reducing vulnerability and adapting to climate change.

The ECOWAS Parliament’s Agriculture, Environment and Natural Resources Committee is mandated to consider climate change and environmental protection, including the harmonisation of environmental policies and programmes among member states.

The Sierra Leonean legislator wants that regional framework to translate into practical preparedness measures that can be implemented consistently across West Africa.

He also called for the ECOWAS Commission to report periodically to the regional Parliament on disaster-preparedness programmes and assess whether they are delivering the intended results.

Such reporting, he argued, would allow policymakers to identify gaps in national preparedness and strengthen coordination between member states.

The proposal comes against the backdrop of growing concerns over the impact of extreme weather events across West Africa, including flooding and landslides.

The ECOWAS Parliament has previously urged governments to integrate climate considerations into national planning and budgets, while advocating regional and national measures to strengthen resilience to climate-related risks.

For the Sierra Leonean legislator, the objective is to establish a system in which countries are prepared to act before disasters occur, rather than waiting until communities have already suffered major losses.

He believes a common ECOWAS framework, backed by appropriate institutions, legislation, early-warning systems and predictable financing, could strengthen the region’s ability to protect lives and property when climate-related emergencies occur.

Ghana News.title: Augustine Boakye: the talent Ghanaians are waiting to see
Ghana News.content:
There was a period in Ghanaian football when some talents seemed to defy football logic. They were not merely good footballers.

They were artists.

And many of them came from West Africa Football Academy (WAFA).

At WAFA, football was played with a particular rhythm: the ball moved quickly, feet seemed lighter, and young men who had barely announced themselves to the country played as though they had been together for decades.

Gideon Waja. Majeed Ashimeru. Richard Danso. Samuel Tetteh. Umar Bashir. Martin Antwi. Richmond Lamptey. Prince Ampem. Emmanuel Boateng. It is a tall list.

Different players. Different personalities. Different journeys.

But somehow, the same football language.

Intricate passing. Delicious touches. Movement without the ball. Courage to receive under pressure. A willingness to play football rather than merely survive it.

For a while, Sogakope became one of the most fascinating places in Ghanaian football.

WAFA's home was not simply a football ground.

It was a factory.

And the factory kept producing talent with incredible substance.

In October 2017, WAFA completed a remarkable 44-match unbeaten run at home after drawing 1-1 with Medeama. Their style was already recognisable: movement, passing and an insistence on playing their way out of trouble.

For six consecutive seasons, they were simply irrepressible, beating at least an opponent four or more goals.

2015

Wafa 4-1 Hasaacas

2016

Wafa 5 - 0 Hasaacas

2017

Wafa 5-0 Hearts

2018

Wafa 5 - 0 Dreams

2020

Wafa 6 - 1 AshGold.

2021

WAFA 5-1 Liberty Professionals

Again and again, the Academy Boys turned Sogakope into a theatre.

When they dismantled Liberty Professionals 5-0, on January 31, 2021, this young kid, Augustine Boakye among the scorers.

It was almost as if the place had its own footballing DNA. And somewhere inside that DNA was a boy from Bompata, a suburb of Ghana’s Ashanti region.

Augustine Boakye in action for WAFA in the Ghana league

His name was Augustine Boakye. When he came through this factory in Sogakope, there was something curious about him. He did not look like a footballer who wanted to merely participate in a game.

He wanted to interfere with it. Give him the ball and he wanted to turn. Put a defender in front of him and he wanted to run at him. Give him a teammate in space and he could find him.

There was mischief in his football. The kind that makes spectators lean forward before anything has actually happened. Ask David Ocloo, former Liberty manager. Ask George Amoako former Liberty captain, and may be Abraham Wayo for the script of that never-to-be-forgotten afternoon.

He tore them apart in a similar fashion football demigod Lionel Messi did to Manchester United that got Michael Carrick depressed in that 2009 Champions League final.

By the end of the 2020/21 Ghana Premier League season, the curiosity had become evidence.

Boakye played 29 matches, scored nine goals, provided 13 assists and won seven Man of the Match awards. Those numbers earned him a place among the nominees for the Ghana Premier League Player of the Season award.

Nine goals. Thirteen assists. Seven individual awards. For a 20-year-old.

But numbers, on their own, do not tell the full story.

They cannot tell you about the first touch that gets neutrals of their feet with gaping mouths screaming ‘wow’ unison.

They cannot tell you about the little pause before the acceleration that gets fans anticipating what is about to happen.

They cannot tell you about the defender who thinks he has closed the door, only to discover that Boakye has already found another entrance.

That was the attraction. He was not simply productive. He was such a talent that one could watch all day without blinking.

And that is a rare quality. Then he disappeared just like many of those with incredible cloth in a fabric of football dynasty.

Football has a strange way of hiding its treasures. Sometimes distance does it. Sometimes timing.

Sometimes a player's development happens quietly, far from the noise that surrounds the biggest names. Boakye left Ghana and began another education in Europe.

Austria became his next classroom.

Wolfsberger became the place where the boy from WAFA had to learn another version of football.

The pitches were different. The opponents were different. The demands were different. The game was less forgiving. But, he kept moving.

At Wolfsberger, he gradually became more than the exciting Ghanaian prospect. He became a professional footballer. He learned to survive without the ball. To make decisions faster.

To understand spaces differently.

To play against defenders who had no interest in being entertained. And eventually, France came calling.

Saint-Étienne.

A club whose name carries history in French football. A club where expectations are not whispered.

Boakye, now 25, arrived in July 2024, having established himself in Austria. He had made 43 league appearances for Wolfsberger, scoring 13 goals and providing nine assists.

The journey had moved from Sogakope to Wolfsberg. Then from Wolfsberg to Saint-Étienne.

Augustine Boakye completed move to Saint-Étienne in July 2024

The boy was becoming the footballer. He was a man! France did not come easy

There is a temptation, when telling football stories, to make every journey look inevitable.

It rarely is.

Boakye's first season in France was about adjustment. Last season was about influence.

He played 31 Ligue 2 matches for Saint-Étienne, scoring five goals and providing nine assists.

Then came this season. And suddenly, something began to happen. The numbers started making noise.

Seven league appearances.

Seven starts.

Four goals.

Three assists.

Seven goal involvements.

Against Metz on 19 September, Boakye scored one and assisted another in Saint-Étienne's 2-2 draw. He had scored in four consecutive league appearances.

Augustine Boakye celebrates goal against Metz in Lig 2

This is the version of Boakye Ghana is now beginning to see.

Not the promising 20-year-old at WAFA.

Not simply the Ghanaian abroad.

But a 25-year-old attacking player who has accumulated several seasons of European football and appears to be entering one of the most productive periods of his career.

Ghana has been waiting. The country knows his name. But it has barely seen him.

Ghanaian football fans and journalists may have watched his career through statistics, clips and reports from Europe. They have heard about the goals. They have heard about the assists.

They have heard about Saint-Étienne. But they have not yet had enough time with him.

Enough minutes. Enough touches. Enough moments.

The Black Stars came close to giving him that opportunity at the 2026 World Cup.

Boakye was named in Carlos Queiroz's squad for the tournament, but the opportunity never quite arrived on the pitch.

Augustine Boakye in Ghana’s camp for World Cup 2026

The ball screamed for him when Croatia were a tough nut to crack. Carlos Queiroz never heard.

It whispered when Colombia were running away with ease, but the Portuguese had other ideas, leaving the young man on the edge of the story.

There’s always that butterfly of ‘if’, but this moment feels different.

With an AFCON qualifying campaign on the horizon. Côte d'Ivoire and The Gambia to look forward to.

Then there is a new beginning under Queiroz.

The timing could not be more interesting.

Boakye is no longer arriving as an unknown teenager.

He arrives with a body of work. And, importantly, he arrives at a time when Ghana's attack has been forced to adjust.

Mohammed Kudus withdrew from the squad after recovering from injury, Antoine Semenyo and Jordan Ayew out plus many others affected by fitness and availability issues. Queiroz has consequently had to make additions to his squad.

Mohammed Kudus withdrew from squad to focus on recovery

Is this Boakye’s time?

Ghana's 2027 AFCON qualifying campaign begins in Bouaké against Côte d'Ivoire on Thursday, 24 September. Bouaké is not a City many Ghanaians would want to be reminded of.

In 1984, when Ghana line-up as defending champions of the AFCON, the team had what many described as disastrous showing on the continental, forcing the team to be disbanded for what many claim was lack of commitment to the national cause.

It was named the ‘Bouaké debacle.’ Quieroz may want to avoid a repeat of history not just against Boauké, but against a nation that has denied Ghana an AFCON title in the last 34 years, before returning home to face The Gambia five days later at the Accra stadium.

Carlos Queiroz leads Ghana’s AFCON 2027 quest

Côte d’Ivoire beat Ghana in 1992 to win its first AFCON title and defeated Ghana in 2015 to win their second title. Both victories were secured after a marathon shootout. The man who denied Ghana an AFCON gold medal in 2015, Herve Renard, leads to Elephants again.

It is not an ordinary beginning.

Côte d'Ivoire are one of Africa's established football powers. AFCON champions two years ago.

And Hervé Renard is beginning a new cycle with the Elephants, having introduced eight new players into his squad.

Herve Renard led Ivory Coast to Afcon success in 2015 against Ghana

Ghana, meanwhile, is beginning its own chapter. Queiroz has inherited a group containing established names and emerging players. A group that failed to qualify for this tournament in 2025, ending Ghana’s 20 consecutive years of participating in the competition.

Ghana cannot afford another slow start. That makes this AFCON qualifying window significant. Players must step up, but who should Quieroz call on?

Does Ghana have the attacking talent?

They have them. The question is what kind of attacker Queiroz wants.

And that is where Boakye becomes fascinating.

Call him an attacking midfielder and you are not wrong. But you are not entirely right either.

This football academian is that left-footed attacker who can operate across the frontline. He can come inside. He can start wide. He can carry the ball. He can combine.

He can create. And, he can score.

His recent Saint-Étienne numbers make the point better than adjectives ever could: four goals and three assists in seven Ligue 2 appearances this season.

But there is another quality that cannot be measured so easily. Freedom.

Boakye likes to play. He likes to receive. He likes to face people. He likes the uncertainty of one-versus-one situations.

And he has something Ghana have always loved in their best attacking players: the instinct to make something happen when nothing appears to be happening.

Think of Kudus. Quincy Owusu Abeyie. Kevin Prince Boateng. Kwadwo Asamoah...

That is the kind of footballer spectators remember.

Boakye did not emerge from nowhere. He came through a football culture that valued the ball. The same academy that produced Waja, Ashimeru, Tetteh, Annan, Lamptey, Ampem and others also produced him.

And the numbers from his breakthrough season confirm that he was not merely passing through.

He belonged.

When WAFA beat Liberty Professionals 5-0 in January 2021, Boakye scored and also assisted Sampson Agyapong.

When the Ghana Premier League Player of the Season nominations were announced months later, his nine goals, 13 assists and seven Man of the Match awards were impossible to overlook.

That was the player Sogakope knew. Europe has since polished him. But somewhere inside him, that WAFA player remains.

The boy who sees the defender. The space behind him. The teammate arriving. And lays the ball.

There is a temptation to make a player's international debut into a referendum on his entire career.

It should not be. International football is its own beast. The spaces are different. The tempo is different. The pressure is different.

A player can dominate a domestic league and struggle to reproduce it internationally. So Boakye does not need to arrive in Bouaké and become Ghana's saviour.

He simply needs an opportunity to begin.

A touch. A run. A pass. A shot. A moment.

Perhaps that is all Ghanaian supporters are asking for.

Because for years, they have heard about Augustine Boakye.

Now they want to see him. Not on a statistical website.

Not through a highlight reel from France. They want to see him in black and white (in Ghanaian parlance).

They want to see whether the player who enchanted Sogakope can carry that magic into the Black Stars. He is no longer waiting

The talent that once needed to announce itself in Sogakope is now producing goals in Saint-Étienne.

The question is no longer whether Europe has seen him.

Europe has.

The question is whether Ghana has.

Perhaps that is what makes this moment so compelling. The country has spent years waiting for the next great attacking talent to announce himself. Maybe he already did. Maybe we simply were not close enough to hear it.

Augustine Boakye is no longer waiting for permission.

He is knocking.

And somewhere between Bouaké and Accra, Ghana may finally open the door.
