World.title: A cheeky response to Trump and Sheinbaum’s first presidential trip to Asia: Wednesday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Listen to this article

Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

🇺🇳 Sheinbaum fires back at Trump’s U.N. remarks: Responding to Trump’s U.N. General Assembly claim that Mexico is the “epicenter” of cartel violence and that it’s “unacceptable” for the U.S. to border a country “controlled by enemy cartels,” Sheinbaum said she could just as easily say it is “very difficult to live next to a country” with such high illegal drug use and gun production.

Responding to Trump’s U.N. General Assembly claim that Mexico is the “epicenter” of cartel violence and that it’s “unacceptable” for the U.S. to border a country “controlled by enemy cartels,” Sheinbaum said she could just as easily say it is “very difficult to live next to a country” with such high illegal drug use and gun production. 🇨🇳 Sheinbaum to attend APEC Summit in China: The president announced she’ll travel to Shenzhen, China, in November for the APEC Leaders’ Meeting — her first trip to Asia as president. Mexico will host the APEC summit in 2028.

The president announced she’ll travel to Shenzhen, China, in November for the APEC Leaders’ Meeting — her first trip to Asia as president. Mexico will host the APEC summit in 2028. 🚆 750-billion-peso investment in rail projects: Sheinbaum said Mexico is investing roughly 750 billion pesos (US $42.95 billion) in railroads this sexenio, with around 60,000 jobs tied to construction.

Why today’s mañanera matters

At her Wednesday morning press conference, President Claudia Sheinbaum offered a riposte to the Mexico-related remarks U.S. President Donald Trump made during a 37-minute speech to the U.N. General Assembly on Tuesday.

Her retort was significant as it demonstrated — once again — that Sheinbaum is prepared to forcefully counter Trump’s rhetoric on Mexico, while simultaneously seeking to maintain a positive and productive working relationship with the U.S. president and his administration.

Also of note at today’s mañanera was Sheinbaum’s disclosure that she will travel to China in November to attend the APEC Leaders’ Meeting. The trip will be Sheinbaum’s first to Asia as president. She has visited seven foreign countries since she was sworn in on Oct. 1, 2024: Panama, Brazil, Honduras, Canada, Guatemala, the United States and Spain.

Sheinbaum responds to Trump’s UN address

A reporter asked the president about Trump’s U.N. General Assembly address, highlighting that the U.S. president described Mexico as the “epicenter” of cartel violence and declared that it is “unacceptable” for the United States to share a 2,000-mile border with a country “controlled by enemy cartels.”

Sheinbaum’s first response was to note that Trump also said “something else.”

“Let’s see, what did he say?” she asked, prompting the reporter to acknowledge that the U.S. president also said that his administration has “a very good relationship with the Mexican government.”

“They take one part of the statement and not the other,” Sheinbaum said without specifying who she was referring to.

She then gave a pointed response to Trump’s declaration that it is “unacceptable” for the U.S. to share a border with a country “controlled by enemy cartels.”

“I could say it’s very difficult to live next to a country that has such a high level of illegal drug use,” Sheinbaum said.

“Or I could say it’s very difficult to live next to a country that produces so many guns,” she said.

“But I’m not going to say it,” Sheinbuam said, eliciting laughter from the press corps.

“I’m not going to say it because we have a good relationship with President Trump and the U.S. government,” she said.

“We’re working in a coordinated way [on security challenges] and we’re making progress,” Sheinbaum said.

La presidenta Sheinbaum no quiso pronunciarse sobre las declaraciones de Trump ante la ONU Afirma que es difícil vivir a lado de un país que es consumidor de drogas Nada menciona sobre la protección de su gobierno a narcopolíticos de Sinaloa pic.twitter.com/jTmGlGH0UU — Manuel Lopez San Martin (@MLopezSanMartin) September 23, 2026

Sheinbaum to attend APEC Summit in China

Asked why she decided not to travel to New York to participate in the 81st session of the U.N. General Assembly, Sheinbaum responded:

“There are moments and then there are moments when one decides to go or not go. I felt that this wasn’t the time to attend the [General] Assembly. I didn’t go last year either.”

Foreign Affairs Minister Roberto Velasco is representing Sheinbaum at the General Assembly. The president noted that he has not yet addressed the General Assembly.

She told reporters that she will attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Leaders’ Meeting in Shenzhen, China, on Nov. 18 and 19. Sheinbaum noted that Mexico will host the APEC Leaders’ Meeting in 2028.

In China, “we’re going to receive the baton,” she said, although Vietnam will host the 2027 APEC event before Mexico gets its turn the year after.

Sheinbaum highlights 750-billion peso investment in rail projects

After an update on the various railroads currently under construction, Sheinbaum told reporters that the total investment in the projects is around 750 billion pesos (US $42.95 billion).

“That’s what we’re investing in trains in the sexenio,” she said, referring to her six-year period of government (2024-30).

Sheinbaum said that trains have “many virtues,” noting that they “connect regions” and “cities” and help to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by taking cars and buses off the roads.

She also highlighted that railroad projects create jobs. Sheinbuam told reporters that around 60,000 people are currently employed in jobs directly related to the construction of railroads. She also said that rail projects help drive economic growth.

“We’re very happy with the work being carried out,” Sheinbaum said, referring to the various railroad projects under construction, including lines linking Mexico City to Querétaro, Mexico City to Pachuca and Saltillo to Nuevo Laredo.

By Mexico News Daily chief staff writer Peter Davies (peter.davies@mexiconewsdaily.com)

World.title: Washington Flirts With a 90-Day Diesel Export Ban: What It Means for Expats in Latin America
World.content:
UNITED STATES · ENERGY & LATAM

Key Facts — The report The White House is preparing a 90-day ban on diesel exports , with the legal route being worked out and President Trump inclined to announce it by the end of the week, Politico reported Wednesday, citing five people familiar with the discussions.

— The denial A White House official said Wednesday the report is “not true” . Energy Secretary Wright, reported to oppose a total ban, has publicly called export bans a “blunt tool” that “definitely doesn’t work” and favors voluntary redirection of supply instead.

— The price pressure US diesel averages about US$6.52 a gallon (AAA), up roughly 90 cents in a month and about 76 percent in a year; diesel futures fell about 4 percent Wednesday on the report (Reuters).

— The precedent If imposed, it would be the first US curb on energy exports in more than a decade — the crude-oil export ban was lifted in 2015. Russia is separately weighing its own fuel export restrictions.

— The LatAm angle Latin America buys heavily from US Gulf Coast refineries — Mexico is consistently the largest buyer of US diesel in US trade data. A ban would push import prices up across the region in the short term.

— What to watch Whether an announcement comes by Friday, and whether it is a ban or Wright’s voluntary approach. Nothing had been formally announced as of Thursday morning.

Washington is debating something it has not done in more than a decade: restricting energy exports. The reported target is diesel, the fuel that moves Latin America’s trucks, buses and food supply — and much of the region’s imported diesel comes from US Gulf Coast refineries. For expats, the story is not the US pump price; it is what a ban would do to freight and food costs from Mexico to Chile.

A Pemex fuel station at night in Mexico. Mexico is consistently the largest buyer of US diesel in US trade data, which makes it the country most exposed to the export ban reported to be under discussion in Washington. (Photo: Rio Times media library)

What Washington Is Reported to Be Preparing

Politico reported Wednesday, citing five people familiar with the matter, that the White House is preparing a 90-day ban on diesel exports, that lawyers are working out the legal route, and that President Trump is inclined to announce the measure by the end of the week. Energy Secretary Wright called energy-company executives on Tuesday night to say a ban was likely within days, the report said.

The same report describes a split at the top: Wright, Treasury Secretary Bessent and Interior Secretary Burgum are opposed to a total ban. And on Wednesday a White House official publicly denied the report outright — “not true”. Trump himself, speaking at the UN on Tuesday, framed the idea in his own terms: “let’s not send out the diesel.”

As of Thursday morning, nothing had been formally announced. Treat the ban as reported preparation, not policy — the denial and the preparation can both be true while the decision sits on the president’s desk.

Why Diesel Is the Pressure Point

US diesel averages about US$6.52 a gallon according to AAA — up roughly 90 cents in a month and about 76 percent in a year, making it the most politically sensitive fuel price in the country. Diesel futures fell about 4 percent on Wednesday as traders digested the report: a ban would trap supply in the domestic market, lowering US prices while raising them everywhere else.

The context is global. Russia is separately weighing fuel export restrictions of its own, and the OECD’s interim outlook published Wednesday projects Brent peaking near US$105 a barrel late in 2026 — a forecast, not a fact. A US diesel ban would be the first American curb on energy exports since the crude-oil export ban was lifted in 2015.

What It Means for Latin America

US Gulf Coast refineries are the region’s fuel station. US trade data consistently show Mexico as the largest buyer of US diesel, with Brazil and Chile also among the big importers. If exports stop, even for 90 days, buyers bid against each other for Atlantic Basin supply from elsewhere — and the price rise lands in import markets within weeks.

For expats, diesel rarely shows up at a pump you visit; it shows up in bus fares, trucking rates and supermarket logistics. The region is already running two live experiments in diesel policy: Mexico’s voluntary cap holds regular diesel at MXN 27 a liter (about US$1.54) at a cost one analyst estimates at MXN 163 million a day (about US$9.3 million), and Bolivia raised its administered diesel price to Bs17.95 a liter (about US$1.49) — an 83 percent rise — in June, a decree drivers marched against in Oruro on Wednesday. A US export ban would squeeze both: the cap gets more expensive to hold, and the alternative suppliers get pricier.

What Happens Next

The reported window is days: an announcement “by the end of the week” means Friday at the latest if the reporting holds. The alternative outcome is Wright’s voluntary approach — asking refiners to redirect supply without a legal ban — which would leave export flows intact. Either way, the first place the decision shows up in Latin America is the wholesale diesel price, and from there freight. For today’s full regional money picture — Banxico’s 1 p.m. decision, Argentina’s country risk at 566, Colombia’s TRM jump — see our daily guide for Thursday 24 September.

Will the United States ban diesel exports? As of Thursday morning, nothing had been announced. Politico reported Wednesday that the White House is preparing a 90-day ban and that President Trump is inclined to announce it by the end of the week; a White House official denied the report the same day, and Energy Secretary Wright — reported to oppose a total ban — favors voluntary redirection of supply instead. Both the preparation and the denial can be true at once; the decision sits with the president. Would a US diesel export ban raise fuel prices in Latin America? Yes, in the short term, if imposed. Latin America imports heavily from US Gulf Coast refineries — Mexico is consistently the largest buyer of US diesel in US trade data. A ban would force buyers to compete for supply from farther away, raising import prices within weeks. Diesel moves freight, buses and food logistics, so the effect reaches consumers who never buy diesel directly — in bus fares and supermarket prices rather than at the pump. Why is diesel suddenly so expensive in the United States? US diesel averages about US$6.52 a gallon according to AAA, up roughly 90 cents in a month and about 76 percent in a year — the sharpest fuel-price increase in the country, driven by the global crude rally. That domestic price is the politics behind the reported ban; the OECD’s interim outlook published Wednesday projects Brent peaking near US$105 a barrel late in 2026, a forecast that suggests the pressure is not expected to fade quickly.

World.title: Investment-Grade Talk and a US$7 Billion Energy Package: What Argentina’s New York Week Means for Expats
World.content:
ARGENTINA · MONEY & POLICY

Key Facts — The package The US State Department announced Wednesday it would set aside up to US$7 billion through 2027 for Argentina, largely for energy — the EXIM-backed package first reported by Reuters; Argentine outlets put about US$6 billion of it behind the Argentina LNG project. No loan contracts were signed, and the department said no signing was imminent.

— The forum The announcement followed the week’s meetings around an investor forum at Argentina’s New York consulate, with Foreign Minister Quirno, US envoy Landau, YPF chief Marín and EXIM’s Whitten involved.

— The investment-grade talk JP Morgan’s regional chief, Gómez Minujín, told Bloomberg Línea on Wednesday that Argentina could regain investment grade if Milei is re-elected in October 2027 — with policy continuity, lower inflation and reserve accumulation. A conditional path, not a rating action.

— The counter-signal Country risk rose for an eighth straight session to 566 points on Wednesday, and the Merval fell 0.94 percent as banks were sold; YPF rose 1.6 percent on the energy news.

— The cash test A US$803 million payment to the IMF falls due on Friday 25 September, with the Fund’s third-review mission still working in Buenos Aires without a public statement.

— Your money The blue dollar is 1,540 / 1,560 (US$100 buys ARS 154,000); a US$1,000 card purchase costs about ARS 1,995,500 at the tarjeta rate.

Argentina spent the week in New York selling a future — investment grade, American energy money, a seat back at the creditors’ table — while the market back home quietly charged it more to borrow. Both things are real. For expats, the skill this week is separating what is signed from what is said.

The Casa Rosada in Buenos Aires. While the government pitched investors in New York this week, country risk — the premium markets charge to hold Argentine debt — rose for an eighth straight session to 566 points. (Photo: Rio Times media library)

The Week in New York

The centerpiece was money for energy — and this time it moved from report to announcement. The US State Department said Wednesday it would set aside up to US$7 billion through 2027 for Argentina, the EXIM-backed package that Reuters had first reported from a planning document; Argentine outlets put about US$6 billion of it behind Argentina LNG, the roughly US$51 billion project to liquefy Vaca Muerta gas and export it by ship. No loan contracts were signed, and the State Department said no signing was imminent in the coming days — the announcement is a commitment of intent, not a disbursement.

Two guardrails for reading the headlines. First, this is EXIM — the US export-credit agency — not a US Treasury swap line: it finances American-linked exports and projects, which is why the money points at energy. EXIM reopened cover for Argentina on 3 February 2026, so Wednesday’s announcement builds on an existing channel rather than creating one. Second, until contracts are signed — and the State Department says none are imminent — the number is a ceiling, not a commitment.

The Investment-Grade Question

JP Morgan’s regional chief executive, Gómez Minujín, told Bloomberg Línea on Wednesday that Argentina could regain an investment-grade rating if President Milei is re-elected in October 2027 and the program holds — the conditions he named were policy continuity, lower inflation and reserve accumulation. That is a bank executive’s conditional path, not a rating-agency action; no agency has moved Argentina’s rating this week.

The OECD’s interim outlook, published the same day, frames the distance still to travel: it cut Argentina’s 2026 growth forecast to 2.6 percent (3.0 percent for 2027) and sees 2026 inflation at 30.8 percent — far better than the triple digits of the recent past, and far from investment-grade norms.

The Counter-Signal at Home

While the delegation pitched in New York, the Buenos Aires market marked its own card. Country risk — JP Morgan’s spread on Argentine dollar bonds over US Treasuries — rose for an eighth straight session to 566 basis points on Wednesday. The Merval fell 0.94 percent to 2,969,545 points as investors took profits in banks — Supervielle lost 3.0 percent, Grupo Galicia 2.9, Banco Macro 2.7 — while YPF gained 1.6 percent on the energy news, the session’s most-traded stock. The wholesale peso closed at 1,516 per dollar, the very top of its one-year range.

The politics ran in parallel: Milei devoted much of his UN General Assembly speech on Wednesday to the Malvinas — a “causa nacional”, with legal actions announced against companies operating in the islands — and again called the UN “useless”. The meeting that mattered more for markets came on the sidelines: Secretary of State Rubio, with Economy Minister Caputo in the room.

What It Means for Expats

None of this week’s headlines changes today’s exchange counter. The blue dollar is 1,540 / 1,560 — US$100 buys ARS 154,000, and ARS 1,000,000 is about US$641 at the selling rate. The oficial is 1,485 / 1,535, the MEP financial rate sits at 1,537.6 / 1,542.9, and card spending remains the expensive way to pay: a US$1,000 charge lands at about ARS 1,995,500 at the tarjeta rate of 1,930.5 / 1,995.5.

What the week does change is the medium-term frame. If the EXIM package signs and the LNG financing closes, Argentina’s export-income story strengthens into 2027 — the backdrop for the peso you will be exchanging into. If Friday’s IMF payment or the review mission stumbles, the country-risk climb gets a ninth session. Watch the signatures, not the speeches.

What Happens Next

Thursday brings INDEC’s July economic-activity print (EMAE) and first-half poverty data during the day — the statistical backdrop for the IMF review. Friday 25 September is the cash test: the US$803 million payment to the IMF falls due. After that, the calendar runs to the EXIM signature, if it comes, and the long road to the October 2027 election on which the investment-grade talk is conditioned. For the full regional picture — Banxico’s decision, Colombia’s TRM jump, Brazil’s pre-election real — see our daily guide for Thursday 24 September.

Is Argentina about to regain investment grade? Not this week, and not this year. JP Morgan’s regional chief, Gómez Minujín, told Bloomberg Línea on Wednesday that Argentina could regain investment grade if Milei is re-elected in October 2027, with policy continuity, lower inflation and reserve accumulation — a conditional path described by a bank executive, not a rating-agency action. The OECD the same day cut Argentina’s 2026 growth forecast to 2.6 percent and sees 2026 inflation at 30.8 percent, which shows the distance still to travel. What is the US$7 billion package, and is it signed? It is support announced Wednesday by the US State Department — up to US$7 billion through 2027, largely for energy, the EXIM-backed package first reported by Reuters; Argentine outlets put about US$6 billion of it behind the Argentina LNG project. No loan contracts had been signed as of Thursday morning, and the department said no signing was imminent. It is EXIM export-credit support, not a US Treasury swap line, and until contracts sign, the number is a ceiling rather than a commitment. What does country risk at 566 mean for my money in Argentina? Country risk is the premium investors demand to hold Argentine bonds over US Treasuries; 566 basis points after eight straight rises means markets are charging more to lend even as the government pitches in New York. For daily life the rates that matter moved less: the blue dollar is 1,540 / 1,560 (US$100 buys ARS 154,000; ARS 1,000,000 is about US$641), and a US$1,000 card purchase costs roughly ARS 1,995,500 at the tarjeta rate. The near-term markers are Friday’s US$803 million IMF payment and the review mission’s eventual statement.

01 Getting Around

Mexico’s Pacific coast remains the day’s travel story, and the warning zone has grown. The tropical storm warning now runs from Tecpan de Galeana to Manzanillo — extended westward overnight — with a tropical storm watch from west of Manzanillo to Playa Pérula. Tropical storm conditions are expected within the warning area overnight and are possible in the watch area late tonight and on Thursday, the NHC says. The port of Acapulco remains closed to small boats and coastal fishing, and Michoacán and Jalisco keep 19 and 38 shelters open respectively. The army’s DN-III-E preventive phase and the navy’s Plan Marina remain active along the Pacific.

Puerto Vallarta stays outside the warning zone on blue alert, the lowest level of Mexico’s cyclone warning system; the cruise ship Island Princess, which moved its call from Wednesday, is scheduled today. Swells from Polo will spread northward along the west-central coast and toward Baja California Sur on Friday and into the weekend — the NHC warns of life-threatening surf and rip currents. If you are flying or sailing along the coast this week, check with your airline, the port captaincy and Mexico’s weather service (SMN) before setting out.

Elsewhere: Bolivia’s Oruro drivers marched peacefully on Wednesday against the diesel decree, DS 5716, and the drivers’ confederation has called a national 24-hour vehicle withdrawal for Monday 28 September, threatening escalation to an indefinite strike; intercity travel is running, with police and soldiers guarding the main highways under the state of exception. Uruguay’s SUPRA port union holds its general assembly at 10 a.m. today, with port activity cut from 8 a.m. — check operations if you are shipping or traveling by ferry. In Ecuador, a nightly curfew (midnight to 5 a.m.) runs through 30 September in Guayas, Manabí, Los Ríos and El Oro under Decree 498, and 185 factories have been ordered to cut power use; plan evening movements accordingly.

02 Cost of Living & Money

All rates below are from live sources on the day, with the measure named. Argentine figures are Wednesday’s closes from dolarapi; the TRM is Colombia’s official rate, valid today only; PTAX is Brazil’s official central-bank fixing; FIX is Banxico’s official reference; the observado and UF are Chile’s official daily values. Where only a market estimate exists, we say so.

Argentina. The gap between a calm peso and a rising risk premium widened again: the blue dollar moved five pesos to 1,540 / 1,560 (US$100 buys ARS 154,000), but country risk — JP Morgan’s spread on Argentine dollar bonds over US Treasuries — rose for an eighth straight session to 566 on Wednesday. The wholesale rate closed at 1,516 per dollar, the top of its one-year range, and the Merval fell 0.94 percent as investors took profits in banks; YPF rose 1.6 percent on the energy news. In New York, Milei met Secretary of State Rubio with Economy Minister Caputo in the room, and JP Morgan’s regional chief raised the prospect of investment grade — conditional on re-election in 2027 and continuity. Friday brings the US$803 million payment to the IMF. For your money: card spending remains the expensive way to pay (a US$1,000 card charge costs about ARS 1,995,500), and the MEP rate sits near the blue at 1,537.6 / 1,542.9. Our standing country-risk explainer has been updated this morning, and the New York week standalone has the investment-grade detail.

Colombia. The TRM — the official reference rate that governs card settlements and many contracts — jumps to 3,264.39 today, up 1.7 percent from 3,208.66 on Wednesday and valid today only; a new one is certified this afternoon. At today’s rate, US$1,000 converts to COP 3,264,390 and a COP 3,000,000 rent costs about US$919, roughly US$16 less than at Wednesday’s rate. The jump tracks a global dollar surge that hit the whole region on Wednesday. The political story is Monday: the government is due to issue the economic-emergency decree on 28 September that will enable the farm-sector debt freeze.

Brazil. Wednesday’s PTAX fixed weaker at 5.1408 / 5.1414, and spot closed at 5.1703 per dollar, down 1.36 percent on the session as the dollar firmed globally; the Ibovespa fell 0.86 percent to 185,814. Ten days before the first round, an AtlasIntel poll for Bloomberg put a runoff in a statistical tie — Lula 47.7, Flávio Bolsonaro 47.4, with a one-point margin of error — and a new Datafolha national survey is expected as early as today (fieldwork 22–24 September, registered with the electoral court; release timing is Datafolha’s). The electoral court ordered the Lula campaign to delete a video filmed at the presidential residence within 24 hours. On the data front, the central bank’s quarterly monetary policy report is due at 8 a.m. and the IPCA-15 mid-month inflation print on Friday at 9 a.m.; consensus forecasts a return to positive monthly inflation after August’s −0.40 percent — a forecast, not a fact. Our election explainer is updated daily.

Mexico. Banxico determined the FIX at 17.5030 on Wednesday, published in today’s Diario Oficial; the rate applicable to payments today is 17.3015. Spot closed at 17.531 after a 1.37 percent slide — the sharpest one-day move in months, per El Financiero, which cited the narrowing US–Mexico rate gap dulling the carry trade. MXN 10,000 is about US$571 at Wednesday’s determined FIX. The decision lands at 1 p.m. Mexico City time, hours after the mid-month inflation print at 7 a.m.; Barclays expects a hold at 6.50 percent — a bank forecast, not guidance. The OECD raised its 2026 growth forecast for Mexico to 1.5 percent from 0.8 in its interim outlook published Wednesday. Our Banxico standalone sets out what today means for expat budgets.

Chile. The dollar observado weakened to 959.39 today from 945.87 on Wednesday, and the spot rate closed at 962.375, the peso’s weakest in about a year, as copper slipped to US$6.68 a pound. The UF — the inflation-indexed unit used in rents, insurance and many contracts — stands at 41,008.10, about US$42.74. A monthly rent of 20 UF is CLP 820,162, about US$855. Politically, the Senate approved the political-system reform 28–3 on Wednesday, leaving only the Chamber vote — timing not fixed — and a Data Influye poll put President Kast’s approval at 25 percent for September, down 11 points from August.

Peru, Uruguay, Costa Rica. Peru’s sol is around 3.3809 per US dollar on market estimates (S/1,000 ≈ US$296) — the tax authority’s feed we normally use was unavailable this morning, so this figure is labeled an estimate — ten days before the 4 October local elections tracked in our Peru elections standalone. Uruguay’s peso is around 40.12 on market estimates (UYU 40,000 ≈ US$997), with the port union’s assembly today. Costa Rica’s colón is near 452.34 (CRC 700,000 ≈ US$1,548), also a market estimate, and a tax bill filed Tuesday would charge foreign-source income for tax residents — details in section 03 below.

03 Visas, Residency & Tax

Where What changed What it means for you Costa Rica Bill 25.796, filed Tuesday, would tax foreign-source interest, dividends, royalties, rents and capital gains at 15 percent for tax residents (more than 183 days in the country). Pensions and salaries are excluded, and foreign tax already paid would be credited first. A rival bill, 25.734, takes a different approach. Neither is law; there is no start date. Nothing changes today. If you are tax-resident in Costa Rica with foreign investment income, this is the bill to watch — territorial taxation is what draws many expats, and both bills would narrow it. Colombia Standing deadline: the permanent-visa transfer under Resolución 9316 of 2024 must be completed by 31 October 2026 — 37 days from today. Nothing new was published today. If your permanent visa was issued before October 2022, book the transfer appointment now; slots tighten as the deadline nears. Argentina No new migration or tax measures today. Decree 681/2026, tightening permanent-residency and citizenship rules, has been in force since 31 July; the tax agency’s updated personal-assets thresholds continue to apply. If your residency file is in progress under the pre-decree rules, confirm with your gestor which regime applies to your case. Peru No detention decree has been published as of this morning. The OAS observer mission is in place for the 4 October local elections, ten days away. If your visa or residence permit is valid, nothing changes — carry proof of status. Our Peru standalone has the checklist.

04 The Week’s News in Brief

Where What happened Why it matters Argentina & the UN Milei devoted much of his General Assembly speech on Wednesday to the Malvinas — a “causa nacional” — announcing legal actions against companies operating in the islands, and again called the UN “useless”. Economy Minister Caputo joined his meeting with Secretary of State Rubio. On the money track: JP Morgan’s regional chief laid out a path to investment grade, and the US State Department announced it would set aside up to US$7 billion through 2027, largely for energy; no loan contracts were signed, and the department said no signing was imminent. The money story — not the speech — is what moves your cost of living in pesos: our Argentina standalone separates what is signed from what is talk. Brazil An AtlasIntel poll for Bloomberg put a runoff in a statistical tie: Lula 47.7 percent, Flávio Bolsonaro 47.4, margin of error one point. Monday’s Quaest national survey had Lula ahead 37–33 in the first round and tied 41–42 in a runoff. The electoral court ordered the Lula campaign to delete a residence-filmed video within 24 hours. A new Datafolha is expected as early as today. Ten days out, every poll moves the real — and your rent in reais. Our election standalone tracks the campaign daily. United States & diesel Politico reported Wednesday that the White House is preparing a 90-day ban on diesel exports, with President Trump inclined to announce it by the end of the week; a White House official publicly denied the report the same day. US diesel averages about US$6.52 a gallon, up roughly 76 percent in a year. Latin America buys heavily from US Gulf Coast refineries; a ban would push diesel — and freight — costs up across the region. Our diesel standalone has the details. Venezuela President Trump pulled aside interim president Delcy Rodríguez at the Lotte Palace on Tuesday evening, with Rubio, Bessent, Wiles and Miller present; no readout or deal emerged, and sanctions are unchanged. Rodríguez addressed the General Assembly on Wednesday. The first known direct contact at this level since the transition — movement without substance so far; relevant for expats with Venezuelan family, property or pension ties. Mexico The OECD raised Mexico’s 2026 growth forecast to 1.5 percent from 0.8 in Wednesday’s interim outlook, and sees Brent peaking near US$105 late in 2026 — a forecast, not a fact. Banxico decides at 1 p.m. today. The rate call, the peso and the diesel cap decide what your money buys this month — our Banxico standalone previews all three. Chile The Senate approved the joint-committee text of the political-system reform 28–3 on Wednesday; only the Chamber vote remains, with timing not fixed. A Data Influye poll put President Kast’s approval at 25 percent for September, down 11 points from August. The reform’s final vote is now a single step away; the approval slide frames the government’s weaker hand heading into it. Peru A Caraz judge on Tuesday ordered 15 days of preliminary detention for two foreign nationals over the killing that has reshaped the campaign; police recalibrated their account of the sicariato angle, and the elections of 4 October proceed as scheduled. Ten days out, security is the campaign’s central theme — our Peru elections standalone tracks it.

05 Weather & Safety

Mexico, Pacific coast — Hurricane Polo: In its 9 p.m. CST Wednesday advisory, the National Hurricane Center held Polo at Category 5 with maximum sustained winds of 160 mph (260 km/h) and a central pressure of 923 millibars, centered about 130 miles (205 km) south-southwest of Zihuatanejo and 240 miles (390 km) south-southeast of Manzanillo, moving northwest at 6 mph. Some additional near-term strengthening is possible, and Polo is expected to remain a powerful major hurricane for the next few days; a turn toward the west-northwest is expected today and Friday. On the forecast track, the core stays offshore through this morning before moving farther out to sea. A tropical storm warning now runs from Tecpan de Galeana to Manzanillo — extended overnight — with a tropical storm watch west of Manzanillo to Playa Pérula. Rainfall of 4 to 6 inches, isolated 8, is forecast for coastal Guerrero through today, and 2 to 4 inches for coastal Michoacán, Colima and Jalisco, with life-threatening flooding, mudslides and dangerous surf the main risks. Hurricane-force winds extend 40 miles from the center, tropical-storm-force winds 115 miles. Swells spread northward toward Baja California Sur on Friday and into the weekend; the NHC’s probability table gives Cabo San Lucas an 8 percent chance of tropical-storm winds by early Sunday 27 September, rising to 12 percent by early Monday. The next intermediate advisory is due at midnight CST, the next full advisory at 3 a.m. CST. Our Polo standalone has the expat checklist.

Brazil, south: Utilities are still restoring power after this week’s storms in Rio Grande do Sul, Santa Catarina and Paraná, which killed four people; expect debris and intermittent closures on southern highways.

Rio de Janeiro: A rainy day with a high near 22°C; yellow flags on the beaches — swim with caution. Sunset is at 5:50 p.m.

Elsewhere: Ecuador’s nightly curfew (midnight to 5 a.m.) runs through 30 September in four coastal provinces under Decree 498, with 185 factories ordered to cut power use. Bolivia’s highways are open after Wednesday’s peaceful Oruro march, guarded by police and soldiers under the state of exception. No other regional emergencies are in force this morning.

06 What’s On

Rio de Janeiro: With rain forecast for much of the day, the indoor circuit earns its keep: the CCBB is open 9 a.m. to 8 p.m. with free entry, the Real Gabinete Português de Leitura is free 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., and the Paço Imperial is free noon to 6 p.m. The Jardim Botânico opens at 8 a.m. (R$40 residents, R$80 foreigners — about US$7.78 and US$15.56 at Wednesday’s PTAX), and Parque Lage is free. The metro is R$7.90 a ride, about US$1.54, per our desk’s What’s On brief.

São Paulo: The Pinacoteca is open 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. (R$40, about US$7.78) and the Museu da Língua Portuguesa 9 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. (R$25, about US$4.86); Ibirapuera park and the MAC USP are free. Coffee Lab and Santo Grão are the desk’s coffee picks. For the evening, Vila Madalena: Salve Jorge, the Beco do Batman graffiti alley, and Pirajá. Sunset is at 6:03 p.m.

Ahead: Anette Olzon’s orchestra shows open tonight in Belo Horizonte, then São Paulo on the 26th and Rio on the 29th; the Ópera de Colombia gala is 3 October in Bogotá; World of Coffee Panama runs 23–25 October with tickets from US$52; Jovanotti plays Buenos Aires on 22 October; Luciano Pereyra is at the Movistar Arena on 24 October; and Carmina Burana is staged in San José, Costa Rica, on 17–18 October.

07 The Calendar Ahead

When What Where Why it matters Today, Thursday 24 September Banxico rate decision at 1 p.m. Mexico City time; Mexico mid-month inflation at 7 a.m.; Brazil’s central bank publishes its quarterly monetary policy report at 8 a.m. and the CMN meets; Datafolha expected in the evening; INDEC publishes July EMAE and first-half poverty during the day; Uruguay port-union assembly; Anette Olzon shows begin; NHC advisories at midnight and 3 a.m. CST Mexico, Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay The peso’s worst day in six months meets the rate call; the Argentine prints frame the IMF review’s backdrop. Friday 25 September Argentina’s US$803 million payment to the IMF falls due; Brazil’s IPCA-15 mid-month inflation at 9 a.m.; Polo forecast to move farther out to sea; the White House is reported to be inclined to announce the diesel decision by end of week Argentina, Mexico, United States The first cash test of the mission week; the diesel call, if it comes, reprices freight across the region. Sunday 27 September Polo’s swells reach Baja California Sur — the NHC gives Cabo San Lucas an 8 percent chance of tropical-storm winds by early Sunday, rising to 12 percent by early Monday Mexico Low odds, but the day Los Cabos travelers should recheck. Monday 28 September US–Mexico formal trade talks resume in Washington (28–29 September); Colombia’s government is due to issue the economic-emergency decree enabling the farm-debt freeze; Bolivia’s drivers hold a national 24-hour vehicle withdrawal United States, Mexico, Colombia Tariff reductions are on the table after the Sheinbaum–Trump call; the decree would open the farm-debt freeze; Bolivia risks escalation. Wednesday 30 September–Thursday 1 October G20 trade ministers meet in Milwaukee, hosted by USTR Greer — Brazil hopes for a tariff meeting on the sidelines; Bolivian urban teachers march nationally on the 30th; Ecuador’s nightly curfew ends on the 30th United States, Brazil, Bolivia, Ecuador The next dated chance to move the US–Brazil tariff track before the first round. Around Friday 2 October IMF board expected to consider Bolivia’s US$1.9 billion program United States, Bolivia An expectation stated by Bolivian officials, not a confirmed schedule. USA & Canada Intelligence Dossier — Wednesday, 23 September 2026 · Web edition Take it with you. The full dossier is published on the web and updated through the day. Read the web dossier → · Every edition on the dossier page →

The White House — Courting one autocrat while fighting its own reporters, as three newsrooms go before a judge and Xi Jinping lands. American voters — Angry and frightened about money, and not consoled by the opposition offered to them. The Senate Armed Services chairman — Embarrassed by his own president’s guest, and saying so on the floor. Ottawa — Deliberately looking past Washington, and taunted for it the same morning.

The White House spent Wednesday courting one autocrat while fighting its own reporters. Trump drove out to an air base in the evening to greet China’s Xi Jinping on the tarmac; his lawyers had stood in a federal courtroom hours earlier, defending a ban on three American newsrooms.

The two quarrels met in a single sentence. A government lawyer asked the judge to leave the reporters locked out at least until the Chinese president has gone home, because, he said, national security matters most during such a visit.

American voters are angry about money and not consoled by the alternative. In a CNN poll published on Wednesday, 44 per cent of registered voters call their vote for Congress a message of opposition to Trump, against 19 per cent who call it a message of support, yet only about a quarter approve of each party in Congress.

The chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee is embarrassed by his president’s guest. Senator Roger Wicker, a Republican of Mississippi, told the chamber on Tuesday that Trump should not have invited Xi, and called him “a brutal, unelected and oppressive dictator”.

Ottawa is deliberately looking past Washington, and was taunted for it. Prime Minister Mark Carney spent the week in New York building coalitions with Europeans and never met Trump, who wrote on Wednesday morning that Canada is “destroying itself” through immigration.

Canada now has three votes running at once, and Trump is on every ballot. British Columbia’s premier called a snap election for 24 October in which he named the American president more than twenty times, while Quebec votes on 5 October and Alberta holds its referendum on 19 October.

Read across CNN, NPR, the Associated Press through PBS, NBC News, the White House’s own briefing page and the Press Democrat of California. Then the Canadian Press through BNN Bloomberg and the Chronicle-Journal of Thunder Bay, the Prime Minister’s Office in Ottawa, the Hill Times and the Bank of Canada.

The full USA & Canada Intelligence Dossier is updated daily by the Rio Times Intelligence Desk. It carries the editor’s leader, the deep dive on the state visit and the press ban, the country health check and the people who matter. Open the dossier · Browse the archive

Washington Rolls Out The Carpet, And Bolts The Door

The welcome for Xi Jinping was designed to flatter, and it went ahead on Wednesday evening. Xi arrived in Washington and “was met with a rare planeside greeting” from Trump at Joint Base Andrews, the military airfield outside Washington that receives visiting leaders, rather than being driven to the White House, the Associated Press reported after the event.

The First Lady gave the reason in plain terms. Melania Trump told Fox & Friends, the morning programme of the Fox News Channel, on Wednesday that her husband chose to go himself because “they have a great relationship”, adding: “He’s coming on our soil, and we need to welcome them with the most respect.”

The staging at the airfield was exact. A red carpet 100 feet long was unfurled at the foot of the aircraft steps, where a 21-person honour guard waited with Trump and Melania Trump, and Xi and his wife Peng Liyuan came down and shook their hands, the Associated Press reports.

Thursday carries more of it. The Office of the First Lady says the arrival ceremony on the South Lawn will feature 479 military personnel from every branch of the armed forces, a review in the Rose Garden, and a flyover by one B-2 Spirit bomber and four F-22 Raptor fighters.

It is a repayment, not a first meeting. The visit reciprocates the ceremony that met Trump in Beijing in May, where, the Associated Press reports, a red carpet, an honour guard and about 300 Chinese youths waving both flags chanted “Welcome, welcome! Warm welcome!” — though Xi himself was not at the airport.

What steadies the reading is that nobody expects much of it. The Associated Press writes that “expectations are low that the trip will produce any major breakthroughs”, with tensions high over trade, artificial intelligence, Trump’s war with Iran and China’s designs on Taiwan. The black-tie dinner on Thursday evening will seat technology chiefs including Nvidia’s Jensen Huang and SpaceX’s Elon Musk.

This desk read no Chinese source today, so the account above is an American one. The Associated Press describes a three-day visit beginning on Wednesday, while the Office of the First Lady calls Thursday 24 September the day of the state visit proper. Both are correct, for different things.

A Judge Starts Where The White House Is Weakest

The ban that Trump announced on Friday 18 September reached a courtroom on Wednesday afternoon. Judge Timothy J. Kelly of the United States District Court for the District of Columbia, whom Trump himself appointed, heard the emergency request on Wednesday afternoon. CNN, the cable news network, MS NOW, the cable channel formerly called MSNBC, and Politico, a Washington political news site, asked him to restore their reporters’ passes.

He opened not on free speech but on fair procedure. Courts have held that the White House cannot revoke a journalist’s pass without notice or a chance to appeal, and Kelly told both sides that process “wasn’t played out here”, CNN reports.

He said so before either lawyer spoke. Kelly told them “I just say to both sides that’s where I am”, and set out his order of business: “Before we get to any core first amendment issues, there is a due process claim and a due process issue that seems to me the first stop in figuring out how to resolve the motion.” That sequence favours the newsrooms.

The newsrooms’ lawyer said the government had changed its story. Theodore Boutrous of the law firm Gibson Dunn argued that national security was never mentioned when the ban was announced, and appeared only after the lawsuit was filed: “All of the sudden this is a national security case,” he said, as though “a light bulb went off”.

He put the principle bluntly. The administration is “literally arguing that reporters shouldn’t scrutinize national security” matters, he said — “That’s the sin” — and the stories the White House cited “are just garden variety reporting”.

The government asked for delay rather than victory. Justice Department lawyer Michael Velchik urged Kelly, at a minimum, not to restore the passes until after Xi’s visit, saying the security concerns are paramount during it and that the judge should not override the President’s “personal determined judgement over that period”.

The judge tested the newsrooms too. Kelly asked whether a president could pull the pass of a reporter found to have “passed on classified information to a foreign enemy”, and then whether the substance of a story could ever justify a ban; Boutrous said it could not, because “Once you go down that road, it is … blatant viewpoint discrimination”.

Nothing has been decided. The hearing ended without a ruling from the bench, and Kelly said he would “try to get an answer as soon as I can”, so a decision is expected at any time; when this desk last read CNN’s live coverage at 22.41 UTC on Wednesday, CNN reported that he “did not issue an immediate ruling”.

The paper trail is the newsrooms’ best material. The White House sent the three companies letters on Tuesday, filed in court that night, listing stories it said “threatened national security and/or spread falsehoods”.

Executives at two of the outlets answered in writing. They told the court that several of the listed stories were written by reporters who hold no White House pass, and that the letters to CNN and to MS NOW each named a pass-holder whose pass was renewed after the story ran, CNN reports.

Key Facts — The welcome for Xi Jinping. Flattery on the tarmac: Trump greeted Xi beside his aircraft at Joint Base Andrews on the evening of 23 September, on a red carpet 100 feet long, the Associated Press reports. — Thursday’s arrival ceremony. Pomp as a message: 479 military personnel and a flyover of one B-2 bomber and four F-22 fighters are planned for 24 September, the Office of the First Lady says. — The press ban in court. Unresolved: Judge Timothy Kelly heard the three banned newsrooms on 23 September, opened on due process and ended without a ruling, CNN reports. — The government’s request in court. Two quarrels in one sentence: on 23 September a Justice Department lawyer asked that passes not be restored until after Xi’s visit, CNN reports. — American anger without consolation. 44 per cent of registered voters call their congressional vote a message of opposition to Trump, against 19 per cent for support, CNN’s poll of 16 to 17 September finds. — The Greenland agreement. Signed, not in force: the accord Trump, Denmark and Greenland signed in New York on 22 September enters into force only after Danish and Greenlandic parliaments act. — A third Canadian election. British Columbia votes on 24 October after Premier David Eby named Trump more than twenty times in calling it, the Canadian Press reports. — Ottawa’s cheque at the United Nations. Carney pledged C$82 million (about US$58 million) for ocean monitoring on 23 September while never meeting Trump in New York, the Canadian Press reports.

Anger That Finds Nothing To Vote For

The American mood this week is fury without relief. A poll by SSRS for CNN, taken online and by telephone from 16 to 17 September among 1,206 adults and published on Wednesday, finds 44 per cent of registered voters describing their vote for Congress as a message of opposition to Trump and 19 per cent as a message of support.

CNN calls that a high for an incumbent president going back to the presidency of George W. Bush. The margin of sampling error is 3.5 percentage points for the full sample and 4.1 points among registered voters.

The money numbers are worse than the political ones. Just 27 per cent approve of Trump’s handling of the economy, down 22 points from 2018; 20 per cent approve of his handling of inflation; and 28 per cent call economic conditions good, a fall of 41 points from 2018.

The poll also asks how people feel, and the answers are anxious. Some 57 per cent say they feel uncertain about their own finances, and more than a third are not confident of keeping their present standard of living — worse, CNN notes, than the readings at the end of the Great Recession.

The doubt reaches inside his party. Only 35 per cent of Republicans strongly approve of Trump, against 66 per cent in September 2018; half of Republicans disapprove of his handling of inflation, and 59 per cent say the war in Iran has hurt their finances.

What stops this becoming a rout is that the opposition inspires nobody. Democrats lead the congressional vote by 49 to 41 per cent, a narrower margin than the 12 points CNN found in its September polling before the 2018 midterm elections, and about a quarter of Americans approve of each party in Congress.

Prices are the mechanism behind all of it. Two-thirds of Americans say Trump has worsened economic conditions, and majorities say the war in Iran and the new tariffs have hurt their own finances.

The United States Capitol. A CNN poll finds 44 per cent of registered voters call their congressional vote a message of opposition to Trump, against 19 per cent who call it a message of support. Photo: Martin Falbisoner, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

A Signature In New York That Is Not Yet A Law

Tuesday brought the document behind one of Trump’s boldest claims. He, Denmark’s Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenland’s Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen signed a security agreement at United Nations headquarters in New York on Tuesday, after months of quiet talks, the Associated Press reports.

Trump had described it in grander terms at the General Assembly. He said a deal with Denmark gives the United States “permanent control over security and all other needs” in Greenland, the Arctic island under Danish sovereignty, NBC News reported on Tuesday.

The text says something more careful. It reaffirms “the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Denmark” and recognises Greenlanders’ “right to self-determination”, according to the Associated Press’s reading of the accord.

What the United States gains is room to build. It may “modernize and expand” its activities at the Pituffik Space Base in the north-west, set up “defense areas” at Narsarsuaq in the south and Mestersvig in the east, and “may establish additional defense areas in Greenland”.

It also shuts the door on Moscow and Beijing. The accord provides that “no state that is not a member of NATO shall be allowed to establish its own manned or unmanned military installations in Greenland”, nor keep a lasting military presence there.

The gap between the claim and the paper is the point. The agreement “does not have an end date”, but it will only “enter into force” once the “necessary parliamentary processes of the Kingdom of Denmark, in conjunction with Greenland, have been completed” — a signature, not yet a law.

Trump called it “a dream come true” for the United States, NBC News reports. The network’s own assessment is cooler, headlining the result as “No invasion, a few compromises and the status quo”.

Ottawa Looks Past Washington, And Is Taunted For It

Canada’s answer to a broken negotiation is to spend its week elsewhere. Carney and Trump were both in New York and did not meet, on Carney’s first trip to the United States since trade talks collapsed last month, the Canadian Press reports.

The government says so in its own voice. Its release of Wednesday opens by declaring that the international order faces a rupture and that Canada is building a new one. It quotes Carney: “At this pivotal moment in history, the world can count on Canada.”

The money is modest and pointed. At an event on ocean monitoring co-hosted with Ursula von der Leyen, the President of the European Commission, Carney pledged C$82 million (about US$58 million). “Canada is an ocean nation,” he said; von der Leyen said 30 countries have promised support, and that “We must listen to the ocean and we must protect it much more.”

The larger cheque went to Gaza and the West Bank. Ottawa announced a further C$100 million (about US$71 million) for Palestinians, of which C$80 million (about US$57 million) is humanitarian aid. That brings its total since October 2023 to more than C$600 million (about US$426 million).

Carney himself did not give Canada’s set-piece speech. Foreign Minister Anita Anand addressed the General Assembly for the second year in a row, Global News, a Canadian television news service, reports.

Trump answered the week’s diplomacy with a post. On Wednesday morning he claimed Canada is “destroying itself” by admitting millions of people “essentially unchecked and unvetted”. He called it a “Liberal takeover that will end very badly”; the Canadian Press notes that he offered no evidence.

The grievance behind the courtesy is trade. Trump has imposed tariffs of 50 per cent on a range of Canadian goods, and is set to block imports of others later this month. He has also ordered Canadian-origin products removed from United States government purchasing systems, the Canadian Press reports.

Europe is the hedge, and it is not yet a deal. Von der Leyen last week opened the door to Canada becoming what she called the first “associate member” of the European Union, and the two sides meet in Montreal on 29 October.

At home the fight is over a single bill. The Building Canada Strong Act, or Bill C-39, was introduced on 21 September by Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon. It runs to 232 pages and amends both impact-assessment law and the Canada Labour Code, the Hill Times, an Ottawa politics weekly, reports. Unions and the New Democratic Party call it an attack on labour; the government says Canada needs it to build.

Three Canadian Ballots, And Trump On All Of Them

The newest of the three came as a surprise on Tuesday. Premier David Eby, whose New Democratic Party is the centre-left party governing the Pacific province, went to Government House in Victoria to ask Lieutenant-Governor Wendy Cocchia to dissolve the legislature, setting voting day for 24 October, the Canadian Press reports.

He called it a firebreak. Eby mentioned Trump more than twenty times outside Government House, called the moment an “existential” one for the province, and said: “When you smell smoke you don’t sit and wait to see what happens next.”

He accused his opponents of going easy on the American president. Trump is “targeting our businesses and he is threatening our sovereignty”, Eby said. He added: “At a time when Trump is creating more uncertainty, the last thing we need to do is abandon the front line.”

His timing is what his critics attack. Eby governs on the one-seat majority he won at the 2024 election, and called the vote a week after scheduled municipal elections, despite pleas from local leaders not to overlap the campaigns, the Canadian Press reports.

The opposition united within two hours. Seven legislators from CentreBC, the breakaway caucus that split from the British Columbia Conservatives, rejoined that party, the Canadian Press reports.

Their interim leader is new to the job. Lorne Doerkson, who called Trump “the bully south of the border”, said of the election call: “I think David Eby is going to regret this.”

The province’s books are the vulnerability. Finance Minister Josie Osborne said last week that the deficit forecast had grown by C$450 million (about US$319 million) to a record C$13.8 billion (about US$9.8 billion). The Canadian Press reports that the rise was largely a “calculation error” on natural gas royalties.

Quebec, the French-speaking province, votes first, on 5 October. Its leaders were preparing on Wednesday for the third and final debate, hosted by Radio-Canada, the French-language public broadcaster.

The pro-independence Parti Québécois is ahead and the appetite for change is the story. Léger’s survey of 1,001 Quebec voters for Le Journal and TVA puts the party at 29 per cent among decided voters, and finds 65 per cent wanting a change of government, up four points.

Alberta, the oil-producing western province, votes on 19 October on ten questions, the last of them on staying in Canada. Premier Danielle Smith said on Monday that she is “not a neutral party” and wants Alberta to remain, after her own party president complained about a C$4 million (about US$2.8 million) advertising campaign.

What This Means From Latin America

The state visit is the item to watch from São Paulo. Any easing of tariffs between Washington and Beijing would move demand for the ore, soya and copper that South America sells to both. The Associated Press reports that expectations of a breakthrough are low.

The oil price is the transmission line. November West Texas Intermediate settled at US$92.16 a barrel in New York on Wednesday, up 1.8 per cent, after Iran’s President told the General Assembly that Tehran would not surrender. That is dearer fuel for the region’s importers, and better receipts for its exporters.

Canada’s search for company includes Brazil. Ottawa lists Brazil among the founders of a new coalition on multilateralism launched at the United Nations on 21 September, alongside Australia, Barbados, the European Union, India and Kenya. That places Brasília beside Ottawa among governments assembling coalitions of the willing.

The Greenland text is a precedent worth reading closely. A great power obtained wide military access while the document reaffirmed the smaller party’s sovereignty and left ratification to its parliament — the shape of bargain a region used to asymmetric negotiation will recognise.

What We Are Watching

Judge Kelly’s ruling on the press ban — expected at any time. The hearing ended on Wednesday without a decision, and the judge said he would “try to get an answer as soon as I can”, CNN reports. The government asked him to wait until Xi has left.

— expected at any time. The hearing ended on Wednesday without a decision, and the judge said he would “try to get an answer as soon as I can”, CNN reports. The government asked him to wait until Xi has left. The Trump–Xi summit at the White House — 24 September. The arrival ceremony on the South Lawn carries 479 military personnel and a flyover, the Office of the First Lady says. Trade and artificial intelligence are the practical tests.

— 24 September. The arrival ceremony on the South Lawn carries 479 military personnel and a flyover, the Office of the First Lady says. Trade and artificial intelligence are the practical tests. The close of the state visit — 25 September. Xi and Peng Liyuan take tea at the White House and then visit the National Archives, where the Trumps will see them off.

— 25 September. Xi and Peng Liyuan take tea at the White House and then visit the National Archives, where the Trumps will see them off. Ratification of the Greenland accord — no date set. The agreement enters into force only when the parliamentary processes of Denmark, together with Greenland, are complete.

— no date set. The agreement enters into force only when the parliamentary processes of Denmark, together with Greenland, are complete. The Quebec general election — 5 October. The Parti Québécois stands at 29 per cent among decided voters in Léger’s survey for Le Journal and TVA. The final debate closes the campaign.

— 5 October. The Parti Québécois stands at 29 per cent among decided voters in Léger’s survey for Le Journal and TVA. The final debate closes the campaign. The Alberta referendum on its future — 19 October. Ten questions, the last on whether to stay in Canada. The premier says she is not neutral and wants the province to remain.

— 19 October. Ten questions, the last on whether to stay in Canada. The premier says she is not neutral and wants the province to remain. The British Columbia election — 24 October. Premier David Eby called it citing an “existential” threat from Trump, and governs on a one-seat majority, the Canadian Press reports.

— 24 October. Premier David Eby called it citing an “existential” threat from Trump, and governs on a one-seat majority, the Canadian Press reports. The Canada–European Union summit — 29 October, in Montreal. It will show whether von der Leyen’s talk of Canada as an “associate member” becomes anything.

— 29 October, in Montreal. It will show whether von der Leyen’s talk of Canada as an “associate member” becomes anything. The American midterm elections — 3 November. Democrats lead the congressional vote by 49 to 41 per cent in CNN’s poll, and about a quarter of Americans approve of either party in Congress.

— 3 November. Democrats lead the congressional vote by 49 to 41 per cent in CNN’s poll, and about a quarter of Americans approve of either party in Congress. The United States funding deadline — 11 December. The House of Representatives passed the Senate’s extension on 1 September, moving the cliff past 30 September, CNN reports. This desk has not verified that Trump signed it.

Go deeper in the paid web dossier. It carries the deep dive on a White House that courts one autocrat while fighting its own reporters, and three ways the press case can run. It also carries a health check of the continent, the North American calendar and today’s verification notes.

For how these stories developed, see the USA & Canada Intelligence Brief for 22 September and 21 September. Those editions carry the United Nations speech and the filing of the lawsuit.

North American politics and trade policy and their bearing on this hemisphere run through our pillar coverage of The United States & Canada. That section carries the daily record behind this brief.

Frequently Asked Questions

What happened at the hearing on the White House press ban on 23 September?

Judge Timothy J. Kelly of the United States District Court for the District of Columbia, appointed by Trump, heard the emergency request on Wednesday afternoon from CNN, MS NOW, the cable channel formerly called MSNBC, and Politico to restore their reporters’ access. He began with fair procedure rather than free speech, telling both sides that the notice the law requires “wasn’t played out here”, CNN reports. The newsrooms’ lawyer, Theodore Boutrous, said national security was raised only after the lawsuit. “All of the sudden this is a national security case,” he said. Justice Department lawyer Michael Velchik asked that the passes not be restored until after Xi Jinping’s visit. The hearing ended without a ruling; Kelly said he would “try to get an answer as soon as I can”, so a decision is expected at any time. When this desk last read CNN’s live coverage at 22.41 UTC on Wednesday, CNN reported that he “did not issue an immediate ruling”.

Does the Greenland agreement give the United States control of the island?

No. Trump told the General Assembly on 22 September that a deal with Denmark gives the United States “permanent control over security and all other needs” in Greenland, NBC News reported. The text was signed that day in New York by Trump, Denmark’s Mette Frederiksen and Greenland’s Jens-Frederik Nielsen. It reaffirms “the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Denmark” and recognises Greenlanders’ “right to self-determination”, the Associated Press reports. It lets the United States expand at Pituffik Space Base and create “defense areas” elsewhere, and bars non-NATO states from military installations. It has no end date, but it enters into force only once the parliamentary processes of Denmark, together with Greenland, are complete.

What do the new American polls say about the midterm elections of 3 November?

A poll by SSRS for CNN, taken from 16 to 17 September among 1,206 adults, was published on 23 September. It finds 44 per cent of registered voters calling their congressional vote a message of opposition to Trump, against 19 per cent for support — a high for an incumbent president back to George W. Bush, CNN says. Democrats lead the congressional vote by 49 to 41 per cent, narrower than the 12-point lead CNN found in its September polling before the 2018 midterm elections, and about a quarter of Americans approve of each party in Congress. Just 27 per cent approve of Trump on the economy and 20 per cent on inflation. The margin of sampling error is 3.5 points overall and 4.1 points among registered voters.

Why is British Columbia holding an election on 24 October?

Premier David Eby, whose New Democratic Party is the centre-left party governing the Pacific province, asked Lieutenant-Governor Wendy Cocchia to dissolve the legislature on Tuesday 22 September, the Canadian Press reports. He called the moment an “existential” one and named the American president more than twenty times. “When you smell smoke you don’t sit and wait to see what happens next,” he said. He governs on the one-seat majority he won at the 2024 election, and his opponents united within two hours, with seven legislators from CentreBC, the breakaway caucus that split from the British Columbia Conservatives, rejoining that party. Their interim leader Lorne Doerkson said: “I think David Eby is going to regret this.”

Sources: CNN, NPR, PBS News carrying the Associated Press, NBC News, the Press Democrat of Santa Rosa, California carrying the Associated Press, and the White House briefing page. Then the Canadian Press through BNN Bloomberg and the Chronicle-Journal of Thunder Bay, the Prime Minister’s Office in Ottawa, Global News, the Hill Times and the Bank of Canada. Canadian-dollar amounts are converted at the Bank of Canada daily average rate for 23 September, C$1.4096 to the US dollar. The one market figure printed, November West Texas Intermediate at US$92.16 a barrel, is Wednesday 23 September’s New York settlement, taken after the 20.00 UTC close; Tuesday’s closes did not verify, so no change on the day is printed anywhere. The desk last checked for a ruling from Judge Kelly at 22.41 UTC on Wednesday, and CNN reported that he “did not issue an immediate ruling”. The account of the welcome at Joint Base Andrews follows the Associated Press’s copy filed after the greeting, not its morning preview. No Chinese source was read today, so the account of the state visit is an American one. Reporting window 22–23 September 2026.

Asia Intelligence Brief — Wednesday, 23 September 2026

The National Diet, Japan’s parliament, in Tokyo. Sanae Takaichi came away from her meeting with Donald Trump in New York with warm words and no document.
