World.title: Honduras Adopts El Salvador-Style Prison Measures Against Gangs
World.content:
Yesterday, Honduras adopted measures that tighten prison conditions, similar to those imposed by the government of Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele, as part of a strategy against gangs and drug trafficking. Gangs such as Barrio 18 and its archrival Mara Salvatrucha operate in Honduras and have been linked to drug trafficking and the country’s high homicide rate of 24 per 100,000 inhabitants, four times the global average.

The prison restrictions approved by Congress, at the request of the right-wing government of President Nasry Asfura, follow last Friday’s designation of several criminal groups, including gangs, as terrorist organizations. The measures are aimed at isolating high-risk prisoners and eliminating alternatives to imprisonment for alleged members of those criminal organizations.

The package amends the Criminal Procedure Code and establishes that suspected members of those groups will be sent to maximum-security prisons following their arrest. It also stipulates that prisoners belonging to those criminal groups will be allowed only one hour of sunlight and outdoor time, either individually or in small groups of no more than two people.

The measures also call for the creation of specialized courts dedicated exclusively to cases involving members of those groups. The provisions were approved on the same day that Shield of the Americas, the Washington-led regional anti-drug alliance, announced an agreement to combat around 20 criminal organizations across the region.

Bukele’s anti-gang campaign, which has reduced homicides to historic lows, has been carried out under a state of exception that has led to the imprisonment of about 92,000 people without judicial warrants since 2022. Asfura, an ally of U.S. President Donald Trump, took office in January with reducing crime as one of his main objectives.

World.title: ‘If there’s a vacancy, definitely I’ll take that’: Darrell Bradley says he is prepared to lead UDP
World.content:
‘If there’s a vacancy, definitely I’ll take that’: Darrell Bradley says he is prepared to lead UDP

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Former Belize City Mayor Darrell Bradley says he would be prepared to take over leadership of the United Democratic Party if the position becomes vacant, while insisting he is not presently campaigning against Opposition Leader Tracy Taegar Panton.

Appearing on Channel 7’s Uncut with Jules Vasquez, Bradley was pressed on whether he would leave his current studies in Canada and return to Belize to lead the UDP if Panton’s leadership were to become untenable.

“If there’s a vacancy in the leadership of the UDP, definitely I’ll take that,” Bradley said. He later said he is actively working toward making a contribution at the “top level” of national politics, describing himself as “an option” for the party rather than declaring that he must become leader.

Bradley repeatedly stressed, however, that he has no personal quarrel with Panton. He said he communicates with her regularly, met with her within the past two weeks and wants to see the UDP unified rather than divided.

Bradley also revealed that he remains in frequent communication with former UDP leader Shyne Barrow. Asked directly whether he was working in tandem with Barrow, Bradley said the two do not speak every day but are in “frequent communication.” He used his relationships with both Barrow and Panton to reject suggestions that he is aligned with one faction of the UDP against another, saying there is “no division” between himself and Panton and that his focus is on bringing people together.

Later in the interview, Bradley also praised Barrow personally, describing him as a “tremendously remarkable individual” who had overcome significant adversity and saying that Barrow still has something to offer the UDP, even if that does not necessarily mean serving as its leader. Barrow, who previously served as UDP Leader and Leader of the Opposition, has remained politically active and has continued publicly commenting on the direction of the party since leaving its leadership.

Panton remains Leader of the Opposition and UDP leader. Bradley said his conversations with various elements of the party are aimed at rebuilding the UDP around what he described as a reform agenda focused on cost of living, organizational strength, new candidates and stronger leadership.

There is also a constitutional hurdle for Bradley. The UDP Constitution requires its party leader to be a member of the National Assembly, an issue that has affected Bradley before. He previously sought the UDP leadership while serving as President of the Senate.

Bradley, who served two terms as Belize City Mayor, said he intends to return to electoral politics but again declined during the interview to identify the constituency in which he would run.

Throughout the interview, he maintained that rebuilding the UDP cannot depend on a single “savior,” but said he believes he can help provide the organization, communication and unifying approach needed to make the party competitive again.

World.title: One detained, licensed .223 rifle seized after Alfred Mahler shot in Maya Ranch area
World.content:
One detained, licensed .223 rifle seized after Alfred Mahler shot in Maya Ranch area

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police have detained one person and seized a licensed semi-automatic rifle as they investigate a shooting in the Maya Ranch area of western Belize on Wednesday afternoon.

According to preliminary information, sometime between 1:00 p.m. and 1:30 p.m. on September 23, 2026, Alfred Mahler and another man were inspecting land in the Maya Ranch area when they were approached by persons in a grey pickup truck.

Police say the two men were subsequently followed along Pine Ridge Road by a red pickup truck, from which shots were reportedly fired. Mahler was struck by gunfire, while the red pickup fled the scene.

Investigators have since detained one person in connection with the incident and seized his licensed .223 semi-automatic rifle. Mahler is receiving medical treatment. Police have not yet disclosed the extent of his injuries or identified the detained individual.

The shooting comes against the backdrop of a contentious land dispute at Maya Ranch involving local farmers and Maya Ranch Limited. Farmers have gone to court claiming rights to portions of the property through years of occupation and cultivation, while records previously reported by Channel 7 show the property is titled to Maya Ranch Limited.

Tensions in the area have previously turned violent. In March, Police Sergeant Dalon Kelly was shot while responding to a disturbance at Maya Ranch, and farmer Dan Lopez was subsequently charged with attempted murder, use of deadly means of harm and grievous harm. More recently, on September 4, farmers were involved in a heated confrontation with developer Nigel Petillo, who said he had been hired to work on behalf of the property’s owner.

Police have not indicated whether Wednesday’s shooting is connected to the ongoing land dispute, and say no further information is available at this time.

World.title: Second suspect remanded in $8,214 Crooked Tree armed robbery
World.content:
Second suspect remanded in $8,214 Crooked Tree armed robbery

By Breaking Belize News Staff: An 18-year-old Belize City man has become the second person charged in connection with the armed robbery of a businessman in Crooked Tree earlier this month.

Tyler Dominguez, of Flamboyant Street, appeared in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Wednesday, September 23, where he was read a single charge of robbery.

Police allege that Dominguez, along with 26-year-old Tafaree Rohan Sanchez and others, carried out the robbery on September 2 while armed with a firearm.

The alleged victim was reportedly robbed of $800 in cash, three bottles of Johnnie Walker Black Label rum, three iPhones and two Toyota Hilux pickup truck keys. The total value of the cash and property was reported at approximately $8,214.

Dominguez, who turned 18 on August 31, is facing his first reported criminal allegation as an adult.

Sanchez, a call center agent, was the first suspect charged in connection with the incident. He was arraigned on September 8, pleaded not guilty and was remanded to the Belize Central Prison.

Dominguez was likewise remanded to prison and now joins Sanchez behind bars while the case proceeds through the court.

Both men are expected to return to the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on November 13, 2026.

World.title: Woman 7 months pregnant with twins released from prison after 1 night; Minister Gilroy Usher donates $100 to $155 fine, Ladyville Highlights getting her help
World.content:
Woman 7 months pregnant with twins released from prison after 1 night; Minister Gilroy Usher donates $100 to $155 fine, Ladyville Highlights getting her help

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A seven-month pregnant mother expecting twin boys is free today after spending a night at the Belize Central Prison because she was unable to pay an outstanding $155 court fine dating back to 2025.

Thirty-five-year-old Leeann Monique Samuels was released on Wednesday after Port Loyola Area Representative and Minister of State Gilroy Usher contributed $100 toward clearing the outstanding fine through Ladyville Highlights, while the balance was covered with assistance from the organization and its founder, Albert Magdaleno.

Samuels had been taken to prison on Tuesday after appearing in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on a new charge of possession of utensils used for smoking a controlled drug. Police alleged that they found her with a silver pipe measuring approximately 3¼ inches during a search at a Belize City residence.

Samuels initially pleaded guilty; however, after the police facts were read to her, she disputed a key part of the allegation, telling the court that the pipe had not been in her hand as police claimed. She said the object was beneath the chair where she had been sitting and fell when she stood up.

Because her explanation amounted to a denial of the prosecution’s facts, the Magistrate treated the guilty plea as equivocal and entered a not guilty plea on her behalf. Samuels was offered bail of $400 plus one surety, but an outstanding $155 fine from August 2025 prevented her release.

Unable to pay the old fine, a warrant was prepared and Samuels was sent to the Belize Central Prison. Her imprisonment came on the fourth birthday of her first set of twins, two girls.

The case returned before the Chief Magistrate on Wednesday morning, when a support officer from the Women’s Department was also brought into court. The Chief Magistrate subsequently dismissed the new possession-of-utensils charge against Samuels. No reason for the dismissal was stated in court.

Attention then shifted from prosecution to getting Samuels support ahead of the birth of her twin boys, who are expected in November. The court discussed assistance for the expectant mother and her children, and Samuels was eventually released into the care of the Women’s Department support officer and Magdaleno.

According to Magdaleno, Usher contacted him Wednesday morning and offered $100 toward Samuels’ outstanding court debt after learning that she had been remanded because she could not pay the $155.

Usher is the PUP Area Representative for Port Loyola and currently serves as Minister of State in the Ministry of Public Utilities, Energy and Logistics.

Ladyville Highlights, operated by Albert and Fiona Magdaleno, has previously assisted Belizean families facing medical, housing and financial difficulties by using its social media platform to connect people in need with donors.

After one night behind bars, Samuels walked out of court a free woman, with efforts now focused on securing assistance for her and her unborn twins.

World.title: Belizeans are encouraged to stay cool with Winchester air conditioners
World.content:
Belizeans are encouraged to stay cool with Winchester air conditioners

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): With Belize’s warm weather making air conditioning an important part of many homes and businesses, Belizeans are reminded that Winchester air conditioners are available at various hardware stores across the country.

The Winchester brand is being promoted under the message, “Stay Cool with Winchester.”

Customers looking to cool bedrooms, living spaces, offices or other areas can visit any retail store that sells hardware or household appliances and inquire about available Winchester air conditioning units.

The units are distributed in Belize by Nando’s Wholesale LLP, giving customers a local option when shopping for cooling solutions.

World.title: Woman robbed of purse and cellphone while walking in Trial Farm
World.content:
Woman robbed of purse and cellphone while walking in Trial Farm

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Police in Orange Walk are investigating a theft reported by a 37 year old woman who says two men approached her from behind while she was walking along Flamingo Street in Trial Farm Village on Monday night.

According to police information, the woman was walking with her aunt at around 9:30 p.m. on September 21 when two Hispanic men reportedly came up behind them.

Police say one of the men was walking while the other was riding a small beach cruiser bicycle.

The man who was on foot allegedly grabbed the woman’s white sling purse before both men fled the area.

The purse reportedly contained three Social Security cards, several bank and credit cards, and a Tecno Digi cellphone.

The woman told police that one of the suspects was wearing a white cap, white T shirt and black short pants and was approximately 5 feet 5 inches tall. She could not recall how the second man was dressed.

After the incident, the woman reportedly ran to a nearby shop and asked for assistance. The shop owner contacted the Trial Farm Police Sub Station, and she was later assisted in making a report.

Police say the matter remains under investigation.

World.title: Benque Viejo man says longtime friend stole his cellphone from verandah
World.content:
Benque Viejo man says longtime friend stole his cellphone from verandah

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Police in Benque Viejo Town are investigating a theft complaint after a 50 year old man reported that his cellphone went missing from his verandah shortly after a longtime acquaintance visited his home.

According to police information, the complainant was at his residence on Providence Street at around 8:00 p.m. on Sunday, September 20, when a man he had known for about 30 years arrived at his home.

The two reportedly sat on the front verandah before the complainant told the visitor to leave.

Police say the complainant then went inside to use the bathroom, leaving his cellphone on a chair.

When he returned, the phone was gone.

The missing device was described as a black touchscreen Alcatel cellphone valued at $100.

The complainant told police he would be able to identify the phone if it is recovered and requested court action.

Police identified the person named in the complaint as Luban Salazar.

The matter remains under investigation.

World.title: Woman says relatives took her dog and never returned it
World.content:
Woman says relatives took her dog and never returned it

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Police at the Raccoon Street Police Station are investigating a theft report involving a missing dog.

According to police information, a 30 year old woman reported that on August 8, her children went outside to play from their home near Mile 1½ on the George Price Highway.

The family dog, described as light brown and responding to the name Clown, reportedly followed the children outside and later went missing.

The woman told police that on September 22, two of her nieces visited her home while selling cosmetics.

When she questioned them about the dog, they allegedly admitted that they had taken the animal at the request of their mother.

The complainant said she, along with other family members, made efforts to recover the dog but were unsuccessful.

She later visited the Raccoon Street Police Station and made a formal report.

Police say the woman did not request court action.

World.title: MINING MESS
World.content:
Mining and quarrying operation in progress Stock photo

THREE mining companies owed the Government penalties to the tune of US$13.7 million (approximately $2.2 billion) at the end of 2025 after they failed to rehabilitate 264.14 hectares of mined-out land as required by law.

At the same time, the March 2026 Schedule of the Mines and Geology Division (MGD) of the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries identified US$828,000 in royalty principal and US$2.58 million in interest and penalties outstanding from two operators.

These are among the key findings of a performance audit by the Auditor General’s Department (AGD) dated July 2026, of the licensing, monitoring and enforcement actions of the MGD.

The audit report was tabled in the House of Representatives on Tuesday.

Auditor General Pamela Monroe Ellis noted in her overview that the MGD is responsible for regulating the sector under the Mining Act of 1947 and the Quarries Control Act 1984, to ensure that mining and quarrying operations are properly authorised, monitored, and enforced in keeping with the law and the public interest.

The audit found that one lessee accounted for 169.68 hectares (64 per cent of the area not rehabilitated) and US$9.89 million (72 per cent of the total monetary exposure).

“The weaknesses in enforcement were linked to the absence of a single, auditable, rehabilitation register; non-use of the security deposit mechanism during the review period, and the absence of finalised rehabilitation guidelines for quarries.

“Consequently, MGD could not demonstrate that all lease renewals were supported by the required information, reducing assurance that operators had the financial capacity to meet their obligations, and that Government had adequate protection, through the security deposit, against future rehabilitation or restoration costs,” said Monroe Ellis.

She added, “The long-outstanding rehabilitation obligations remained unresolved, and MGD could not demonstrate that the polluter-pays principle embedded in Sections 53A–55 of the Mining Regulations was being effectively enforced.”

Monroe Ellis said the audit assessed whether MGD’s licensing, monitoring, and enforcement arrangements were effective in supporting orderly and compliant mining and quarrying operations for the period 2019-2020 to 2023-2024.

“In particular, the audit examined whether applications were properly assessed before approval, inspection activities were adequately planned and targeted, breaches were followed up in a timely and consistent manner, and whether MGD maintained reliable records to support regulatory decisions,” she explained.

Among the other key findings was that one operator continued mining for six years after its licence had expired, in breach of Sections 25 and 31 of the Mining Act and Section 8 of the Quarries Control Act.

Monroe Ellis also found that six quarry operators continued operations after their quarry licences had expired. Five of them submitted renewal applications between 30 and approximately 607 days after expiry, while one submitted no renewal application.

“MGD also did not consistently issue reminder notices before licences ended, or take timely enforcement action after expiry. Continued operation beyond the authorised licence period weakened the licensing regime; reduced the deterrent effect of enforcement; and increased risks related to revenue collection, environmental oversight, and public confidence in the regulatory system,” said Monroe Ellis.

She also pointed out that mining leases were renewed without key documents, and the resulting risk materialised in unenforced rehabilitation obligations.

The auditor general explained that the Mining Act, and the Mining Regulations, require that lease renewals be supported by current financial statements, evidence of public notice to allow objections, and security deposits or letters of guarantee sufficient to protect the Government against rehabilitation or restoration costs.

“The regulations also require mined-out lands to be rehabilitated within the prescribed time frame; with statutory tools such as security deposits, restoration bonds, and penalty assessments to be used to enforce rehabilitation obligations.”

According to the audit, of the eight active operators reviewed, only four submitted up to date financial statements, two submitted none, and two submitted outdated statements.

“Further, there was evidence of public notice being issued for only four of the eight leases. In addition, four of the operators that were non-bauxite entities did not provide the required security deposits.”

Monroe Ellis said MGD advised that the security deposit requirement had been relaxed to promote investment but did not provide documented approval for this concession.

The audit also found that quarry inspections were not guided by a documented risk-based approach.

Said Monroe Ellis: “Good practice for regulatory oversight requires that inspection activities be guided by a documented, risk-based methodology. MGD’s own operational plans and the Quarries Control Act envisage inspection frequency and priorities being determined by risk factors such as size of operation, environmental sensitivity, compliance history and complaints, with inspection targets assigned and monitored.”

Yet, MGD did not have a documented method for prioritising quarry inspections, and managed only 243 inspections in fiscal year 2022/23 against a target of 400.

According to the audit, royalty arrears and quarry tax obligations were not systematically tracked.

It said MGD did not maintain accurate records on the status of royalty payments and quarry taxes, and the records were not reconciled in a timely manner.

Alarmingly, the audit also found that enforcement records were incomplete, even while MGD’s standard operating procedures require the maintenance of complete and reliable records of enforcement action, including reported breaches, investigations, referrals, corrective action, and outcomes.

“We could not confirm that enforcement action was consistently pursued for 14 of the 15 illegal quarrying cases recorded in MGD’s complaints register,” said Monroe Ellis. She outlined that nine police reports were reviewed; however, only one matched an entry in the register and showed evidence of follow-up actions.

World.title: Chuck to meet with protesting lawyers over Firearms Act discontent
World.content:
Several members of the Jamaican Bar Association and the Advocates’ Association in association with bar associations across the island armed with placards outside the Supreme Court on King Street in downtown Kingston Wednesday morning demanding that their concerns about the Firearms (Prohibition, Restriction and Regulation) Act, 2022 be addressed through meaningful reforms. (Photo: Karl Mclarty)

JUSTICE Minister Delroy Chuck on Wednesday voiced disappointment with the protest action taken by members of the defence bar to show discontent with the 2022 Firearms Act, but said it is hoped that a meeting scheduled for 2:00 pm today will help stave off further plans by the attorneys to abandon the courts all of next week if their demands are not met.

“I am really disappointed that members of the Jamaican Bar Association and the Advocates’ Association have taken the action today by demonstrating around the Supreme Court. On Sunday, September 13 during the Assize service I indicated that the matter was under consideration and told the association that I was prepared to meet with them,” the justice minister said.

In referencing the pending meeting today, he said the “government is very concerned about the prevalence of gun crimes and the need to protect law-abiding citizens of this country but remains open to dialogue on the Firearms Act 2022”.

Wednesday, members of the Jamaican Bar Association and the Advocates’ Association in association with bar associations across the island, armed with placards, demanded that their concerns about the Firearms (Prohibition, Restriction and Regulation) Act, 2022 and its impact on “justice, due process, and the rule of law” be taken on board for reform.

The protest came just over a week after the justice minister’s comments at the annual Assize Service of the judiciary. Chuck, in his statements which evoked inflamed commentary from several quarters, said while the mandatory minimum sentences contained in the provision were being reviewed because of widespread concerns, “the security forces and a number of my colleagues feel that the Act is working and it is bringing down murders and shootings”.

“It is under consideration, but firearms are a major problem in our country, and that is why we don’t want to send a signal that we are going to relent on the enforcement to condemn the possession and the use of firearms. But it is under consideration,” the justice minister said then.

A week later, Saturday, September 19, members of Jamaica’s legal profession met to consider what they described as “the operation and impact of the Firearms (Prohibition, Restriction and Regulation) Act, 2022, particularly its mandatory sentencing provisions and the restrictions placed on judicial discretion”.

In a statement issued following that meeting, the attorneys said, “The legal profession supports strong and effective laws to combat gun violence and punish those who use illegal firearms to murder, rob, terrorise and intimidate our citizens. Our concern is not with strong penalties. Our concern is with a sentencing regime that does not adequately allow judges to distinguish between offenders, offences, and individual circumstances.”

The Firearms (Prohibition, Restriction and Regulation) Act, 2022, which prescribes a mandatory 15-year sentence for violations, took effect in November 2022 and, among other things, provides penalties ranging from 15 years to life imprisonment for possession of illegal weapons, and establishes a dual regime — distinguishing between prohibited weapons or unregulated firearms and connected activities and firearms that are duly authorised or registered.

According to the advocates, their meeting on Saturday “identified several areas of serious concern, including the restriction of judicial discretion; the proportionality of mandatory minimum sentences in individual cases; the diminished incentive for early guilty pleas; the resulting increase in matters proceeding to trial and pressure on an already burdened criminal justice system; the treatment of imitation firearms; and the consequences of certain provisions for licensed firearm holders”.

“The legal profession is calling for urgent amendments to the Act, including consideration of an ‘exceptional circumstances’ provision allowing judges appropriate discretion in deserving cases, meaningful sentencing incentives for early guilty pleas, reform of the certificate regime, and a review of the provisions governing imitation firearms and licensed firearm holders. The profession also calls for urgent, structured consultation with the Government, Opposition, Parliament, judiciary, and other relevant stakeholders on the proposed amendments,” the attorneys said in that statement.

Noting that the “concerns are not new” as members of the legal profession and civil society have “written, spoken publicly and proposed amendments”, the professionals said “the time has now come for action”.

They said following those extensive discussions, the meeting resolved to pursue collective action, including a silent protest outside the Supreme Court on Wednesday, September 23 followed by the withdrawal of legal services from criminal courts for one week commencing Monday, September 28.

Wednesday’s protest action was, however, not sanctioned by all segments of the defence bar, with some attorneys voicing discontent over the method employed.

One attorney, in a biting commentary on a social media platform, said while he understood the reason for the concern, professional associations are expected to maintain a high level of discourse without resorting to making public spectacles.

Yesterday, attorney Tamika Harris, a member of the Bar Council of the Jamaican Bar Association and chair of its Criminal Practice and Procedure Subcommittee who was a key figure behind the protest, said the meeting this afternoon will inform the posture of defence attorneys in the island’s courts next week.

World.title: ‘I felt like a fool’
World.content:
File photo shows Pastor Kevin Smith in worship. A witness on the stand in the Home Circuit Court said Wednesday that he was responsible for shearing the pastor’s head, helping him get dressed for church services, and carrying his Bible to the pulpit.

A witness huffed and puffed on Wednesday in the Home Circuit Court murder trial of Andre Ruddock in Kingston as defence attorney Anthony Williams cross-examined him about how he felt when his now-deceased pastor, Dr Kevin Smith, pushed his fingers into gunshot wounds he received in his back that were allegedly inflicted by the preacher.

Ruddock is on trial for murder in relation to the October 17, 2021 killing of Taneka Gardner at the Kingdom Restoration Ministries International in Albion, St James. Smith was the pastor of the church and the witness who is on the stand said he was responsible for shearing the pastor’s head, helping him get dressed for church services, and carrying his Bible to the pulpit. Ruddock’s duties surrounded providing security for Smith.

After trying to avoid the question about how he felt at the time of the incident, the witness eventually told the court that he felt like a fool. He told the court previously that Smith shot him twice in the back and assured him that he was immortal and could not die. He said that while he was in pain on the ground after being shot, Smith walked over to him and stuffed his fingers into the gunshot wounds. The witness also claimed that he was stabbed in the back by another member of the church, who was acting on Smith’s orders.

Williams asked the witness to confirm that he told prosecutors during the trial which began last week, that he was shot in the back by Smith.

“That is correct,” the witness responded.

Williams then prompted him to explain again what he told prosecutors took place after he was shot twice in the back by Smith.

“You said he also used his hands to do what?” Smith asked.

“He pushed his fingers in the wound. I am more than positive [that happened]. I know for a fact, sir,” the witness said.

The attorney asked him how long the pastor had his fingers in his wounds.

The witness, who had a perturbed look on his face, told Williams that he did not know.

It was at the point when Williams began to ask the witness to explain how he felt while Smith was pushing his fingers in his wounds, that the witness started huffing and puffing.

That caused an angry look on his face and a piercing and penetrating gaze at the attorney. He appeared very uncomfortable.

The witness asked the attorney if he could please “move forward from that question”.

Williams expressed to him that that was not how it worked in court and pressed him to answer the question. The witness’ refusal to comply sparked the intervention of Judge Leighton Pusey who called his name, trying to get his attention. It was only after Pusey called his name a few times, that the witness decided to look at the judge.

Instead of scolding the witness, Pusey asked Williams if it was possible to come back to the question at another time during the cross-examination to get the witness to compose himself.

However, Williams expressed to the judge that the questions that were to follow had the potential of making the witness even more uncomfortable and recommended that it was better if the witness simply answered the question.

Pusey instructed the witness that he should try his best to answer the questions that Williams was posing.

The attorney then made another attempt.

“How did you feel?” Williams asked.

“I felt like a fool,” the witness answered.

Williams probed whether he said anything to the pastor while he was pushing his fingers in his wounds.

He told the attorney that he did not, and explained that he was in pain.

Williams asked the witness about the reasons for him not making mention in any of his four statements to the police that Smith had stuck his fingers in the wound.

“You gave four statements to the police. I am suggesting to you that you never told the police in any of those statements that the pastor used his finger and stick in the wound. Do you agree?” Williams asked.

“I don’t remember if I did or not,” the witness said.

He told the attorney that the events which unfolded at the church happened five years ago and that he didn’t carry thoughts about it in his head.

“I don’t want to remember. These were very traumatic events that unfolded in my life,” he said.

The attorney found it difficult to understand why even after telling the police on different occasions that he had amendments made to his multiple statements, he failed to mention anything about the pastor’s fingers in his wounds.

“My suggestion is that the reason why you did not mention it in your first statement about the pastor sticking his fingers in your wounds was because that never happened. You agree?” Williams asked.

“I disagree,” the witness said.

“I am suggesting to you that you are lying,” Williams told the witness, prompting an objection from lead prosecutor LaToya Bernard.

Williams further suggested to the witness that he was not shot by Smith, but by members of the security forces.

The witness disagreed.

“I am suggesting to you that you went to your bus and took out an illegal gun that you had in your bus and came back to where the pastor was and fired shots at the police,” Williams said, to which the witness responded in disagreement.

Williams continued, “I am suggesting to you that it was the police in carrying out their lawful duties, returned fire and shot you. It wasn’t the pastor man who shot you”.

Again, the witness disagreed.

“I suggest that not only were you firing at the police, you fired as a faithful servant to your pastor who was also firing at the police,” the attorney said.

Again, the witness disagreed.

The trial continues today.

World.title: Jackie Jackson, legendary Jamaican bass guitarist, dies at 79
World.content:
Jackie Jackson

Clifton “Jackie” Jackson, the legendary bass guitarist who played on countless hit songs by artistes such as Toots And The Maytals, Jimmy Cliff and Paul Simon, died in Montego Bay on Wednesday.

Jackson, 79, was admitted to the Cornwall Regional Hospital in St James recently. He was a fixture on the Montego Bay hotel scene for many years, mentoring artistes and musicians including his wife, Karen Smith, who died in 2021.

From Central Kingston, Jackson got his start in the mid-1960s at the Treasure Isle recording studio of producer Duke Reid. He was a member of The Supersonics, the house band that played on numerous hit singles including Girl I’ve Got A Date by Alton Ellis, Little Nut Tree by The Melodians and Queen Majesty by The Techniques.

Jackson also played on classic songs for producer Leslie Kong, such as Israelites by Desmond Dekker and The Aces, By The Rivers of Babylon by The Melodians as well as The Harder They Come and Wonderful World, Beautiful People by Jimmy Cliff.

In 1972, Jackson and fellow Jamaican musicians including guitarist Hux Brown and keyboardist Neville Hinds played on Simon’s Mother And Child Reunion, which is from the American singer’s debut album released that year.

Some of Jackson’s best work was done with Toots And The Maytals with whom he toured for 50 years. His patented sound can be heard on that group’s biggest hits which include Pressure Drop, Funky Kingston and Sweet And Dandy.

At the Back-2-Bass-es show last February at the Edna Manley College of the Visual and Performing Arts in St Andrew, Jackson told the Observer Online that it is important to teach Jamaican youth about reggae’s history.

“Mentoring the younger generation is paramount to our music industry. The beautiful thing about the music I’ve played over the years, is that it will always be there to provide inspiration for more generations to come; and that is something I can be really proud of,” he said.

That event featured fellow bassists Boris Gardiner, Lloyd Parks, Daniel “Danny Axeman” Thompson, Donald “Danny Bassie” Dennis and Errol “Flabba Holt” Carter.

In 2012, Jackie Jackson was awarded the Order of Distinction for his contribution to the development of Jamaican music.

World.title: Seprod surges 20% as company seeks approval for 5-for-1 stock split
World.content:
The Seprod Group headquarters in Kingston.

SEPROD Limited’s share price surged nearly 20 per cent Wednesday after the manufacturing and distribution group announced plans to restructure its share capital, including a proposed five-for-one stock split and a resolution authorising the company to raise fresh equity.

The stock was trading at $77.99, up $12.86, or about 19.7 per cent, with 166,914 shares changing hands.

The movement follows Seprod’s announcement that it has called an extraordinary general meeting for shareholders to vote on three proposals: increasing the number of shares the company is authorised to issue, splitting every existing share into five, and giving its board authority to issue new shares in the future, including through an additional public offering, or APO.

Seprod already has about 910.9 million shares in issue against its current authorised limit of one billion shares, leaving relatively little room to issue additional stock under its present structure.

The first proposal would therefore increase the number of shares Seprod is authorised to issue from one billion to 1.9 billion.

Based on approximately 910.9 million shares currently in issue, the five-for-one split of the shares already held by investors would increase that number to roughly 4.55 billion units.

Importantly, that does not by itself make an investor five times richer. Someone holding 100 Seprod shares before the split would instead hold 500 shares afterwards, while retaining the same percentage ownership of the company immediately following the split. The market price of each share would normally adjust lower to reflect the much larger number of shares in circulation.

At Wednesday’s price of $77.99, for example, a straight five-for-one adjustment would put the theoretical share price at about $15.60, assuming nothing else changed.

So an investor with 100 shares worth $7,799 before the split would have 500 shares worth roughly the same $7,799 immediately after it. The practical effect is that Seprod shares would be available in smaller denominations, potentially making individual units more affordable to investors who may find the current price relatively high.

Further, the split itself would not provide Seprod with any new money. But that’s where the third resolution becomes important.

Seprod is also seeking shareholder approval to allow its board to issue new shares in the future, including through an APO. Seprod has not said that an APO is imminent or disclosed how much it might seek to raise. The proposal instead gives the board the ability to issue new equity should it decide additional capital is required.

Chairman P B Scott said the measures are intended to give the company more room to strengthen its finances and pursue further growth.

“Over the past four years we have built the Caribbean’s largest integrated manufacturing and distribution platform for food, pharmaceuticals and premium beverages. We are now focused on integrating our businesses and strengthening our balance sheet,” Scott said in a press statement.

He added that the resolutions would provide Seprod with “greater flexibility” as it pursues those objectives and future growth opportunities.

The proposals come as Seprod continues to work through softer sales but improved profitability.

For the six months ended June 30, group revenue declined three per cent to $72.93 billion from $75.18 billion a year earlier, while net profit climbed 62 per cent to $2.34 billion. The company said the result included a gain from the disposal of International Biscuits Limited.

During the April-to-June quarter alone, revenue fell three per cent to $36.51 billion, largely due to weaker demand from Jamaica’s tourism sector as some hotels continued to operate with reduced room availability or delayed reopening following Hurricane Melissa.

Despite the lower sales, quarterly net profit increased 16 per cent to $688 million, compared with $592 million in the corresponding period last year.

The group has also been reducing debt. Seprod said cash flow generated during the first half allowed it to cut debt by more than $3 billion while declaring $551 million in dividends.

Its financial statements show long-term liabilities declining to approximately $38.1 billion at June 30, from $41.1 billion at the end of December, while stockholders’ equity increased to $50.52 billion from $49.71 billion.

The company has said its priorities for the remainder of the year include debt reduction, regional integration, improving operations and completing capital projects at its manufacturing plants.

Shareholders will vote on the proposed changes at a virtual extraordinary general meeting scheduled for October 12 at noon.

– Karena Bennett

World.title: Dr Gabrielle Henry sues Miss Universe organisation over 2025 fall
World.content:
Miss Universe Jamaica 2025 Gabrielle Henry .

Former Miss Universe Jamaica Dr Gabrielle Henry has filed a lawsuit against the Miss Universe Organisation and two of its parent companies, nearly a year after she fell from the pageant stage during the 2025 Miss Universe competition in Thailand.

PEOPLE magazine reported that Henry filed the lawsuit on Monday, September 21, in Delaware Superior Court, bringing five claims against the defendants, including negligence, premises liability, negligent hiring, retention and supervision, and negligent and intentional infliction of emotional distress.

According to the complaint, Henry was following rehearsed choreography during the preliminary competition on November 19, 2025, when she fell about five feet through an “unmarked and uncovered opening in the stage”. The suit alleges that the opening contained lighting equipment and concrete.

Henry also alleges that intense lighting directed towards her during her rehearsed walk impaired her visibility and contributed to the fall.

According to the lawsuit, Henry lost consciousness upon impact and suffered a traumatic brain injury, including acute subarachnoid haemorrhage, frontal lobe haemorrhagic contusion and subdural haemorrhage. She was hospitalised from November 19 to December 10, 2025.

The complaint describes the incident as the “most traumatic moment” of Henry’s life and alleges that the media attention surrounding the fall caused continuing emotional distress in addition to the effects of her physical injuries.

READ: Miss Jamaica Universe withdraws from pageant after suffering head injury in fall

Henry, who was practising as an ophthalmologist at the time, alleges that her injuries prevented her from resuming her medical residency and have resulted in ongoing neurological and cognitive symptoms requiring continued care, rehabilitation and follow-up.

The lawsuit further alleges that other contestants had raised concerns about the lighting and staging conditions. It claims that following Henry’s fall, the stage was modified to add bright white lights along its edge, PEOPLE reported.

In a statement to PEOPLE, the Miss Universe Organisation said it had not been served with, nor received, any lawsuit, claim, demand letter or subpoena from Henry or anyone acting on her behalf and therefore could not comment on claims it had not seen.

The organisation said the host and production entities, Miss Grand International (MGI) and Miss Universe Thailand, under the direction of Nawat Itsaragrisil, were responsible for producing the 74th Miss Universe competition, including the venue, stage, and on-site safety.

It also said it had paid Henry’s hospital expenses after the incident, despite having no obligation to do so, and later covered her treatment at a specialised hospital in Jamaica following her return home.

The organisation said it had not received any further request for medical expenses and had also offered Henry a position as a goodwill ambassador on the Miss Universe team. According to the organisation, she had not responded to the offer.

Henry’s lawsuit also names MGI, which she alleges was responsible for the staging, lighting and safety arrangements for the event. It further alleges that the Miss Universe Organisation retained and exercised control over those aspects.

The complaint alleges that MGI’s failure to oversee stage safety contributed to Henry’s injuries.

According to PEOPLE, Henry also alleges that the Miss Universe Organisation failed to maintain a safe stage by leaving an opening unguarded, unmarked and unbarricaded, and by failing to identify what she describes as MGI’s unsafe staging and production practices.

The lawsuit comes nearly a year after the incident sparked public speculation about the circumstances surrounding Henry’s fall.

At the time, Miss Universe Haiti Melissa Sapini told PEOPLE that following the incident, the remaining contestants were gathered for a meeting where she alleged a staff member appeared to blame Henry for the fall.

“I don’t know that they handled that correctly,” Sapini told PEOPLE at the time, adding that the first comment made was that Henry had not been paying attention.

The Miss Universe Organisation did not respond to PEOPLE’s requests for comment on Sapini’s claims at the time.

In a December 8, 2025 statement, the organisation said it had assumed all related expenses, including accommodation, airline rebooking, transportation and support for Henry’s family.

MGI, meanwhile, told PEOPLE at the time that the incident occurred primarily because Henry had missed her blocking and may not have been looking at the runway while walking. However, the organisation said no one from MGI had blamed her.

The representative also said the runway was more than five metres wide and had clear, oversized white borders, adding that no other contestant had experienced an accident on the runway.

The Miss Universe Organisation has previously rejected suggestions that Henry was responsible for the incident, saying such claims were inaccurate, unfounded and did not reflect the facts.

World.title: Chilling confession
World.content:
Murder victim 64-year-old domestic helper Hyacinth Rose Johnson, who was also called June.

FRANKFIELD, Clarendon — Police here say a 15-year-old schoolboy has been charged with murder after he confessed to using a screwdriver to fatally stab his 64-year-old neighbour then dragged her body to hide the gruesome crime.

The victim, Hyacinth Rose Johnson, a domestic helper, was killed in Union district, Grantham, north-west Clarendon in July.

“The police continued their investigation, which led them to the arrest of this young man. He was arrested on Saturday and on Monday, while being interviewed in the presence of his mother and two justices of the peace, he confessed to using a screwdriver to stab the female to death. He indicated that he was not provoked by the female, and that he doesn’t know why he [killed] her. The incident occurred at his home, which is in front of the home of the deceased,” a police source told the Jamaica Observer Tuesday.

Police dispelled rumours that Johnson, also called June, had been sexually assaulted by her killer. Police said the teen, who is a student at a prominent high school, confessed to moving the woman’s body to the back of her house.

“We have no evidence that she was sexually assaulted. Her clothing was found in a certain position; that is why persons were of the view that she was sexually molested. She was drawn by him, in a bid to hide the crime, from his premises to another premises. In the process [her underwear] were pulled down to her ankles,” the police source said.

A police report outlined that about 7:00 am on July 1 residents of Union stumbled upon Johnson’s body at the back of her house. Police said the body had stab wounds to the chest. Five days later, placard-bearing residents dressed in red and black marched through the community, protesting Johnson’s gruesome murder.

Member of Parliament for Clarendon North Western Richard Azan said Johnson was a mother of four who lived alone.

“People are outraged about it, because June was not a person who gave trouble. June went around washing and cleaning [homes] for people. She was a hard-working churchwoman. I said it at the funeral [on August 29], and I said it at a community meeting. I said we have to find this one; that was clear in my mind and we arranged community meetings and all of that with the police and everybody,” said Azan.

“I am so disappointed that a young person could be able to [allegedly] commit a crime on someone in a community who gave service to the same community by helping other persons. She could be the grandmother of the person [accused of] committing the crime,” added Azan.

World.title: Royal Caribbean Group and Sandals Resorts announce landmark partnership
World.content:
Royal Caribbean Group Chairman and CEO Jason Liberty (left) and Sandals Resorts and Beaches Resorts Executive Chairman Adam Stewart sign the partnership agreement.

Royal Caribbean Group and Sandals Resorts on Wednesday, September 23, 2026 announced the signing of an agreement to form a partnership in the all-inclusive resort space with a 50 per cent investment from Royal Caribbean Group.

“Building on Sandals and Beaches Resorts’ more than four decades of leadership in Caribbean hospitality, the joint venture will create new opportunities for continued resort growth while broadening the experiences across Royal Caribbean Group’s vacation platform,” both entities said in a joint news release.

The partnership brings together two of the travel industry’s most celebrated vacation companies, pairing Sandals and Beaches’ all-inclusive resort expertise with Royal Caribbean Group’s vacation platform, including industry-leading brands — Royal Caribbean, Celebrity Cruises and Silversea — a portfolio of private destinations, new river cruising offering, and an industry-first loyalty programme.

“United in a shared history in the Caribbean and connected by a love for their communities, the companies will offer travellers an unparalleled collection of cruise, private destination and resort experiences, serving guests across more vacation occasions and establishing their undisputed leadership in Caribbean vacations,” the release added.

“The joint venture expands Royal Caribbean Group into an adjacent vacation category, growing its participation in the approximately US$2 trillion global vacation market, and meets the growing global demand for Sandals and Beaches Resorts by accelerating their expansion,” the release stated.

“The partnership will include Sandals and Beaches’ collection of premier all-inclusive properties across the Caribbean, and the companies will explore opportunities to broaden distribution, deepen guest engagement, and make it easier for travellers to discover vacation experiences offered across both portfolios,” they added.

“For nearly 60 years, we’ve reimagined what a vacation can be, constantly expanding the ways we inspire our guests to explore, connect and create lifelong memories,” the release quotes Royal Caribbean Group Chairman and CEO Jason Liberty.

“We have been building a vacation platform that brings joy to millions of people around the world and creates meaningful relationships that last with our guests. Our partnership with Sandals and Beaches Resorts is an important next step on that journey, bringing together two iconic leading vacation companies to further strengthen and grow one of the most admired resort portfolios in the world,” Liberty said.

“The Stewart family has created powerful and beloved brands, and we are honoured to build on that legacy. Together, we see tremendous opportunity to expand the reach of Sandals and Beaches Resorts and continue turning the vacation of a lifetime into a lifetime of vacations,” he added.

“My father, Gordon ‘Butch’ Stewart, founded Sandals Resorts with the belief that a company built in the Caribbean could stand on the world stage alongside the most respected names in hospitality. Today is proof of how far that vision can go,” said Sandals Resorts and Beaches Resorts Executive Chairman Adam Stewart.

“This partnership is the natural next step in building on that conviction. It gives us the ability to grow faster with a partner that shares our values of exceptional hospitality, long-term investment, and the power of enduring brands. Together, we will introduce more guests to Sandals and Beaches Resorts while creating even more extraordinary experiences for those who have made our resorts part of their lives for decades.” Stewart added.

“As we continue to grow, we will remain true to what has always defined us: delivering authentic vacations that exceed expectations while creating opportunities for our team members, travel advisor partners and the communities we call home. The future has never been brighter, and I know this moment would make my father incredibly proud,” Stewart said.

The joint venture will be governed by a board under the shared leadership of Stewart and Liberty. Stewart will maintain a leadership role in guiding the company’s long-term strategic growth as executive chairman of Sandals and Beaches Resorts. Existing reservations, loyalty programmes, resort operations, and cruise operations will continue as usual, with the partnership bringing additional resources to support future opportunities.

Under the terms of the agreement, Royal Caribbean Group will acquire a 50 per cent equity interest in Sandals and Beaches Resorts for approximately US$3 billion, representing a forward EBITDA multiple of approximately 10x.

Royal Caribbean Group has secured committed debt financing from Morgan Stanley to fund the investment. The transaction is expected to close in early 2027, subject to customary approvals and closing conditions, and is expected to be accretive to earnings next year.

BofA Securities and PJT Partners acted as financial advisors, and Latham & Watkins and Jones Day acted as legal advisors to the Sandals Group. Perella Weinberg Partners and Morgan Stanley acted as financial advisors and Kirkland & Ellis LLP acted as legal advisor to Royal Caribbean Group.

World.title: SONDAGE EXCLUSIF 2027. Face à Le Pen, Mélenchon et Philippe au duel, Glucksmann garde la tête hors de l’eau
World.content:
PARIS — Qui pour faire face à Marine Le Pen ? Donnée entre 30 et 31 % des intentions de vote dans le sondage Cluster 17 réalisé en exclusivité pour POLITICO entre le 15 et le 16 septembre, la candidate du RN confirme sa position de large favorite pour accéder au second tour de l’élection présidentielle de 2027. Le match pour la deuxième place est en revanche plus serré que jamais : pas de véritable favori entre Edouard Philippe (Horizons) et Jean-Luc Mélenchon (LFI).

Dans le premier des deux scénarios testés, le maire du Havre porte seul les couleurs du centre-droit — Gabriel Attal (Renaissance) n’est pas sur la ligne de départ — et atteint 19% d’intentions de vote, à égalité parfaite avec Jean-Luc Mélenchon, en légère progression par rapport à la moyenne des sondages parus en septembre (voir notre agrégateur de sondages maison). Raphaël Glucksmann, lui, rassemblerait 12% de Français dans une telle configuration.



Dans l’hypothèse où Edouard Philippe s’efface au profit de Gabriel Attal, l’Insoumis se qualifierait en revanche facilement, avec 20% des voix, devant Raphaël Glucksmann, crédité de 14% d’intentions de vote dans ce scénario. Le président de Renaissance, lui, recueillerait 13,5% des voix selon Cluster 17.

Le social-démocrate Raphaël Glucksmann, actuel favori de la primaire socialiste, parvient donc à garder la tête hors de l’eau, comme le note Jean-Yves Dormagen, président de Cluster 17, malgré le match à trois bien installé entre les pôles dominants — LFI, centre-droit, RN — et progresse même très légèrement. Mais il ne peut espérer, à ce stade, décrocher un ticket pour le face-à-face final.

World.title: Accessibility: Europe’s hidden growth engine
World.content:
Europe faces major challenges to its competitiveness, including low productivity growth, labour shortages, demographic decline and technological gaps. While these issues dominate economic discussions, a significant opportunity often remains overlooked: accessibility. Around 90 million people in the European Union live with disabilities, and this number is expected to increase as the population ages. Yet employment rates among people with disabilities remain far below the EU average, leaving a substantial pool of talent, skills and purchasing power underutilized.

Accessibility is not only a social or legal issue; it is also an economic strategy. By making products, services, buildings and digital platforms accessible, businesses can reach a wider audience, including people with disabilities, older adults, individuals with temporary limitations and consumers who simply benefit from better design. Rather than serving a niche market, accessibility expands markets and improves experiences for everyone.

For many organizations, accessibility is still perceived as a compliance requirement or an additional cost. In reality, it should be viewed as an investment in quality, innovation and growth. Barriers that exclude people with disabilities often create difficulties for all users. Removing those barriers improves usability, customer satisfaction, brand reputation and commercial performance. Accessibility therefore contributes directly to competitiveness and business success.

The European Accessibility Act, which entered into application in June 2025, reflects this changing perspective. It establishes common accessibility requirements for products and services such as e-commerce, banking, smartphones, computers, ticketing systems, self-service terminals and e-books. By harmonising standards across the single market, the legislation reduces fragmentation, lowers compliance costs and enables companies to scale accessible solutions more efficiently across Europe.

Accessibility is not simply a matter of rights or compliance — it is a proven tool for driving innovation and strengthening Europe’s long-term competitiveness.

Accessibility should also be understood as a quality standard. Many features originally developed for people with disabilities have become mainstream benefits. Captions, for example, were introduced to support deaf and hard-of-hearing users but are now widely used by all audiences. Likewise, clear navigation, readable content, intuitive interfaces, effective color contrast and logical information structures are not special accommodations. They are characteristics of products and services that simply work better.

Research consistently shows that accessible digital design can increase web traffic, improve conversion rates, reduce cart abandonment and generate strong returns on investment. Conversely, poor accessibility often reflects wider usability failures. Many websites still contain basic barriers such as inadequate color contrast, missing labels or inaccessible forms, creating friction for all users and limiting overall performance.

Accessibility is also economically efficient. When incorporated from the beginning of a project, costs remain relatively low. Retrofitting products, websites or services after launch is often far more expensive and less effective. For this reason, accessibility should be built into design and development processes from the outset rather than treated as an afterthought.

Accessibility also reduces the environmental and economic cost of artificial intelligence.

For decades, digital accessibility has been defended on three main grounds: it is a fundamental right, it is a legal obligation, and it opens access to a large and often underserved market. All three arguments remain valid. However, the rise of artificial intelligence (AI) introduces a fourth dimension that is increasingly relevant for Europe’s competitiveness: efficiency.

Accessibility is fundamentally about making information understandable. Accessible websites and documents clearly identify headings, buttons, form fields, images, languages and relationships between pieces of content through structured, semantic coding. These features were originally designed to support people using assistive technologies, but they provide an additional and increasingly important benefit: they help AI systems understand content more efficiently.

AI relies on context and structure to interpret information. When digital content is properly labeled and organized, AI systems can process it directly. When that information is missing, the system must infer meaning, perform additional processing and consume more computational resources. In practice, inaccessible content requires more machine work, increasing electricity consumption, water usage in data centers, processing costs and response times.

Recent research modeling the interaction between AI systems and digital content found that accessible versions of the same webpages, documents, and online transactions can reduce AI processing work by between 70 percent and 99 percent, depending on the use case. The same reductions apply to electricity consumption, water usage, and associated carbon emissions because these factors are directly linked to computational effort.

The implications are significant. At scale, organizations receiving millions of AI-powered queries each year could reduce operational costs while simultaneously lowering energy consumption and environmental impact. Accessibility therefore becomes not only a tool for inclusion and usability, but also a practical mechanism for improving the efficiency and sustainability of AI systems.

This emerging reality is particularly relevant in Europe. For the first time, European legislation is advancing along two complementary paths: requiring digital products and services to be accessible while also increasing transparency and accountability regarding the energy and water consumption of data centers. Accessibility contributes to both objectives through the same technical measures.

When incorporated from the beginning of a project, accessibility costs remain relatively low. Retrofitting later is far more expensive.

Demographic trends further reinforce its importance. Europe’s growing silver economy, driven by consumers aged 50 and over, represents one of the continent’s largest and fastest-growing markets. These consumers increasingly demand products and services that are simple, safe and intuitive to use. Tourism provides another example, as accessible destinations attract more visitors, encourage longer stays, foster customer loyalty and generate greater spending while improving experiences for all travelers.

Accessibility is also becoming increasingly relevant in the age of AI. The same features that make digital content accessible to people, such as structured information, semantic coding, alternative text and properly tagged documents, also make it easier for AI systems to process information accurately. Accessible content improves data quality, reduces inefficiencies and helps AI systems perform more reliably, making accessibility an enabler of innovation rather than a constraint.

Achieving these benefits, however, requires more than legislation. Organizations need knowledge, skills and implementation capacity. This is the role of AccessibleEU, the European Accessibility Resource Centre. Through training, technical guidance, knowledge-sharing and collaboration, AccessibleEU helps businesses, public administrations and professionals translate accessibility requirements into practical solutions and build expertize across Europe. By creating a common knowledge base and sharing best practices, it helps ensure that accessibility is implemented consistently across sectors and countries.

Spain’s ONCE Social Group provides a compelling example of accessibility as an economic asset. Through ONCE, Fundación ONCE and ILUNION, the organization has demonstrated that inclusion and business success can reinforce one another. Today, it is the fourth-largest employer in Spain and the world’s largest employer of people with disabilities, showing how accessibility can unlock talent, improve productivity, stimulate innovation, and expand markets while generating social and economic value.

The conclusion is clear: Europe should treat accessibility as both competitiveness infrastructure and a quality standard. Alongside digital transformation, skills development, energy policy and the single market, accessibility should become a central element of economic strategy. Properly understood, it is not simply a matter of rights or compliance but a proven tool for improving products, driving innovation, expanding markets, increasing employment and strengthening Europe’s long-term competitiveness. Accessibility is no longer the social dimension of economic policy; it is increasingly one of Europe’s most powerful and underappreciated engines for growth, resilience and prosperity.

Barriers that exclude people with disabilities often create difficulties for all users. Removing them improves usability for everyone.

Jesús Hernández Galán

Director of a ccessibility and i nnovation, Fundación ONCE

World.title: Mélenchon’s allies try to temper his debt write-off rhetoric
World.content:
But Berr and other left-leaning economists have tried to reframe the debate around what they see as the grip of financial markets over sovereign debt.

However, Mélenchon isn’t tamping down his language. With polls suggesting he could qualify for the first time in a second-round face-off against far-right leader Marine Le Pen, and as rivals from more moderate parties are struggling to emerge from a jam-packed field, the 75-year-old appears keen to set France’s fiscal debate on his own terms.

Playing hot and cold

In a press conference with online media and influencers last June, the presidential candidate outlined his idea of “freezing the public debt held by the Bank of France at a zero interest rate,” echoing a proposal from his previous presidential campaign to convert these debts into perpetual zero-interest debt — in other words, loans with no repayment date and no interest payable.

The French central bank holds less than one-sixth of French debt, totaling some €488 billion.

Mélenchon’s proposal would be like “putting the debt in the fridge,” he first said — before going on to talk about “throwing it to the fire.”

The latter metaphor sparked a Europe-wide controversy later in the summer, fueled by a viral post on X reposting the clip in August. Political opponents have predicted a “financial crisis,” “ruin” or “bankruptcy” should the state fail to follow through on its financial commitments.

World.title: Rebellion in a tiny English village reveals Burnham’s peril on migration
World.content:
The village’s declaration of “independence” from the rest of the U.K. came in a symbolic referendum, which took aim at the use of a military barracks on Piddington’s periphery to house up to 1,250 asylum seekers. The result was an overwhelming 285 in favor of leaving the U.K., with just 26 villagers opting to remain.

Now this very British protest threatens to spread to other shires. It has become a magnet for Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s critics — handing them fresh ammunition to use against him as they push to leave the European Convention on Human Rights.

All the while, Britain’s far-right is threatening to shift attention away from the watery frontier of the English Channel toward “defending” Piddington from newcomers. That raises the prospect of unwanted, balaclava-wearing activists descending on an otherwise tranquil village.

Tea and trouble

When POLITICO headed down rural roads to reach the bucolic breakaway “state” this week, Kemi Badenoch was there by pure coincidence. The Conservative Party leader was following a line of right-wingers pledging their support for this tiny patch of Middle England in revolt.

Over plates of biscuits and mugs of tea in the small village hall that has been the nerve center of this pseudo-secessionist movement, Badenoch listens attentively to the fears of the more than 40 assembled local women.

And she leans in to the darkest fears the villagers harbor. Not only is this about migration, she said, but it’s a “huge safeguarding risk” too. She warns of a “criminal element” being housed on Piddington’s doorstep — the arrival of hundreds of men whose identities are little known, up against cherished playing fields that back onto the military base (albeit through barbed wire fencing).

World.title: Don’t believe the doomers: Europe’s tech industry slams AI panic
World.content:
“Sadly, it has jumped up to the Terminator is coming,” James Wise, a partner at Balderton Capital and chair of the U.K. government’s sovereign AI fund, said of the current narrative. “I don’t think the Terminator is coming at all.”

Those fears land atop the agendas of world leaders this week, with U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping meeting for a Thursday summit after AI security was debated at the United Nations General Assembly and a special G7 meeting. Leaders from 22 nations adopted a declaration on Monday saying that AI must remain under human direction, oversight and control, and suggesting the creation of a global supervisory regime.

Yet for those tasked with defending computer systems, the daunting chorus of warnings about advanced AI models — and the political scramble to respond — risks applying the wrong solution to the wrong problem.

“We should spend more time making the rules and standards we have work at scale, and less time focusing on fears about theoretical risks or news reports from the Silicon Valley AI doomer bubble,” said Alexandru Voica, policy lead at U.K.-based AI firm Synthesia.

“Many third-party narratives, and even frontier labs’ own narratives, completely neglect to factor [hacker] behavior and capabilities into their doomsday theories,” said Marcus Hutchins, a cyber threat researcher and former hacker best known for stopping the huge WannaCry ransomware attack in 2017.

Getting down to business

A recent example of AI voices arguably missing the mark is a warning by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei that an AI agent could take over the internet. That claim, which was widely reported, was derided and debunked in cybersecurity circles.

World.title: Europe's security and prosperity start before people reach its borders
World.content:
The opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not represent in any way the editorial position of Euronews.

It is spending increasing political energy asking how to stop people reaching its borders, when the more consequential question is what happens long before they get there. If Europe wants to use its external aid to strengthen its own security and prosperity, it must answer that question in the next seven-year budget cycle.

 

Lasting prosperity and security require investment much earlier – where displacement begins, where refugees are first received and where fragile societies are most at risk of buckling under such prolonged pressure. Most solutions are there, not at Europe's border.

The distinction matters – and so does where Europe puts its money

Europe is increasingly tempted to view external assistance through the narrow lens of migration control: more money for partners willing to contain movements or accept returns.

Some of these objectives are legitimate. Governments have a responsibility to manage their borders, maintain functioning asylum and integration systems and where necessary, return those without a legal right to stay while complying with line with international law.

But a foreign aid policy built principally around preventing people from reaching the European territory is not a strategy for managing forced displacement. It risks simply moving the pressure elsewhere, making others – often with fewer resources than Europe – responsible for managing it, while potentially allowing others to instrumentalise migration flows and erode trust in Europe as a partner.

Where Europe puts its money, it advances its vision of what the world of tomorrow should look like. If Europe leaves the space empty, others – often with very different values – will fill it.

The EU is surrounded by countries facing extreme fragility risks. Many host refugees at a scale that would test far stronger institutions. Close to two-thirds of those arriving in Europe through irregular routes and seeking asylum come from these countries. That pressure is unlikely to disappear – and could grow – if underlying needs are not addressed earlier. Traffickers and actors with extremist agenda prey on precisely these vulnerabilities.

Addressing displacement means addressing its consequences before they cascade into wider instability. It means keeping children in school, keeping health systems functioning, creating livelihoods, supporting host communities, and strengthening institutions.

This is not charity, it is strategic investment

The next EU budget (MFF) offers Europe a crucial opportunity to put this principle into practice. The question is not only how much money Europe allocates to external action, but what it is intended to achieve and what Europe expects in return.

The MFF will determine which countries, crises and priorities receive sustained European backing. It will shape Global Europe, the EU's principal framework for development and humanitarian action, and therefore Europe’s ability to use its financial weight to advance its own security and prosperity.

Related EU to further tighten migration policy after Ceuta crisis

This is not a technical exercise in dividing budget lines. It is a strategic choice about where European resources can deliver the greatest return: reducing instability, strengthening economic resilience, opening markets and building partnerships before crises become more costly to manage .

Refugees who work contribute to local economies. Stronger infrastructure supports trade. More resilient economies create markets for European goods and services. Stronger public institutions help societies withstand polarisation and resist extremist political movements.

This is why the design of Global Europe matters. Europe needs the capacity to finance the full displacement cycle: reducing fragility and conflict; protecting people when displacement occurs; supporting host countries and communities; creating livelihoods; and investing in solutions, including safe return where conditions permit, as well as resettlement and labour or education mobility.

The principle is simple: invest European money to the problem where it can deliver the greatest return – including for Europe's own security and prosperity.

Money spent strengthening a fragile health system today reduces the risk of a pandemic tomorrow. Money spent helping a refugee find work strengthens a host economy and provides a stronger trading partner for the EU. Money spent supporting the rule of law reduces the risk that instability and political extremism will spill across borders.

Not soft investments – investments in Europe’s own interests

Europe has a finite pool of resources and an expanding set of demands. Defence, cohesion, competitiveness and stronger public services will rightly compete for political attention and money. These priorities are closely linked to Europe’s external choices. A safer and more prosperous Europe depends in large part on what happens beyond its borders.

The next MFF will determine whether Europe puts its money behind short-term crisis management or long-term resilience; whether it strengthens relationships or creates transactional dependencies; and whether its external spending generates returns for Europeans as well as its partners.

Related Five EU countries aim to send migrants to return hubs by 2027

Europe cannot prevent every conflict or stop every person from moving. But it can influence whether people have a viable future closer to home, whether host countries remain resilient, whether markets and partnerships grow, and whether crises extend across borders.

The choice is straightforward: use Europe’s money to manage the consequences of forced displacement on Europe, or invest more decisively in preventing those consequences from becoming Europe’s problem in the first place.

Jean-Nicolas Beuze is the UNHCR (United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees) Representative to the EU.
