World.title: The EU wants to protect children online. What about everyone else?
World.content:
Children deserve a safer internet, said European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen when presenting the EU Kids Act on 17 September. The proposal sets graduated thresholds for social media access, bans addictive design features like infinite scroll for under-18s, and requires platforms to verify age using a privacy-preserving "yes/no" token instead of a birth-certificate check.

 

Commission Executive Vice-President Henna Virkkunen presented it as a delay, not a ban. Children get eased into risky platforms at 13, 15, and 18 rather than being locked out entirely.

That framing worries digital rights groups. “The way the proposal is framed is that age is the problem," says Simeon de Brouwer, policy advisor at European Digital Rights (EDRi), a Brussels-based network of digital rights NGOs.

He argues that by delaying rather than fixing the underlying design, "the Commission does not address the causes of the harm, the business model and the addictive design, the manipulative practices, which young people will be exposed to as soon as they reach the different thresholds."

Age as a proxy for vulnerability

De Brouwer's core objection is that the Act treats age as the only marker of vulnerability worth legislating for. "The sole factor of vulnerability that is taken into consideration is young age, not even age. But there are many other factors," he says.

EDRi represents member organisations working across civil society, and according to de Brouwer, the organisation tries "to take into account marginalised groups whose voice we don't hear that much in Brussels."

That matters because age verification requires everyone, not just children, to prove they are old enough to pass through the gate. "If we really need to know who's underage to protect them better, that means we know everybody's age, or we need everybody's age," de Brouwer continues. "We are turning smartphones and identity documents into prerequisites for accessing online spaces and exercising fundamental rights." He lists who gets caught in that net: "people who don't have state identities, people who are stateless, people from migration backgrounds and not integrated yet, people who by choice don't have a smartphone."

Who could be marginalised?

The same restrictions risk harming some of the young people the Act is meant to protect, including those with disabilities who rely on the internet to socialise.

De Brouwer points to "young people who also are marginalised, so people who are handicapped and don't have that many physical interactions, people who are in rural spaces and don't have friends around, people whose parents are not very present or willing to support them and therefore need online spaces to find, to talk to, to find people like them." He concludes that "the range of young people who will lose out is immense."

Francesca Pisanu, senior policy officer at Eurochild, a network focused on children's rights, broadly welcomes the Act's ambition but agrees the accessibility question deserves scrutiny. She says: "It is known that social media platforms or the online world in general is a space where children, or people in general, can be included in society. They can find people with shared identities succeed. They can also see more diversity."

She adds a caveat, "people that are discriminating [in] the offline world are also likely to be discriminated [against] in the online world," so it's important that "all these inclusive features" are "activated at the same time as the protective features," so the two do "not contradict" each other.

Pisanu pointed to a Eurochild-linked study in the Netherlands that found that "children with disabilities or the children with mental health issues were the ones that were actually in favour of a ban," a reminder that marginalised groups do not speak with one voice on this question.

Overlapping and overriding other Acts

For de Brouwer, the deeper problem is political timing. He argued the Kids Act risks overriding the Digital Fairness Act (DFA), a parallel initiative meant to strengthen consumer protection "everywhere, regardless of which service you use", not just for children.

"The risk is that we lose out by focusing so much on children and young people. We lose the political momentum that we had to improve everyone's protection through the DFA," he said, warning it could now arrive "in a diluted fashion."

He was equally clear that many of the Act's protections should not be limited to minors. "Who doesn't want to be protected from AI companions designed to be addictive and to entice you to keep coming back?" he asked, arguing that platforms should instead be "forced to be non-addictive" and that "we should have, for example, a right to services which are not personalised."

Pisanu's institutional position is less confrontational: Eurochild wants safety-by-design to be binding law, not just DSA guidelines, and welcomes that some protections, like recommender-system defaults, would extend even to unregistered users, since some of these "safety features would apply also to those that are not registered." But both interviewees converge on one point: the current draft answers "how do we protect children" without fully answering "how do we protect anyone who is vulnerable but not underage."

The European Parliament and the Council must take positions on the Kids Act, and the Commission must review the rules' effect on fundamental rights by 31 August 2030, leaving the balance between protection and exclusion unsettled.

World.title: Carrara marble: Can a sculpture created by an AI robot be considered as art ?
World.content:
Robotic arms are being used to carve complex sculptures from blocks of marble, guided by software that turns digital designs into precise instructions for the machines.

 

The technology is being developed by Italian companies LITIX and ROBOTOR, which say it could make marble sculpture more accessible.

"The goal is to be able to create something out of your idea, even if you don't have the skill to do that," says Giacomo Massari, founder and CEO of LITIX and ROBOTOR.

A digital image can be converted into a 3D file before software generates the toolpaths used by the robot. The machine can then carry out most of the carving, leaving skilled workers to refine the sculpture.

A robot carves a marble artwork as technology transforms traditional sculpture in Carrara. AP Photo

A changing role for sculptors

The arrival of robots has prompted mixed reactions among traditional sculptors in Carrara. Some have been uneasy about machines taking over work that has traditionally required years of training.

"You're not killing a job, you're just evolving that job," says Massari. He adds robots can take on as much as 99% of the carving, allowing artisans to concentrate on the final details.

The company also argues that this could make working with marble safer and less physically demanding.

Workers use traditional tools to finish a marble sculpture in Carrara, Italy. AP Photo

But the debate goes beyond jobs. As machines become capable of translating digital ideas directly into physical objects, artists are also having to consider what constitutes the creative act.

'Algorithmic sculpting'

Italian Artist Davide Quayola uses algorithms and robotic machines as part of his own practice.

Rather than seeing the robot as an independent creator, he describes it as an extension of his artistic gesture.

"I am actually feeling that I'm completely in control," he says. Quayola calls his approach "algorithmic sculpting".

He says he and his studio programme the machine's movements, making the robot part of the process through which the artwork is created. For him, the distinction is important. The machine may perform the physical work, but the artist decides how it operates and what the finished work is intended to become.

The future of marble

Carrara has long been associated with traditional craftsmanship and the white marble used by some of history's most celebrated sculptors.

Carrara's white marble quarries have supplied stone to sculptors for centuries. AP Photo

Now, the same material is being shaped using technology that would have been unimaginable to earlier generations of artists.

The change does not necessarily mean an end to traditional craftsmanship.

Instead, the role of the sculptor may increasingly shift from physically removing stone to designing, programming and refining the final work.

As robots take on more of the physical process, one question remains: where does the work of the machine end and the work of the artist begin?

World.title: Swiss voters expected to reject bid to enshrine stricter neutrality in constitution
World.content:
Switzerland will vote on a heavily debated proposal to tighten their country's traditional neutrality on Sunday, amid fears that an expected "no" could be interpreted as abandoning the principle altogether.

 

The Swiss widely embrace their neutrality, but an initiative to enshrine a strict definition into the Alpine nation's constitution has exposed deep disagreement over what that neutrality entails.

During the heated debate, it has appeared that Swiss identity itself was on the ballot.

While initial opinion polls had indicated that the vote might be tight, the final two surveys published last week suggest a clear majority of voters, well above 60%, plan to heed government advice and reject the initiative.

Switzerland's traditional position is one of well-armed military neutrality, but Russia's war in Ukraine reopened questions over its non-engagement in foreign conflicts.

Concerned over Bern's decision to back the European Union's economic pressure, the pro-sovereignty Pro Switzerland organisation collected enough signatures to trigger a public vote under the country's direct democracy system on better anchoring neutrality in its constitution.

People queue to Zurich City Hall to cast their ballot in a referendum, 28 November, 2021 AP Photo

'Lost our way'

"We have lost our way in recent years by taking very strong stances against Russia, while conversely adopting extremely weak positions regarding Israel," former Swiss diplomat Jean-Daniel Ruch told the AFP news agency at an event backing the initiative.

"This is an opportunity to restore the credibility of our neutrality."

Moscow, which has slammed Switzerland for joining the EU sanctions and accused Bern of abandoning its neutrality, has praised the initiative, dubbed "pro-Russian" by some opponents.

Russian President Vladimir Putin "would rub his hands together with glee if we accepted this initiative," Socialist parliamentarian Samuel Bendahan warned during a recent debate.

The proposal calls for the constitution to guarantee that Swiss neutrality is "armed and perpetual."

Rescuers look from the windows of an office building damaged by a Russian drone strike in Kyiv, 23 September, 2026 AP Photo

It would prevent Switzerland, whose neutrality dates back to 1516 and has been internationally recognised since 1815, from establishing closer ties with NATO and would rule out any military alliance except if the country were attacked.

And it would prohibit imposing sanctions unless called for by the United Nations.

All sides in the debate argue that they want to maintain Switzerland's neutrality.

But the government and parliament have both rejected the proposal, arguing it is too dogmatic and would limit the country's room for manoeuvre at a time of soaring geopolitical tensions.

'Degree of flexibility'

"Neutrality has always been applied with a degree of flexibility," Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis insisted during a recent televised debate.

While Switzerland had no plans to lift a ban on selling arms to countries in conflict, he stressed that "neutrality does not mean indifference."

The country, he said, would "not look away when we see violations of the very international rules that allow us to live in peace."

Nearly all major political parties have also opposed the initiative.

The only exception is the populist right-wing Swiss People's Party (SVP) which has been closely tied to the initiative from the start.

But backers have emerged from various political persuasions.

A soldier poses with a drone during a press event of the Swiss Army in Elm, 18 May, 2026 AP Photo

Samuel Sommaruga, a doctor who claims no political affiliation but is the son of a prominent Socialist senator and the grandson of a former president of the International Committee of the Red Cross, is a leading proponent.

He told AFP he feared Switzerland would "sink" if it did not adopt a strict neutrality definition, warning that it would be seen internationally as having "renounced its neutrality" altogether.

Without a clear neutral stance, he maintained that Switzerland risked being sucked into NATO and losing its privileged status as mediator and influential host of international organisations and negotiations.

"I think that if we vote no, we risk losing that," he said.

According to polls, the Swiss are also expected to reject another initiative on Sunday's ballot, calling for the country to raise its food self-sufficiency rate to 70 percent, up from 42 percent in 2024.

World.title: Night-time grape harvest is Alentejo estate's answer to extreme heat
World.content:
In the pitch-dark night, the grapes are lit up by the beams from helmets and tractors moving across the fields. At Herdade das Servas, an estate in Portugal’s Alentejo region, the grape harvest now takes place at night. And those who work here do not seem to mind.

 

Maria Jerónima Mendes is one of dozens of people involved in picking the grapes. She told AFP that the change has not disrupted the work and that, thanks to the light she carries with her, she even "sees the grapes better than in daylight".

"It sounds like a lie, but it isn’t. The body gets used to turning day into night and night into day," she explained.

On this estate, picking grapes at night began in 2024 as a test and has been adopted as standard practice since last year. It is a response to intense heat and increasingly frequent extreme weather events.

"This night-time harvest came from the need to provide better working conditions for the teams, because Alentejo has a very harsh climate in summer," Renato Neves told AFP. For this winegrower and oenologist, harvesting at night is no longer just an option: it is becoming an unavoidable reality for producers in the region.

"In future, it will be inevitable. In my view, more and more companies will start picking at night, because it is going to become very hard for people to carry on harvesting from 11 am or midday, in temperatures of 40, 41 or 42 degrees," he said.

Alentejo is one of the hottest and driest regions in mainland Portugal, where summer highs of between 35 and 38 degrees are common and peaks are even higher during heatwaves, episodes that specialists increasingly link to climate change.

World.title: Markets mixed as investors eye oil price volatility and US bonds
World.content:
Ahead of European markets opening, Japan's benchmark Nikkei 225 gained 1.3% in morning trading to 65,883.41, as some chipmakers got a boost from the recent interest in artificial intelligence. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 fell 0.7% to 8,700.50.

 

Hong Kong's Hang Seng lost 0.5% to 24,715.95, while the Shanghai Composite dipped 0.8% to 3,902.33. Trading was closed in South Korea for the Chuseok autumn harvest holiday.

In energy trading, benchmark US crude fell 0.82% to $91.40 a barrel. Brent crude, the international standard, lost 0.83% to $102.22 a barrel.

The price for a barrel of Brent remains much higher than the roughly $72 it cost before the war with Iran began and worries are running high that the war with Iran will keep oil bottled up in the Middle East for a long time. Talks are continuing with mediators between US and Iranian officials, but nothing concrete has come from it yet.

US bond market pressure

Overnight, Wall Street got hit by pressure from the US bond market after a surprisingly strong report on the economy raised worries about inflation.

The S&P 500 fell 0.8% after finishing the prior day just 0.4% below its record set last month. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 352 points, or 0.7%, while the Nasdaq composite sank 1.1% from its own all-time high.

The yield on the 10-year Treasury jumped to 5.10% from 4.96%, a considerable move for the bond market. High yields undercut prices for stocks and other investments, while also slowing the economy by making it more expensive for everyone to borrow money.

Wednesday’s jump briefly sent the 10-year yield near 5.14%, back to where it was in 2007 before the global financial crisis caused yields to crater. Yields have accelerated recently because of worries about high inflation, the US government’s heavy debt and other concerns.

Related Fed raises rates for the first time since 2023 in unanimous vote defying Trump

Worries about inflation got a jolt after a preliminary report suggested growth in US business activity surged to its strongest level in more than five years.

US inflation has remained so stubbornly high that the Federal Reserve raised its short-term interest rate last week for the first time in three years. Fed Gov. Michael Barr said in a speech this week that further hikes “are likely to be needed” to get inflation to the Fed’s 2% target.

Although the Bank of Japan recently raised its benchmark interest rate to stem the slide in the Japanese yen, the move was largely figured in for weeks. And so the yen hasn't really bounced back. A weak yen works as a negative for oil-importing Japan when oil prices are soaring.

In currency trading, the US dollar edged down to 157.94 Japanese yen from 158.30 yen. The euro cost $1.1382, little changed from $1.1388.

All told, the S&P 500 fell 58.61 points to 7,706.03. The Dow dropped 352.10 to 51,511.59, and the Nasdaq composite sank 308.24 to 26,936.04.

World.content:

09/24/2026 September 24, 2026 Fire on sleeper bus kills nine outside of Delhi

Nine passengers were killed late on Wednesday after an overnight sleeper bus caught fire outside of the national capital, New Delhi, according to media reports.

A police report, cited by the media, said the bus' air conditioning unit caused the fire while on the Yamuna Expressway in Greater Noida.

Police added that the bus driver and conductor managed to escape the fire and are have absconded.

A passenger who managed to escape the tragedy told ANI news agency that the bus was packed with passengers.

"I was sleeping when someone woke me up saying the bus had caught fire, and we all scrambled to get out," the passenger said. "It was not an easy situation to escape, there was a lot of smoke. We somehow managed to get out."

The police are investigating the incident.

World.title: US judge blocks Trump ban of CNN, MS NOW, Politico from White House, orders him to restore access
World.content:
A judge has ordered President Trump to restore White House access to CNN, MS NOW and Politico after he banned the media outlets from the premises.

​A federal judge on Thursday said US President Donald Trump must lift his ban on journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico accessing the White House.

The ruling came in response to a lawsuit filed by the news organizations contesting the ban, issued on September 18.

In his order, District Judge Tim Kelly said the ban was likely unconstitutional.

Kelly said his order must remain in place for 14 days.

"This is a strong ruling vindicating freedom of the press, due process and the rule of law," Theodore Boutrous Jr., attorney for the outlets, said in a statement emailed to the AP news agency. "We greatly appreciate the court’s swift action."

What did the judge say about the ban?

Kelly rejected the government's claim that national security concerns promoted the ban.

"The record lacks factual support for defendants’ contention that the revocation of plaintiffs' hard passes will ​in fact protect national security or that national security will be endangered if the court orders their passes reinstated while this litigation ​proceeds," he said.

He pointed out that Trump himself had initially cited only an "alleged lack of truthfulness and negativity" in reporting by the outlets as the reason for the ban.

At a Wednesday hearing, Kelly said two previous rulings from the US Court of Appeals for the ⁠District of ​Columbia Circuit had established that White House press passes can be revoked only after due process.

He said the banned news outlets did not appear to have been given a proper chance to contest the ban.

Kelly, who was nominated by Trump in 2017, ordered a CNN journalist’s access restored in a similar case in 2018.

The ban led other media outlets, including DW, to take action in solidarity by suspending pooled coverage of Trump events.

Department of Justice support for ban

On Tuesday, the Justice Department had argued in a filing that access ⁠to the White House was a privilege, not ​an entitlement, and that the president had the authority to deny access news organizations.

The outlets, in turn, argued they were singled out because of the content of their coverage and called the ban a "blatant violation" of the First Amendment, which prevents government infringement on freedom of speech and freedom of the press in the United States.

World.title: OpenAI agent hacked Australia government portal: PM Albanese
World.content:
The hack of Australian health data marks the world's first known AI-led breach of a government website.

An OpenAI agent infiltrated an Australian government health data portal, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said Thursday, in what is the first known instance of an artificial intelligence hack of a government system.

Albanese said the breach occurred in June when an autonomous OpenAI program accessed both "public and non-public" files on the statistics reporting portal of Medicare — Australia's publicly funded universal health insurance scheme.

The available evidence did not indicate a broader network compromise, Albanese said, adding, "Nonetheless, this situation is obviously unacceptable."

Albanese said he spoke to OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman to express Australia's "extreme concern" over the incident.

OpenAI, the developer of ChatGPT, said in a statement that it spotted the breach while carrying out an "extensive review" of its AI tools, adding that "our models took actions we did not intend".

Altman had earlier on Wednesday addressed the UN Security Council, apprising the risks AI poses as the world faces the technology's development.

What did Australia's Albanese say about the OpenAI breach?

Albanese told reporters that OpenAI informed Australia about the breach only on September 10, three months after the incident, through an email sent to a public mailbox.

The Australian leader said he expressed his "disappointment" to Altman that it took OpenAI "way too long to inform the government" on what occurred.

Albanese also deemed the nature of the notification "unacceptable."

The prime minister announced that a probe into the security breach would determine whether OpenAI could face criminal charges.

He added that the investigation would also examine how the breach went past Australia's security agencies, which were unaware of it before OpenAI notified them.

How did the breach take place?

The breach occurred as OpenAI ran training exercises to rate the performance of AI models.

Government Services Minister Katy Gallagher said OpenAI asked the model to search the internet for data showing how much Australia's government spent on medicine.

She said the portal had since been closed and the data moved to more secure systems.

Albanese said no personal information is believed to have been accessed during the incident.

"I think OpenAI know that they need to have better protocols in place. And they're one of the businesses that themselves have warned of the risks which are there," Albanese said.

What has OpenAI said?

OpenAI said in its statement that it discovered the rogue activity in an August review.

"During this review, we identified activity involving several Australian government websites and services as our models attempted to look up answers and available statistics for questions about Australia during an internal evaluation," it said.

The San Francisco-based company added that it had found no evidence of Australian patient records being accessed.

Australia's Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles called the breach "fundamentally unacceptable."

"It was not sitting behind a particularly high fence. This AI agent scaled the fence ... and the point is it was unintended. It wasn't asked to. That's our concern here," Marles said.

In July, OpenAI disclosed that its advanced AI model went rogue during a security test and carried out a dayslong hacking spree into the Hugging Face AI technology digital repository.

Days later, rival company Anthropic announced that three separate versions of its AI broke out of cybertesting environments and hacked three firms.

World.title: Germany sets out plan to phase out fossil fuels by 2045
World.content:
Germany sets out a plan to phase out coal, oil and gas by 2045, reaffirming a climate strategy focused on electrification.

Germany has presented a roadmap to phase out fossil fuels by 2045.

Germany's Environment Minister Carsten Schneider told the UN General Assembly on Wednesday that the plan "combines independence, affordability, and climate protection."

Europe's largest economy is now the third country to have provided a solid plan for the phaseout — to which nearly 200 countries committed at the 2023 COP28 climate conference in Dubai — following France and the Netherlands.

What did Berlin say about the fossil phaseout plan?

Schneider, of the center-left Social Democratic Party, said the decision was linked to the Iran war and its impact on fuel supplies worldwide.

"It is not just extreme weather events around the world that demonstrate how urgently we need to do more to protect the climate," he said. "If the situation in the Strait of Hormuz determines whether people can still afford their daily commute to work, that is not a good state of affairs."

Germany's chemical industry hit by high energy prices To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

He said he believed the 19-year deadline was feasible.

"Our roadmap is intended to set an international example. I am sure that many other countries will follow."

Schneider said that fossil fuels accounted for 65% of Germany's energy consumption in 2024.

The majority of that — 98% of its oil and 95% of its natural gas — was imported at a cost of €76 billion ($86.5 billion). The minister stressed that the figure has since risen sharply due to the Iran war.

How have environmental organizations reacted to the plan?

Several environmental organizations welcomed Berlin's plan, though some highlighted that it contradicted some recent government decisions.

"With this announcement, Germany is showing a sign of life in international climate policy," said Greenpeace energy expert Mira Jäger.

However, she noted that "at the same time, the federal government is subsidizing the oil industry, breaking the heating transition, and slowing down the expansion of renewables."

How does natural gas harm the environment? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Fentje Jacobsen, a climate policy advisor at the World Wide Fund for Nature, argued that the roadmap largely rehashed existing initiatives without adding "new ideas or additional ambitions."

"The current government is meanwhile planning to rely less on renewables and more on gas," she added.

Energy Minister Katherina Reiche of the conservative Christian Democrats has advocated building new gas-fired power plants, arguing that this would help stabilize the electricity grid and highlighting the intermittent nature of renewable sources such as wind and solar.

Reiche has also demanded preserving a larger role for combustion-engine vehicles using alternative fuels, a position that contradicts the phaseout plan, which foresees battery-electric cars accounting for 100% of new passenger car registrations by 2035.

Germany's car industry is a pillar of the country's economy, and the recent struggles it has faced have naturally been reflected in the broader economy.

Edited by: Roshni Majumdar

World.title: Trump welcomes China's Xi for high-stakes summit
World.content:
Skip next section Trump wants Hong Kong's Jimmy Lai to be freed from prison — report

Chinese President Xi Jinping has arrived in Washington to a rare planeside welcome from his US counterpart, Donald Trump.

As Xi walked down a long red carpet on the airport tarmac, a White House spokesperson said that Trump believes Hong Kongdemocracy advocate Jimmy Lai should be released from prison and "wants to see that happen," the DPA news agency reported.

"The United States urges the authorities to grant Mr. Lai humanitarian parole," DPA quoted the spokesperson as saying.

Lai, a 78-year-old media tycoon, was sentenced to 20 years in prison earlier in the year under the National Security Law that China imposed in 2020 following massive pro-democracy protests in Hong Kong.

At a congressional hearing in Washington last week, Lai's son, Sebastien, repeated his appeal for his father's release.

Trump raised the issue of Lai's release when he met Xi in Beijing in May, but the US leader said the Chinese president told him Lai's case "would be a tough one."

On Tuesday, US outlet Politico reported that British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has asked Trump to discuss the release of Lai, who is a British citizen, with Xi.

World.title: Berlin Airport briefly suspends flights over drone sighting
World.content:
Airspace over the German capital was closed for about 45 minutes after a drone was spotted on the runway. Flights have resumed but are experiencing delays.

Berlin's airport briefly suspended flights on Wednesday evening after a drone sighting, Germany's DPA news agency cited airport and police officials as saying.

A drone was spotted on the Berlin Brandenburg Airport's northern runway at 8:00 p.m. (1800 GMT). Airspace above the airport was closed minutes later and operations were suspended for at least 45 minutes.

Several flights were diverted to Dresden.

As of 9:05 p.m., airspace was reopened but flights were experiencing delays.

Drone sightings on the rise

Drone sightings have become a common occurrence for airports in Europe, with Berlin's airport recording the highest number of sightings in Germany in the first part of the year.

Some 28 drone sightings were recorded during the first six months, as per figures by the German air traffic control (DFS). In seven of those cases, flight operations at the airport were temporarily suspended.

This is a jump from last year, when eight drones were detected at the airport and its surroundings in the whole of 2025, according to DFS.

World.title: Harvey Weinstein resentenced to 15 years for sexual assault
World.content:
The disgraced Hollywood mogul was found guilty of sexually assaulting former production assistant Miriam Haley. The man whose case spurred the #MeToo movement awaits a separate sentencing in a California rape case.

Disgraced movie mogul Harvey Weinstein was resentenced on Wednesday to 15 years in prison for sexually assaulting former production assistant Miriam Haley in 2006.

Once one of Hollywood's most powerful kingpins, churning out hits such as "Pulp Fiction", "Shakespeare in Love" and "Chocolat," Weinstein's fall from grace came when sexual assault allegations compounded against him in 2017, spiraling into Hollywood's #MeToo movement.

Accounts of several women who worked with him across the years showed a pattern of abusing his power in Hollywood and ability to make or break careers to extract sexual favors and sexually assault women.

What do we know about Haley's case?

Weinstein was found guilty of forcibly performing oral sex on Haley in 2006.

The former producer said she had accepted an invitation to his Manhattan apartment when he lunged to kiss her, and though she rebuffed him, he grabbed her and sexually assaulted her, ignoring her pleas to stop.

Weinstein was sentenced in 2020 to 23 years for the sexual assault of Haley, but the sentence was overturned in 2024 on appeal. A jury found him guilty again in 2025.

What happened in court?

On Wednesday, a 74-year-old, wheelchair-bound Weinstein made an appeal for leniency, apologizing to those he may have hurt.

"I do have remorse for Miriam Haley's pain, but I have to reiterate my innocence," he told the judge.

Haley stressed the assault was akin to "a life sentence."

"Having been sexually assaulted by Harvey Weinstein has had a devastating effect on my life and sense of security that may never go away. Making the decision to speak up will have me looking over my shoulder for years to come," she said.

Prosecutors had sought a 20-year sentence for the disgraced producer, but his lawyers warned that a longer sentence would likely see him die in prison.

Is violence against women an epidemic no one cares about? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What other cases await Weinstein in court?

Weinstein also awaits a resentencing in a separate rape and assault case in California, where he is accused of assaulting an actress in a Los Angeles hotel room in 2013. In June, an appeals court upheld his conviction but scrapped his 16-year prison term.

Meanwhile, prosecutors said they will not pursue a fourth trial in the case of him sexually assaulting actor Jessica Mann.

In May, a New York judge declared a mistrial after the jury failed to reach a verdict. It was the third time Mann had taken the stand against Weinstein and she said she could not bear to testify again.

Another 2020 verdict for Weinstein in the Mann case was overturned due to mishandling of witnesses, and a 2025 case ended in mistrial.

Weinstein's lawyers have called for leniency, arguing their client is in failing health as he battles blood cancer, congestive heart failure and kidney issues.

World.title: Eviction of 87-year-old woman sparks housing protests in Madrid
World.content:
Police escorted Maricarmen Abascal from the apartment she had called home for more than seven decades. The case has reignited debate over Spain's housing crisis, rising rents and protections for long-term tenants.

The dramatic eviction of an 87-year-old woman sparked protests in the Spanish capital Madrid on Wednesday.

Maricarmen Abascal was evicted from her residence on Alcalde Sainz de Baranda Street, where she had lived for at least 70 years of her life.

"I have lived here for 71 years and I don't want to leave," Maricarmen told reporters as the eviction was being carried out.

Dozens of people protested behind the police cordon, chanting, "Maricarmen, you are not alone" and "Murderers!"

Dozens of protesters gathered as Maricarmen Abascal was removed from her home. Image: Susana Vera/REUTERS

The case highlights the growing pressure on long-term tenants in Spain's major cities, where rental prices have surged in recent years. Gentrification and the shortage of affordable housing have fueled public discontent.

With only 30 minutes to gather her belongings, Maricarmen was escorted by riot police officers. She was removed from her home on a stretcher and taken to an ambulance.

An 8-year-long battle

Spanish newspaper El Pais reported that Maricarmen had rented the apartment from a private landlord until 2018, when a real estate company acquired the property and took over its management.

According to the newspaper, the legal dispute between Maricarmen and the real estate company has lasted eight years, and this was the fourth attempt to evict her from the home.

The elderly woman's lawyer, Beatriz Duro, said that the real estate company had rejected proposals from the legal team as well as requests to postpone her removal from the property.

The company has not made any public statements on the matter.

The case has highlighted the housing crisis in Spain's major cities Image: Susana Vera/REUTERS

Alicia del Rio, spokesperson for Inquilinas de Madrid, a tenants' association that seeks to combat what it describes as the "rental bubble" in the Madrid region, said that Maricarmen was taken by ambulance to a local hospital.

She also announced that a writer, who wishes to remain anonymous, had offered to pay the elderly woman's rent, but the real estate company rejected the proposal.

Spain's housing crisis

Spain remains divided over how to address the worsening housing crisis.

The country's left-wing coalition government has pushed for stronger tenant protections and broader rent controls. However, it argues that as long as Parliament remains divided, it will be difficult to pass such measures.

Meanwhile, Madrid's regional government, led by the conservative People's Party, has favored a more market-oriented approach.

The president of the Community of Madrid, Isabel Diaz Ayuso, is currently embroiled in a controversy related to the purchase of luxury properties valued at €6.3 million ($7.2 million).
