World.title: Kazakhstan’s GDP grows 29% to $306B over seven years
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 24. Kazakhstan’s GDP has grown by 29% over the past seven years, reaching $306 billion, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said at the first session of the Kazakhstan People’s Council.

This was announced in a statement published by the press service of the Kazakh president.

He said the country’s foreign exchange reserves and National Fund assets have exceeded $138 billion, while more than $162 billion in investments have been attracted to Kazakhstan over the period.

“The share of small and medium-sized businesses in the economy has exceeded 40%. Every year, more than 20 million square meters of housing are built in Kazakhstan,” Tokayev said.

He noted that 1,342 schools with capacity for more than 1 million students had been built since 2019. The president also said that the average life expectancy in Kazakhstan had reached 76 years, while more than 1,200 healthcare facilities had been opened.

More than 35,000 kilometers of roads have been built and repaired, Tokayev said, describing these figures as record indicators in the country’s history.

“Thanks to active efforts, Kazakhstan has entered the group of the 40 most competitive countries in the world,” he said.

Tokayev also outlined the political changes carried out following the constitutional reform.

“Undoubtedly, the Constitution will become an eternal guide for our people and an unshakable foundation of a Just, Progressive and Clean Kazakhstan, leading the country toward a bright future,” he said.

He noted that the first elections to the new legislative body, the Kurultai, were held as part of the constitutional reform. According to Tokayev, foreign experts assessed the elections positively, while five parties that received public support entered the Kurultai.

The deputies began their work on August 28, while an updated government was formed and a Vice President was appointed, he said. A new state institution, the Office of the Security Council of Kazakhstan, was also established, Tokayev added.

“Today, the Kazakhstan People’s Council begins its work. Dear compatriots, this historic moment will remain in our memory forever,” the president said.

According to Tokayev, Kazakhstan carried out fundamental transformations within just one year that directly affect the future of the country.

“In a short period, we successfully implemented large-scale reforms that have changed the appearance of the entire state and society. Today, we can confidently say that such a task is possible only for a progressive, constructive and united nation,” he said.

World.title: Legal action lodged over the SA government’s plans for a MotoGP circuit
World.content:
Legal action has been lodged over the South Australian government's plans for a MotoGP circuit in the Adelaide CBD.

Documents filed with the Federal Court on September 18 showed the case has been brought by Joshua Hogan against the state of South Australia.

Attorney-General Kyam Maher said the government would defend its position.

"The South Australian government is aware of the application in the Federal Court seeking an urgent injunction in relation to the works associated with the MotoGP," he said in a statement on Thursday afternoon.

SA Attorney-General Kyam Maher said the government will defend its position. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

"The Crown Solicitor's Office is currently considering the application, including the orders sought and the grounds on which they are sought.

" The government intends to defend its position and will respond through the appropriate court process. "

Designs for the $96 million street circuit, which will require the removal of nearly 400 trees from the eastern parklands, were released in August.

A period of community consultation ended on Sunday, with construction of the track due to begin in December.

A map showing the design for the MotoGP circuit in Adelaide. (Supplied: SA Government)

A separate, unrelated Federal Court case, aiming to stop the controversial North Adelaide Golf Course redevelopment, is still underway.

In that case, applicants Edwin Kemp Attrill and Janette Milera have argued the state government should have referred the redevelopment to federal environment minister Murray Watt.

The Crown Solicitor has refuted their stance, claiming it was not necessary because the development did not alter the key attributes of the parklands.

A judgment is due to be handed down next month.

World.title: 'Catastrophic failure': Cheryl Grimmer family gives Premier deadline
World.content:
Cheryl Grimmer's family has accused the state's top prosecutor of a "catastrophic failure of public accountability" and given the NSW premier an ultimatum to order an independent audit of the 56-year-old cold case.

If the government does not respond by September 29, the family says it will ask supportive members of the NSW Legislative Council to seek government records relating to the case.

The ultimatum, in a letter sent to Premier Chris Minns and Attorney-General Michael Daley on September 22, follows a decision by director of public prosecutions Sally Dowling to uphold the discontinuation of a murder prosecution.

"We refuse to roll over or accept bureaucratic brush-offs," the letter read.

Cheryl Grimmer went missing, believed kidnapped, from outside a Fairy Meadow beach changing shed in 1970. (Supplied)

Cheryl was three when she disappeared from outside a shower block at Fairy Meadow Beach in Wollongong in January 1970. Her body has never been found.

In 1971, a 17-year-old boy told police he had abducted and killed her. Investigators sought evidence to confirm his account but were not satisfied they had enough to charge him.

Why was the prosecution dropped?

Detectives revisited the interview decades later, and the man, known by the court pseudonym "Mercury", was charged with murder in 2017. He pleaded not guilty.

The prosecution was discontinued in 2019 after Justice Robert Hulme ruled the police interview could not be used as evidence. Prosecutors said their case could not succeed without it.

Justice Hulme acknowledged there was "no such requirement in 1971" for an adult support person to attend the interview.

He found police had a proper reason for the adult's absence, but ruled that a child protection law introduced in 1987 governed whether the interview could be used at the later trial.

He excluded it after considering how Mercury was questioned and his vulnerability at the time. The judge separately found it would be unfair to use the interview as evidence under the Evidence Act.

Family challenges review

Earlier this year, the family secured the review by the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions and provided 54 submissions.

In a determination dated September 16, Ms Dowling upheld the decision to discontinue the case, finding it was not reasonably open to challenge the court's exclusion of the interview.

The family says her response failed to address its legal arguments and information about potential witnesses.

It also says the DPP did not explain how the public interest in prosecuting Cheryl's case was considered.

"In a child homicide, evaluating the public interest requires an explicit balancing of the community's right to an open trial against perceived legal hurdles," its letter says.

In a statement on September 17, an ODPP spokesperson said the review considered "the evidence, the law, the trial judge's reasons and detailed submissions made by the family", and concluded the decision to discontinue the prosecution was correct.

The spokesperson said the office understood the outcome was "deeply disappointing" for Cheryl's family and acknowledged its pain and grief.

Pursuit of justice

The family has declined Ms Dowling's offer of a meeting and requested detailed written reasons. It says all communication should be in writing after "the 56-year history of this case".

For years, Paul Grimmer and Ricki Nash have campaigned for justice. (ABC Illawarra: Kelly Fuller)

In its letter to Mr Minns, the family calls for a full, independent audit of the case.

" We demand that you immediately exercise your executive authority to order a full, independent ministerial audit of this file. "

The family says it will seek a Standing Order 52 Legislative Council motion to obtain government records if it receives no response by September 29.

In a statement, Mr Daley said he understood the family was disappointed with the review's outcome.

"The key question considered by the review was the exclusion of the recorded interview. That is a legal question and one which has already been determined by the Supreme Court," he said.

Mr Daley said NSW Police was still working to give the family answers and a $1 million reward for information remained on offer.

His statement did not address the family's request for an independent examination.

Call to 'find a fix'

NSW upper house MP Jeremy Buckingham has been advocating for the family and on Thursday attempted to move an amendment to a bill that would clear a path for a prosecution.

It would have made all police statements made by children before 1988 exempt from the later rule requiring an adult support person.

Treasurer Daniel Mookhey acknowledged the family's "real and unfathomable" pain, but said the change would remove a safeguard in other cases.

Mr Buckingham accepted the objections and urged the attorney-general and all other MPs to "find a fix".

" There must be a legislative fix that can deal with this issue, we can not have a situation where this stands, where justice is not served. "

World.title: Breaking: Lenders pull out of Bathla group as construction work halts across sites
World.content:
Administrators of failed property developer Bathla have reduced staff down to a "skeleton" and will cease construction work after all but one lender decided not to continue propping up the company.

Only a core team will be retained to support the ongoing administration, with administrators Teneo working with lenders on the orderly sale of Bathla's subdivision and land-bank sites.

Support for sales and settlements will also cease.

"Discussions with lenders for further funding have now concluded," administrators said in a statement.

Administrators say Bathla Group has exhausted all its funding. (ABC News: John Gunn)

Administrators had initially secured a short-term funding deal from six lenders to continue on 13 of those lenders' construction projects.

They said that funding had now been "exhausted".

All other construction projects were suspended while 213 staff were stood down at the beginning of September in the wake of the deal.

The group had around 350 employees to begin with.

"We understand some lenders may want to discuss with us support and assistance for some projects," administrators said to lenders in correspondence seen by the ABC.

"While we are happy to assist where we are funded and have the resources available, these discussions will need to wait until next week as we have quite a bit of work to do today and tomorrow to cease operations, secure sites and stand down the workforce."

World.title: Self-described 'evil' man avoids jail for wire traps on bike path
World.content:
An Adelaide man who labelled himself "so-evil" after setting up wire traps along a bike path and injuring cyclists has avoided jail.

Noarlunga Downs resident Levi Michael Young-Henderson, 20, pleaded guilty earlier this year to two counts of acting likely to cause harm and four counts of damaging property in relation to actions in January, 2025.

He was previously facing the more serious charges of acting likely to cause serious harm.

The court heard Levi Young-Henderson handed himself in to police and identified himself as the man depicted in CCTV footage. (SA Police)

Young-Henderson was given a suspended sentence in Christies Beach Magistrates Court today.

The court previously heard that Young-Henderson, who had a job as a fencing worker, had strung wire across the bike path that runs alongside the Southern Expressway, at Hackham West, on January 10 and 13, 2025.

The court was told that police had obtained footage from his mobile phone of the wire, accompanied by an "emoji of a devil and the words 'I'm so evil' written underneath the video".

The court also heard that in the first incident three male cyclists were "knocked off their bikes while travelling at approximately 35km/h" and sustained "severe grazing". All three bikes were "destroyed".

Wire that was deliberately stretched across the bike path along the Southern Expressway in Adelaide's south. (Supplied: Morgan Billings)

The court also heard that in the second incident a female rider escaped injury, but the handlebars of her bike were damaged.

"We say this is a significant matter. It's serious, it's placed a number of members of the public at risk of serious harm and the defendant's actions have caused [damage] in excess of … $50,000 worth of bikes, when they were bought," the prosecutor said at the time.

Young-Henderson's total sentence came to 11 months and five days behind bars, but was suspended upon him entering a bond of good behaviour for two years.

World.title: Man charged after police pursuit back and forth across NSW-ACT border
World.content:
A 22-year-old man has been charged after leading police on a pursuit back and forth across the NSW-ACT border in the early hours of Thursday morning.

Officers allegedly found a large sword, a flick knife, gloves, and balaclavas in a search after the man was arrested.

According to NSW Police, the driver of a Kia hatchback failed to stop for Monaro Police District officers about 2am in Crestwood, on the NSW side of the ACT-NSW border.

NSW Police pursued the vehicle until it turned onto Canberra Avenue and entered the ACT, when ACT Policing officers took up the pursuit through the suburbs of Tralee, Hume and Tuggeranong.

NSW Police arrested the 22-year-old in Queanbeyan, and charged him with failing to stop for police and driving while disqualified. (ABC News: Abubakr Sajid)

A short time later, NSW Police officers rejoined the pursuit as the car re-entered the state in Jerrabomberra.

The pursuit lead officers through Jerrabomberra Heights, Karabar and Queanbeyan CBD before the driver crossed the border back into the ACT.

ACT Policing continued the pursuit onto Yass Road, where officers successfully deployed road spikes near the intersection of Sutton Road.

The hatchback eventually came to a stop back in NSW, on Crawford Street in Queanbeyan, where the 22-year-old driver allegedly ran from the vehicle.

After a pursuit on foot, the man was arrested and searched, with officers allegedly locating and seizing a flick knife.

A subsequent search of the vehicle allegedly also revealed a large sword, gloves, and balaclavas.

The 22-year-old was taken to Queanbeyan Police station, where he was charged with aggravated failing to stop for police, driving while disqualified, and possession of a knife in a public place.

Second police pursuit in three hours

ACT Policing says the 42-year-old man was subject to a good behaviour order and had been disqualified from driving. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

In the early hours of Thursday morning, ACT police officers were also involved in a separate pursuit with the driver of an allegedly stolen vehicle.

Police said about 4:15am a 42-year-old man was seen driving at excessive speeds in a silver Volkswagen Passat, which they said had been stolen from Lyneham in June.

The car allegedly continued at high speed through Weston Creek and Yarralumla, crossing the median strips and repeatedly driving on the wrong side of the road.

ACT Policing said when officers activated their lights and sirens, directing him to stop, he allegedly continued to drive at speeds of up to 100km/h in 60km/h zones.

The vehicle stopped in Curtin around 4:30am, where the driver was arrested.

He refused to undergo a roadside drug test, and police said they located several quantities of white crystalline substance suspected to be methamphetamine in the Volkswagen.

The 42-year-old, who was subject to a good behaviour order, is facing charges including aggravated furious driving, driving a stolen car, failing to stop for police, refusal to provide an oral fluid sample, and driving while disqualified.

World.title: Two seriously injured in Yarra Ranges bus crash
World.content:
Two passengers on a bus that crashed in Victoria's Yarra Ranges are in a serious condition, while several others have been hospitalised.

Emergency services were called to the incident near Glenburn, north-east of Melbourne, shortly before 3pm.

An Ambulance Victoria spokesperson said paramedics assessed 21 patients at the scene.

The crash happened on the Melba Highway at Glenburn in the Yarra Ranges. (ABC News)

A teenage boy was flown to The Alfred in a serious condition with upper body injuries, while a man in his 50s in a serious condition was taken by ambulance to Box Hill Hospital.

A teenage girl and another teenage boy were also taken to hospital in a stable condition.

Authorities say 16 other patients did not require emergency treatment or transport.

Specialist crews including an Air Ambulance Victoria helicopter and Advanced Life Support units assisted with the response.

Emergency services personnel remained at the scene at about 4:30pm on Thursday afternoon.

Charter company Mee's confirmed the bus involved left Mansfield at about 1pm bound for Melbourne as part of a public transport service.

The ABC understands the bus driver was an experienced, long-term driver for the company, and was not seriously injured in the crash.

Police have closed the Melba Highway after the crash. (ABC News)

Vision from the scene suggests the bus crashed through a road barrier on the side of the road it had been travelling along.

At least two other vehicles appear to have been badly damaged.

The Melba Highway has been closed to traffic between Castella and Yea following the collision.

Motorists are advised to detour through Kinglake and Flowerdale via Healesville-Kinglake, Whittlesea-Kinglake, and Whittlesea-Yea Roads.

World.title: Albanese couldn't have timed his Medicare hack bombshell better
World.content:
Welcome back to your weekly federal politics update, where Courtney Gould gets you up to speed on the happenings from Parliament House.

Anthony Albanese couldn't have picked a better time to drop the metaphorical bomb that a rogue artificial intelligence agent breached an Australian government system.

The prime minister has been on the world stage all week, helping to push a statement by middle powers calling for greater safeguards and for AI to remain under human control.

The statement was almost immediately rejected by US President Donald Trump, despite the chief executives of AI companies agreeing a slowdown in the pace of development for the technology was required.

So, the prime minister's unexpected disclosure that an OpenAI agent had gained unauthorised access to a Medicare statistics website three months ago caused quite a stir, especially coming just an hour after the tech giant's chief executive Sam Altman warned about the need for "accurate and speedy" reporting of incidents.

Loading...

The attack on the portal occurred back in June. OpenAI knew of the incident in August and only informed Services Australia – via an email to a public mailbox – two weeks ago.

"This situation is obviously unacceptable," Albanese told reporters in New York, where he has been attending the United Nations General Assembly.

A clearly frustrated Albanese said the Australian government could not find a precedent for the breach, although he stopped short of calling it a world first.

Who knew what, when?

After sitting on the news for more than a week, the government claims it wanted to get its ducks in a row before going public. The Australian Signals Directorate was given the heads up by Services Australia last Tuesday. The minister responsible, Katy Gallagher, was told two days later.

Albanese and his office were informed some time over the weekend. In the days since, the terms of reference for a rapid review into Australia's preparedness for an AI-driven cyber-attack were drafted. A phone call was organised with Altman.

During that phone call Altman acknowledged the actions of his company were not good enough. But he offered no apology.

Medicare AI hack: What we know An AI agent accessed Medicare data. But what did it get? And what else do we know?

In recent months, the government has been actively courting AI companies to invest in Australia. A report released this week on the outlook of the Australian economy over the next 40 years, the Intergenerational Report, underpinned just how important the government considers AI to our future economic growth.

It's a delicate tightrope the government is trying to walk — enticing tech companies to train their models here by considering scaling back Australian copyright while simultaneously advocating for more controls.

Richard Marles, who has been acting prime minister this week, met with Altman in San Francisco earlier this month. There was no mention of the hack at the meeting.

Marles, who was deployed to answer questions that trickled in over the course of the morning, said he wasn't sure what the OpenAI boss knew at the time of their meeting.

"What we would expect is that the government be notified in the most timely manner possible. And we have expressed our displeasure that that did not occur in this instance," he told reporters in Sydney.

Richard Marles said he wasn't sure what Sam Altman knew of the Medicare breach when they met earlier this month. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

That led to predictable criticism from those across the political aisle. Greens Senator David Shoebridge declared OpenAI treated the defence minister “like a mushroom”.

"It's an insult not just to him, it's an insult to Australia that should not be left untouched," he said.

OpenAI's vice president of global policy Ann O'Leary was in Canberra last week. She didn't touch on it either. While that doesn't mean she knew and didn't pass the message along, as my colleague Stephen Dziedzic reported, it certainly has officials annoyed.

There are several questions yet to answer, such as whether an AI-driven attack like this would even break Australian law as it stands. That's something the rapid review, announced today, will be looking into.

Loading

All smiles for a selfie as daggers drawn

All of this took place in the shadow of the prime minister's trip to the United States, where he was escalating Australia's fight against the social media giants.

From Apple's campus in Silicon Valley to the Big Apple, Albanese has been talking up his government's social media ban for under 16s and spruiking the proposed digital duty of care bill.

The draft legislation would require the tech giants to pre-emptively address harms and pave the way for giving users a choice to opt out of the algorithm.

ABC Politics in your inbox Sign up to the ABC Politics newsletter with Courtney Gould

In a rare intervention the Trump administration described the proposal as "extraterritorial censorship of protected speech" and called for exemptions for US-based platforms.

If that sounds familiar, it's because the opposition has been running a similar line in recent weeks. The Coalition is concerned the bill hands the minister too much power to determine what constitutes online harm.

Albanese hit back at his first opportunity, dismissing the criticism. But he went beyond linking the legislation to the protection of children, pointing also to misinformation, disinformation and polarisation online — exactly the things the Coalition has been saying it was concerned about.

"The truth is, this is having an impact on our entire society and how it functions with misinformation, disinformation, with the increased polarisation that we're seeing as well in the political system, where people are moving away from the centre and more and more to the extremes, be they of the left or the right," he said.

Asked about the apparently off-the-cuff remarks on Thursday, Albanese denied linking misinformation and disinformation to the draft digital duty of care.

US President Donald Trump and Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese smiling in a selfie on the sidelines of the UN on September 23, 2026. (Supplied: X)

Despite daggers being drawn between Australia and the US on social media, Albanese and Trump still posed for a smiley selfie at a welcome reception. A government source described the encounter as "warm".

These events always feel a little like diplomatic speed dating. Nowhere was that on show more than the prime minister's own Instagram account, where he posted several photos of his engagements over the week.

Buried four photos deep was a picture of Albanese and Japanese PM Sanae Takaichi. The pair met for the first time since the furore about the PM's gesture over the two crown melons she gifted him.

Curiously, no comment was provided on that one.

World.title: Cold case murder trial witness admits lying to police
World.content:
A key witness in a cold case murder trial over the disappearance of a Warrnambool man in 2006 has admitted to previously lying to police.

Steven Frederick Johnson, 74, has pleaded not guilty to one charge of murder in relation to the disappearance of 38-year-old Christopher Jarvis on June 13, 2006, from his Wangoom home near Warrnambool.

It is the crown's case that Mr Johnson orchestrated a violent attack on his tenant, Mr Jarvis, over $2,210 in unpaid rent, before disposing of his body and setting his car alight.

The defence argues that Mr Johnson wanted to lawfully solve the rental dispute and he had no involvement in the disappearance.

In the Supreme Court in Warrnambool on Thursday, the jury heard from a key witness, who cannot be legally named, who claimed to have assisted Mr Johnson with the alleged killing.

'Doesn't ring a bell, sorry'

During cross-examination earlier in the trial, defence lawyer Patrick Doyle SC suggested the man was not truthfully recalling events in a number of circumstances, including how well he knew Mr Jarvis.

The man told the jury he had only met Mr Jarvis when he had paid $100 to Mr Jarvis for marijuana, and on another occasion Mr Jarvis failed to provide the drugs or refund the man.

The jury trial is set down for five weeks. (ABC News: Jean Bell)

Mr Doyle suggested that the man knew Mr Jarvis better than he let on, and had met Mr Jarvis many times and had socialised with him.

The man denied this.

On Thursday, audio from a November 2022 police interview with the unnamed man was played in court.

In the recording, police explained to the man that they were speaking to people about the 2006 disappearance of Christopher Jarvis and that Mr Jarvis had the man on his contact list.

During that interview, the police officers asked whether he knew Mr Jarvis and the man told the officers he did not.

"Doesn't ring a bell, sorry," the man said in the recording.

The defence repeatedly put it to the man that he had lied to police in 2022 about knowing Mr Jarvis, before the man admitted he did.

"Well, that's fine. Yes, I did. I lied to them," he told the court.

When questioned on another detail in the 2022 police interview recording, the man denied lying to detectives.

"I didn't lie about it, I just didn't tell the truth," the man told the jury.

"Can you explain that distinction to us, please?" Mr Doyle asked the man.

There was a moment of silence in the court room before the cross-examination continued.

Memory issues

Earlier in the trial, the man told the jury that he had memory problems.

"Are you a bit selective when you invoke this problem with your memory?" Mr Doyle asked the man.

The man replied no, and said he had trouble remembering his children's birthdays.

On Thursday, the man reiterated to the court that he had memory issues.

"I'm not here to recall every single thing," he told the court.

"I'm not here using that as an excuse."

Earlier in the trial, the man had told the court Mr Johnson was "greedy" with money.

On Thursday, Mr Doyle asked the man whether he was exaggerating his client's "meanness" with money, after offering examples of where Mr Johnson might be perceived to have been financially generous.

"Everyone owed Steve money, according to Steve," the man replied.

Earlier, the jury heard the two men had met up numerous times in the days prior to Mr Johnson's arrest in November 2022, after police had been asking questions about Mr Jarvis's disappearance.

During his evidence, the man told the court Mr Johnson said to him on one occasion, "I'm too old to go to jail for this shit".

"He told me to keep me [sic] mouth f*****g shut and not say anything," the man said.

The trial continues.

World.title: Lachie Neale tribunal appeal LIVE: Could Lachie Neale serve his ban in round one next season instead of Saturday’s decider?
World.content:
Anderson has reiterated his earlier argument that the board could change Neale’s penalty to miss round one of next season and play in the grand final.

But he has yet to argue how they could make this finding.

“It needs to be a proportionate sentence - a fine or you miss round one next year are both more proportionate sentences, had the grand final been taken into account,” Anderson said.

World.title: Genre bans, ‘pokies pub’ loophole ditched in new NSW live music overhaul
World.content:
NationalNSWLive music Genre bans, ‘pokies pub’ loophole ditched in new NSW live music overhaul Kayla Olaya September 24, 2026 — 5:19pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Police and other state agencies will no longer be able to discriminate against particular genres played in live music venues under a new NSW music bill. Labor’s contemporary music bill marks its second legislative push to reinvigorate Sydney’s nightlife since the 2014 lockout laws, with the first focusing on venues and hospitality through the vibrancy reforms agenda, and the latest on protecting the music sector. A DJ at the Lord Gladstone in Chippendale. Audrey Richardson Now state government agencies and local councils can’t assess a live music event’s risk based on its music genre, whether through licensing conditions, development applications, or event approvals. In the past, police have tried to stop venues from booking music acts from specific genres, such as rap and drill.



Sydney rap group OneFour was the target of a licensing police campaign that prevented venues across the city from including them on their line-ups, according to a 2023 Netflix documentary. The group’s profile soared after a national tour in 2019 was cancelled. At the time, NSW Police admitted to “shutting down” the group’s concerts. Minister for Music and the Night-time Economy John Graham, who is also arts minister, said the new policy makes it clear that genre alone is not a risk and agencies will be expected to provide evidence to justify risk-based decisions. Young revellers enjoy a free public gig at Sydney Park. Audrey Richardson “Venues routinely were required to only play jazz or not play disco or not play rock music, or that was how we used to regulate by genre, and it’s totally inappropriate. We’ve removed all that,” Graham said. The new bill, passed on Thursday, incentivises venues to prioritise local, live music via additional operating hours and grants, after “pokies pubs” used Labor’s $150 million vibrancy reforms agenda to shove musicians into corners, playing covers, in order to access liquor and trading benefits.



Venues that regularly host original live music will now be tiered as “dedicated”, “significant” or “live music”, making them eligible for programs, extended trading hours or government grants depending on classification, instead of blanket eligibility for any that host live music. “The problem was you couldn’t tell the difference between a pokie venue and a music venue or a venue that was just selling alcohol. They were all treated the same when Liquor & Gaming looked at it,” Graham said. The crowd at DJ Buse Sagaga’s performance at an SES Radio event at Disco Pantera in Circular Quay. Peter V’landys could rule rugby league for another six years after officially becoming the most powerful administrator in the game’s 118-year history on Thursday. V’landys was appointed the code’s first executive chairman, making him effectively the chief executive of the NRL as well as chair of the Australian Rugby League Commission. Peter V’landys is switching from racing to rugby league. Oscar Colman “I am honoured every day to have the opportunity to give something back to rugby league and could not be more excited for the game’s future,” V’landys said in a statement announcing his appointment. “Rugby league is the greatest game of all, and we are going to take it to the world.” It has been speculated that V’landys could be paid as much as $3 million a year in the new position.



The post is set to run for just over three years, aligning with his new term on the Commission that will begin when he is up for re-election in February. Under term limits introduced five years ago, his time on the Commission will then be up in 2030. Loading However, he could be put forward by a majority of the other commissioners for an additional three years, taking him out to 2033, if they consider there are “exceptional circumstances” that justify the re-appointment. V’landys, as chairman, can make the same determination on individual commissioners if he sees fit.



V’landys’ appointment comes in a week in which the NRL has faced criticism over its failure to secure a big-name act to perform ahead of the grand final at Accor Stadium on Sunday week. Negotiations with Australian artist Tones and I fell over a fortnight before the decider and the parties have been at odds over the reasons. Peter V’landys and Tones and I. Tones and I’s management said she was only offered the pre-game slot on September 5, but NRL sources maintain discussions had been going on since early August and details of the proposed deal were communicated in advance of the offer itself. The sources are adamant that the ARIA award-winner’s team accepted the offer, but the arrangement collapsed because she did not want to sing her hit song Dance Monkey, rejecting her management’s claim turned it down because of a scheduling conflict.



The NRL has said it will direct $1 million to junior rugby league rather than using the money to pay a grand final act. World.title: Xuan Anh Banh Cuon

It might look lo-fi, but this pasta bar dials up the warmth and charm. Lampshades are made from pasta colanders, cutlery is held in empty tomato cans and the on-tap sangiovese is poured into tumblers. The living is easy here, so relax.

It might look lo-fi, but this pasta bar dials up the warmth and charm. Lampshades are made from pasta colanders, cutlery is held in empty tomato cans and the on-tap sangiovese is poured into tumblers. The living is easy here, so relax.

World.title: Allegations of favouritism, 'unsustainable' workloads at Education Ministry's curriculum division
World.content:
A damning review has found serious problems including allegations of favouritism and lack of public sector values in the Education Ministry's curriculum division.

The division is responsible for the government's curriculum rewrite and has been under scrutiny this week after multiple whistleblowers alleged attempts to subvert the Official Information Act.

The ministry commissioned the review in response to concerns raised through confidential channels and 107 provided information.

It found:

Widespread concern about favouritism by senior leaders, especially in relation to the many temporary appointments in Te Poutāhū | Curriculum Centre

Widespread concern regarding the application of public sector values and principles including fair and transparent appointment processes, conflict of interest management and concerns about the obligation to give free and frank advice to the minister not being met

Unreasonable or unprofessional workplace behaviours exhibited or tolerated by leaders

Strategy, work planning and commissioning

Organisational design and resourcing, particularly the extensive use of contractors or other temporary arrangements

Deeply held concerns about speaking up. This included fear of negative career consequences, which it was considered others had experienced, and because of

A small number of other examples of concerns relating to diversity, inclusion or equity, and sexual harassment.

The review report said some staff made positive comments, others described the workplace as toxic, and many were in the middle.

"The strongest concerns of almost all participants relate to workload and well-being. Feedback consistently described workloads as unsustainable, characterised by constant urgency and short deadlines. It was considered that more could be done to manage workloads and timeframes," the review report said.

The report said many participants were not convinced senior leaders were giving the government free and frank advice, especially with regard to the time required for implementing changes.

Some participants said some former employees left because they had difficulty being politically neutral, the report said.

"Some people spoken to were extremely passionate about their work, and the reviewer could see how this could give rise to an interpretation that they may not be willing to serve the government of the day if they disagreed with the decisions," the report said.

"However, in many cases participants described a desire for further explanation of the context or rationale of an instruction they received, or clarity about where certain instructions were coming from.

"Many referred to the opaqueness of instructions, in that they were not always sure whether an instruction was coming from the minister's office or whether it was a decision of senior leadership."

Many participants said the curriculum centre's leadership was outdated and authoritarian, the report stated.

Examples included unreasonable and intimidating behaviours, a general prevalence of swearing - though not at people, and rudeness.

Some participants said they had seen bullying, others said they had not but gave examples of less-than-ideal leadership practices.

"However, in the course of other parts of their interviews they would describe behaviours that may amount to 'indirect' examples of unreasonable behaviours (such as exclusion from work, gaslighting, threats about job security, and retaliation for voicing work-related concerns)," the report said.

World.title: Former Kamo Wildlife Sanctuary lion Cleo dies, animal rescue group says
World.content:
One of four lions who faced being put down at a Whangārei animal park has died in her sleep, an animal rescue group says.

In a post on Facebook, HUHANZ said Cleo - a lion based at Kamo Wildlife Park in Northland - had severe non-regenerative anaemia and there was a high suspicion she had internal cancer.

"Before any further intervention was needed, Cleo quietly slipped away in her sleep," the post read.

"Our team have gathered around her, surrounding Cleo with the love, tenderness and respect she deserves. And perhaps there is some comfort in knowing that when Cleo showed us something was wrong, we acted immediately.

"We got her the veterinary care she needed and, importantly, we now understand that there was an underlying illness that we could not have fixed."

Cleo was born at Kamo Wildlife Park and spent her 20 years there.

Cleo is suspected to have had cancer. HUHANZ

Last November, the the directors of Kamo Wildlife Sanctuary announced the sanctuary would close and the five remaining elderly lions would be euthanised.

Operator Janette Vallance said the park's owners, Bolton Equities, made the difficult decision to euthanise the cats, which were aged between 18 and 21.

"There were no real options left. The staff and I are devastated."

HUHA stepped in and the park was purchased by ethical investors and the Lionhearts Project Trust was set up to provide for the animals' going forward, the NZ Herald reported.

At its peak in the early 2000s the park was home to 33 big cats, including lions, white tigers, leopards and cheetahs.

At that time it was called Zion Wildlife Gardens and run by Craig Busch, better known as "The Lion Man", and his mother Patricia Busch.

Busch became a national celebrity in 2004 thanks to the TV series Lion Man, and the park put Whangārei on the domestic tourism map.

However, the park ran into financial difficulties in 2006, and was bailed out by Patricia Busch, who became the sole director.

In 2009, after senior keeper Dalu Mncube was killed by a tiger, the then Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry (MAF) ordered the temporary closure of the park for safety and management improvements.

Another closure was ordered in 2014 for enclosure upgrades, this time by MAF's successor, the Ministry for Primary Industries.

Bolton Equities, which is owned by businessman Murray Bolton, bought Zion Wildlife Gardens in 2014 and reopened it as Kamo Wildlife Sanctuary in 2021.

World.title: Auckland Transport explores changes to level crossing after student's death
World.content:
Audio player for " AT explores changes to level crossing after student death " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/community/1558816%2Fauckland-transport-explores-changes-to-level-crossing-after-student-s-death

AT explores changes to level crossing after student death Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

Two weeks on from a tragedy at a level crossing in Mount Albert, Auckland Transport officials have met with residents to get their views on changes to level crossings in the area.

Intended to improve safety and traffic flow, the changes will be expensive and disruptive.

Auckland Transport is talking to residents about six level crossings from Kingsland to Mount Albert.

Local residents Rob and Merla were among those who went to find out more about the level crossing changes at the Mount Albert Community Centre on Wednesday evening.

"They're not ideal the way they are, and we're keen to see the trains increase in frequency, so something has to be done. Otherwise, the traffic will be banking up into the neighbourhoods more and more, the more they close for a train to come through," Rob said.

Merla was concerned about the risk of more fatalities.

"There's been a recent one here in this neighbourhood, so it's quite prescient at the moment."

Flowers laid at Baldwin Ave train station where a Mount Albert Grammar student was fatally hit by a train. Caitlin McGee

Options for improving the crossings include raising roads, lowering the rail line, building road bridges or underpasses, and even removing homes to make new road connections.

Partial or full closure is an option for some crossings.

Rob said it's frustrating the best options are always the most expensive.

"I'm in favour of doing the right thing rather than the cheap thing. Hopefully they'll take some of that on board and give us the best solution."

Safety was also on the radar for local resident, Mark, after the recent death at Baldwin Ave Station

"When something happens, and my understanding is that's not the first time we've had something happen there, it raises (safety) closer to the top of the list."

Any changes needed to maintain connectivity through the area, he said.

"We've taken the kids through to primary school using the walking buses, and now they're up to high school level we use the public transport as well, so we love the trains. We're glad that we've got the new connections, but ...we don't want to do this at the cost of the liveability of our local areas either."

Ailsa Barr wanted to know how options for the busy Morningside Drive level crossing could impact her property which was affected by the 2023 storms.

"...because of the fact that we were impacted by the flood and everything gets put on hold for a long time, we're now potentially facing that again. I see that as a problem," Barr said.

Jenny Rasch has also been through flooding and the ensuing repairs. She worried about what could happen if the changes go ahead.

Rasch said local businesses had been trying to rebuild after COVID which had a "huge impact".

"Eden Park are now opening up to more concerts and more games and more things like that. So you want the area to become more vibrant and more people in it, but (if) you're going to start getting rid of dwellings and rerouting the roads that's going to impact everybody."

Auckland Transport head of level crossings Tom Willetts said safety improvements had been made to all level crossings in Auckland, including gates at all pedestrian level crossings.

"The next stage from that, as we look to increase train frequencies in future years, is to look to remove or replace level crossings further because that really does mitigate the risk."

Willetts said people are naturally concerned about disruptions from construction tied up with removing or replacing the crossings.

"We're working very hard to better understand the communities so that we can mitigate those impacts both in the design of the final outcome of the removal or the replacement, but also so we can build into our thinking around how the replacements or removals will be constructed."

He said each site had its own challenges.

"We have to consider impacts on the local community, but we also have to consider engineering technicalities such as ground conditions and topography, slopes and such like."

Willetts said once AT has the community feedback, they'll review the options and make a final decision with Auckland Council.

World.title: Political donations tracker: Breakaway Te Tai Tokerau Party gets its first big cheque
World.content:
The breakaway Te Tai Tokerau Party has attracted a $50,000 donation as it aims to win the electorate that bears its name.

RNZ is tracking the money flowing to the parties this election year and where it is coming from.

The donation to Te Tai Tokerau Party came via Richard Allen and is listed as being from the Stanley Howard Fund.

Te Tai Tokerau party was founded by Mariameno Kapa-Kingi, who won electorate from Labour in 2023 when she was a Te Pāti Māori member.

After a split with Te Pāti Māori, Kapa-Kingi announced the formation of the new party in May. She is standing in the Te Tai Tokerau electorate and the party has announced Kyla Campbell-Kamariera as its first list candidate.

Since the last update by RNZ on September 11, ACT has received another two donations, including $50,000 from property developer Christopher Reeve and $25,870 from Mike Johnson. This takes the party’s total of large donations to $2.1 million.

Reeve is a long-time donor to ACT and has given over $500,000 to the party since 2017. He’s given to National once in 2021 via Tawata Farms Ltd.

To date, coalition parties have received 73 percent of declared donations.

Here’s where things stand, as of September 24, across all parties for declared donations of over $20,000.

When the donations made to the parties in the governing coalition are combined, the spread looks as below.

Who are this election's big donors?

The following donors have given $100,000 or more so far in 2026.

Not all donors are individuals. Companies, trusts and unions also give to political parties. The chart below shows the split between organisational and individual giving over $20,000 for each party.

In the 2023 election, unions gave $335,000 to Labour. National received no donations from unions, but did receive more than $1m from businesses.

How much bigger could the donation pot grow?

How we analysed the data

All original data comes from the Electoral Commission website. RNZ's analysis normalises names which may appear more than once, but with different treatment. For example a John Smith and J Smith with the same address are updated to both be John Smith. In some instances where people have given individually as well as jointly their names are collated. Donation dates are taken from the "date received by party" information. In some cases one donation entry will consist of several donations made over time. The date received is the date on the donation return and should be the date the total donated by the donor tipped over $20,000.

World.title: Growth advocacy group wants visas for 'exceptional talent' with no job offer required
World.content:
Audio player for " Growth NZ wants visas for 'exceptional talent' with no job offer required " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/business/1558723%2Fgrowth-advocacy-group-wants-visas-for-exceptional-talent-with-no-job-offer-required

Growth NZ wants visas for 'exceptional talent' with no job offer required Checkpoint Download MP3 7m

A growth advocacy group wants to let up to 300 "exceptionally talented people" a year move to New Zealand with no job offer required.

Growth New Zealand is floating the idea of a "Catalyst Visa", where unlike other options people would not need a job offer or sponsor ahead of their arrival.

Applicants would have to prove they're top talent in their field, with a record of " internationally exceptional achievement".

Successful applications would need to start "qualifying work" within 12 months of arriving, and after three years they'd be eligible to apply for residency, if they're still in the right kind of work.

Growth NZ co-founder Maya Pan told Checkpoint while there was already "outstanding" talent in New Zealand, the country was still lacking specific capibilities.

"People who have scaled global companies, if they've raised serious capital overseas, if they've taken breakthrough ideas from the lab into the market or built high performing technical teams and seen rapid growth, there just aren't as many people like that within a small country."

Pan said that there were a number of areas in need of specific skills.

"Even within existing large corporates in New Zealand, you start to need specialists at that strategic layer."

She said dozens of companies had told her product management was one key area that was missing workers with certain knowledge.

"That's kind of a relatively new domain within New Zealand, and there aren't as many examples of strategic product managers in technical roles here where they actually set a vision for a product area."

Pan said an independent panel would set the specific criteria for the visa applicants, and a dedicated team within Immigration New Zealand would assess individual applications.

While other visa options are already available, Pan said the catalyst visa offered entry on conditions that didn't currently apply to any other visa.

"[One] thing that is not provided with current visa pathways is the ability to be self-employed and start your own business or the ability to work on multiple advisory roles across many companies."

"They could figure out a path with the accredited employer work visa, but one issue with that is you do need to have that job offer up front. So that's quite a lot of pressure both ways to commit in terms of making sure it's the right fit and the right scope and that you'd like living in New Zealand."

After living in the Silicon Valley for the last 13 years, Pan said she had seen first hand the desire to move to New Zealand.

"I have friends and colleagues, former colleagues there, and it's on a weekly basis that I'm hearing from one of them... I'm really interested, I'm seriously looking into moving to New Zealand."

"If you look at the geopolitical environment, if you look at the safety and natural environment and of the benefits of raising a family here, it's never been more appealing."

Pan said 300 was a "modest initial cap" for the number of visas granted, and nowhere near as high as other countries offering the scheme.

"The UK, Singapore, Australia, the US all offer this exceptional talent type of visa where you don't need a job offer... if we were using the same ratio in the US or UK use, we would have 900 of these exceptional specialists a year."

"It's not a high volume of immigration. We have 40,000 or 50,000 accredited employer work visas issued a year. So it's really a drop in the bucket if you look at it that way."

World.title: Myriad of drugs seized after more than 80 search warrants executed across country
World.content:
A myriad of drugs have been seized by police after more than 80 search warrants were executed across the country.

Detective Inspector Tom Gollan said the joint operation with law enforcement in Australia focused on organised crime and - in particular - airports and borders.

Golan said 34 people were arrested.

"We know that these substances create harm amongst communities including addictions, but drugs also attract violence, organised crime and other serious criminal activity," he said.

"Those peddling illicit substances across our community are making profits off of their harm, and authorities are continuing to apply pressure to disrupt their criminal enterprises."

Police found cannabis grow houses in Auckland and seized more than a quarter of a tonne of the class C drug.

Customs Integrated and Targeted Operations Centre Manager, Bruce Berry said the week of action strengthened the coordinated work already taking place across borders.

"Customs works closely with Police and our international partners every day to detect and disrupt the criminal networks moving illicit drugs across borders.

Methaphetamine, cocaine and opium were amongst the other drugs seized.

World.title: Dannevirke Community Hospital pauses new patient admissions as Health NZ seeks staff
World.content:
Audio player for " Health NZ provides workforce support to Dannevirke Hospital " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/health/1558622%2Fdannevirke-community-hospital-pauses-new-patient-admissions-as-health-nz-seeks-staff

Health NZ provides workforce support to Dannevirke Hospital Checkpoint Download MP3 5m

Health New Zealand has put a temporary halt on Dannevirke Community Hospital taking new patients while it finds more clinical staff, following a number of resignations.

Local doctors in the Tararua District have raised concerns about referring patients there because of safety risks, and the health agency has carried out an audit of the hospital this week.

Geoff Gwyn, the regional director planning, funding and outcomes for the central region, said new admissions would be paused for the next 30 days while Health NZ provided "additional clinical workforce support".

The hospital is run by Tararua Health Group, which also operates the Pahiatua Medical Centre, where staff have raised concerns over unsafe workloads and delays.

Gywn said the priority was "ensuring people continue to have access to safe healthcare services while THG works on a plan to stabilise its workforce and support the long-term delivery of services in Dannevirke".

Pausing new admissions to the hospital was a precautionary measure.

He said current patients would be looked after and maternity services would continue as normal.

Patient Voice Aotearoa's Malcolm Mulholland said he was confused by the development.

"It effectively becomes a patient-less hospital, I've never heard of one of those," he told Checkpoint.

GPs were not referring patients to the hospital because of "clinically unsafe practices", Mulholland said.

He did not yet know how many staff would be brought in by Health NZ to help.

THG should not retain the contract to run the hospital, he said.

"They need to kick them out."

World.title: Government hits pause on council amalgamation plan until after election
World.content:
Audio player for " Government pulls handbrake on local government reforms " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/politics/1552378%2Fgovernment-hits-pause-on-council-amalgamation-plan-until-after-election

Government pulls handbrake on local government reforms Checkpoint Download MP3 8m

The Government has told mayors around the country it's deferring decisions on amalgamating councils until after the election.

RMA Reform Minister Chris Bishop and Local Government Minister Simon Watts said they would be taking additional time before deciding which proposals, part of the Head Start local government reform process, should progress to the detailed design stage.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6405514951112

Eighteen proposals were submitted in August against the Government's objectives for a simpler, more effective and accountable local government system.

"While the overall quality of proposals was high, none came with the unanimous view of the region, and some needed further analysis before they can progress. These are important gaps we must fill in prior to making final decisions," Watts said.

Particular areas that required further development included ensuring fair and effective representation with streamlined governance, and the transfer and delivery of regional functions, the ministers said.

Local Government Minister Simon Watts and RMA Reform Minister Chris Bishop when the amalgamation was announced. SAMUEL RILLSTONE / RNZ

"Rather than asking councils to commit further time and resources to finalise proposals now, the Government will now work to fill in these gaps over the next few months. Cabinet will consider these proposals in early-2027."

Watts denied the government had misjudged the complexity of local government reform.

"We haven't underestimated it. We are committed to getting this right.

"We don't want to be making decisions this close to the election, and we've got a few gaps in the proposals that we want to work with councils on."

The reforms were among the largest the country had seen in the past few decades, he said.

"Taking time until after the election to work with the councils to do that is the sensible thing to do."

Addressing criticism over the delay, he said he understood some mayors were "enthusiastic about change and reform".

"It was a voluntary process, and councils put together high-quality proposals.

"There's no wasted effort or wasted money in that regard."

Bishop said the Government continued to expect proposals endorsed by Cabinet to be developed in detail and considered for final approval in 2027, with Head Start changes intended to be in place ahead of the 2028 local government elections."

"Work is also continuing on the backstop process for areas that do not progress through Head Start. Decisions on that process will be informed by lessons from the Head Start pathway, consultation feedback and further advice from officials. We continue to expect decisions on this in early 2027."

RMA Reform Minister Chris Bishop. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Ministers made promises they couldn't keep - Wellington mayor

But Wellington City mayor Andrew Little said the announcement showed the Government was not serious about the process.

Little, who is also co-chair of the Wellington and Wairarapa Mayoral Forum, said councils across the region put forward strong proposals that met the Government's requirements and would have worked, while spending nearly $250,000 collectively to put forward a proposal before the recent deadline - which was "significant time and ratepayer money".

Little told reporters councils had done everything the Government had asked of them, and they had "been let down".

Audio player for " Andrew Little reacts to decision to pause council amalgamations " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/politics/1552378%2Fgovernment-hits-pause-on-council-amalgamation-plan-until-after-election

Andrew Little reacts to decision to pause council amalgamations Midday Report Download MP3 6m

It was "poor organisation" - the government had made a promise it couldn't keep, Little said, as it clearly didn't have the numbers to enact reform.

He said there had been mixed views among residents and ratepayers on whether to amalgamate or not, "but on balance people supported it".

The government's attribution of the delay to the fact that the proposals were not unanimous - an aspect that wasn't requested of them in the first place, Little said - was "effectively shifting the goalposts".

Andrew Little. RNZ / Baz MacDonald

Millions had been spent nationwide by councils in preparing headstart proposals, he said.

If the government wanted change in time for 2028, councils were "rapidly running out of time", Little said.

"Ministers asked us to move quickly. We did exactly that. It is now clear the Government was not ready to follow through, and didn't have enough support around the Cabinet table."

Little said ministers made promises they couldn't keep and have now abandoned the process.

"Wellington ratepayers are entitled to ask why they were asked to pay for an exercise the Government was not prepared to complete.

"At a time when councils are doing everything possible to keep costs under control, facing an arbitrary rates cap that will affect services and facilities that communities rely on, spending nearly a quarter of a million dollars on a process that goes nowhere is unacceptable."

He said the three-month deadline was "totally unreasonable" and criteria continually shifted.

"We met all of the government's requirements to get a proposal in before the deadline.

"The only party that has not thought through their policy is central government themselves. It claims it is wanting to simplify local government, but today it has confirmed it has no plan for how to achieve this."

LGNZ president Rehette Stoltz. RNZ / Angus Dreaver

'Communities will not tolerate ratepayer money being spent on unclear processes'

Local Government New Zealand (LGNZ) president Rehette Stoltz said people were frustrated after they "moved heaven and earth" to meet an unrealistic deadline for proposals.

LGNZ was only informed of the delay on Thursday, shortly before it was announced publicly, she said.

"The minister rang me this morning to give me a heads up that an announcement would be made at 11, and that was the first that we heard, and then our members were informed.

"We have really stretched local government only for us to find out today that nothing will proceed before the election.

"I think it's unfair on local government and councils, councillors, as well as staff.

"The time and money, the effort, the relationships that were damaged with a rushed process, that is all in play now and we are just processing it," she said.

Addressing Watts' comments about gaps in proposals, she said councils did not know what was missing and what needed to change.

"We have not received any feedback yet, but when this was announced earlier in the year we made it very clear with the minister, with officials, that three months is insufficient for us to consult with our communities and our neighbouring councils.

"It's not fair on councils and on ratepayers," she said.

Local government was open to discussions over reform, she added, and hoped that the work they had done would not be wasted.

"There's just too much uncertainty at the moment," she said.

Selwyn district mayor Lydia Gliddon. RNZ / ANNA SAREGNT

More mayors react

Selwyn district mayor Lydia Gliddon said it was disappointing that councils had been asked to quickly develop and submit proposals only for the decisions to now be deferred.

"Selwyn invested significant effort into this process, including consulting with our communities. We owe it to those who took the time to share their views to ensure their voices continue to be heard," she said.

The council remained committed to working with the government to achieve the best outcome for its communities.

"The position of Selwyn residents has been very clear. Through our consultation, people told us overwhelmingly that they wanted Selwyn to become a standalone unitary authority, and we will continue to support and advocate for that view going forward," she said.

"As New Zealand's fastest-growing district, Selwyn faces unique growth, infrastructure and service delivery challenges.

"Our district is experiencing growth at a scale few other parts of New Zealand are facing, and it's important any future local government arrangements recognise those realities and give our communities a strong voice."

The Waitaki District Council straddles two regional council boundaries, working across the different planning systems, regulatory approaches and policy frameworks.

Waitaki district mayor Mel Tavendale. Jackie Tav

Waitaki district mayor Mel Tavendale said it created duplication, burdening ratepayers and the council with added cost, time and pressure, which was unsustainable.

She did not want to lose the momentum for change after councils invested a lot of time, money and effort to develop a solution on a tight deadline.

"The need for reform has not gone away, and we are disappointed because we did the work asked of us," she said.

"Waitaki put forward a credible, practical and well-considered proposal in good faith that reflects communities of interest and responds directly to the need for greater scale, capability and affordability."

Tavendale said Waitaki wanted a seat at the design table so that local communities could decide their own future.

The council has faced flak after originally proposing a 45 percent rates rise to plug a $14 million operating deficit, prompting backtracking, death threats and protest before settling on an average district-wide rates increase of about 17 percent.

Hundreds of Waitaki ratepayers rallied on 25 June 2026 against a 17 percent rates hike they say is unaffordable and will force people to choose between paying their bill or necessities like power and food. RNZ / Tess Brunton

"Ministers have been critical of Waitaki's rates rises, but those increases are being driven in part by a system that clearly needs reform," Tavendale said.

The mayors of Timaru, Mackenzie, Waimate and Waitaki districts lodged a single unitary authority proposal that would see a new region stretch from Aoraki Mount Cook to the coast, and from Ashburton to Waitaki.

Tavendale said it would create a stronger regional voice and ensure rural communities remained heard.

"The government also needs to consider how it will support local communities through the change process, so the weight of reform does not fall entirely on ratepayers."

Labour said the government's plans for council reform were an embarassing and expensive distraction.

Government has delivered a 'false start', Labour says

Local government spokesperson Tangi Utikere said ministers Chris Bishop and Simon Watts had promised a "head start", but delivered a "false start".

"They gave councils three months to spend time and money planning major structural change, only to pull the plug on getting anything done before the election.

"That's a huge embarrassment for a government that has spent months telling councils this was a priority."

He said Labour was not opposed to local government reform.

"There are sensible conversations to be had about councils working together, sharing services and delivering better value.

"But timing matters - local economies are struggling, businesses are under pressure and construction workers and tradies are crying out for work."

World.title: Live: Lachie Neale faces AFL Appeals Board in last-ditch attempt to overturn ban
World.content:
It's crunch time for Brisbane's Lachie Neale as the dual Brownlow Medallist tries to overturn a ban at the AFL Appeal Board so he can play in the grand final against Fremantle.

Neale lost on Tuesday with the AFL Tribunal upholding his ban for striking Hawthorn's Jack Ginnivan.

Now two days before the decider, Neale has his appeal, while we wait for Brisbane and Fremantle to announce their grand final teams later today.

Follow all the proceedings and team news in the live blog.

World.title: Would you travel over 50 hours for your team? This Dockers fan is
World.content:
Would you go to the ends of the earth for your favourite team?

That's pretty much what Rafe English is doing.

The university student, originally from Perth, is undertaking a journey of more than 50 hours across the globe — from Illinois in the US to Melbourne — to see his beloved Fremantle Dockers play in the grand final.

Purple army heads east The Nullarbor has turned purple this week as Fremantle Dockers supporters make the long journey to Melbourne for Saturday's AFL grand final.

"I would fly from anywhere to see Freo play in this grand final," English told the ABC during a seven-hour layover in Dallas, Texas, one of many stops on his epic journey.

"I say every year is our year, but in the back of my mind, I did have that sense that we were going to Docker it up.

"I knew when we strung together those last couple of games that I was going to be flying to Melbourne."

Love and devotion

From his university in Normal, Illinois, English has watched fervently as his team climbed to the top of the ladder.

Footy fans filthy as airfares soar ahead of grand final Return airfares to Melbourne have hit $6,000 ahead of Saturday's AFL Grand Final as Fremantle and Brisbane fans scramble for seats.

"Early mornings, but it's all worth it in the end when you love the club this much," he said.

His journey started with a two-hour train ride from central Illinois to Chicago, where he spent the night.

English then took a bus and a train for an hour to the airport, followed by a two-and-a-half hour flight to Dallas, where he boarded his final 17.5 hour flight to Melbourne.

This is the second ever grand final for the Dockers. They face the Brisbane Lions at the MCG on Saturday. (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor)

Dockers and dad

During his stopover in Dallas, English explained why the Dockers meant so much to him.

"Obviously what the club has built, and what they mean and stand for, but for me it's the memories that I've had with my dad, and growing up, and that real connection," he said.

Mr English is posting about his more than 50-hour journey on social media. (Supplied: Instagram)

He recalled how sad he was when the Dockers lost the 2013 grand final against the Hawthorn Hawks by just 15 points.

"I don't think I spoke for about two or three days, as a nine-year-old, I was devastated," Mr English said.

From disaster to destiny, it's taken a decade to rebuild the Dockers Football is full of sliding doors moments. Just ask the Fremantle Dockers, who crashed and burned in 2016 and are now on the cusp of winning their first-ever premiership.

Many fans are traversing more than 3,000 kilometres across Australia to catch the grand final, but English's journey makes the drive across the Nullarbor pale in comparison.

As the crow flies, the distance between Normal, Illinois and Melbourne is more than 15,000km — which is roughly five times the distance between Perth and Victoria's capital.

English's flight is scheduled to land in Melbourne at 5am on Saturday, where he will reunite with family and watch his team try to take the premiership.

"It would mean the world to me to see Fremantle lift up that cup after all these years of devotion," he said.

World.title: Matildas name three uncapped players in squad for October friendlies
World.content:
After suffering a gut-wrenching ACL injury on the eve of her potential Matildas debut, midfielder Hana Lowry has been handed a national team recall.

Coach Joe Montemurro has named three uncapped players for his 26-player squad, which will face world number three Germany and world number 47 Haiti in Europe in October.

One of them is Lowry, who was previously selected in 2024 but was ruled out with a knee injury, and has been building ever since.

The 23-year-old signed a deal to move from A-League Women's club Sydney FC to Norway earlier this year and has impressed, scoring a goal and assisting another in her first seven games with the new club.

Former Sydney defender Tori Tumeth has also received a maiden call-up after shining for the Vancouver Rise in Canada's Northern Super League. At the same time, Melbourne Victory's Courtney Newbon is the third potential debutant.

But the Australians will be without stars Alanna Kennedy and Charlize Rule due to injury, while Arsenal midfielder Kyra Cooney-Cross also won't join the team as she continues her return to football.

Midfielder Isabel Gomez and goalkeeper Ilona Melegh have been dropped after they were part of the side for their two-game series against Mexico in June.

Superstar Sam Kerr has been named to feature in the friendlies. (Getty Images: Dustin Satloff)

Defenders Charli Grant and Alexia Apostolakis, along with midfielder Daniela Galic, will return to the national team set-up.

European stars Mary Fowler, Caitlin Foord, Ellie Carpenter and Steph Catley have also been named, as well as Gotham City's Sam Kerr.

The October international window marks a crucial stage in the Matildas' preparation for the FIFA Women's World Cup, which gets underway in Brazil next June.

There are only a handful of international breaks before the showpiece tournament, meaning every game is crucial for Australia as they look to build on their fourth-place finish in 2023.

"We have a good mix of experience, players returning to the squad and players earning their first senior call-ups, which is important as we build towards the Women's World Cup," Montemurro said.

"We want to use these games to strengthen our connections, build confidence and continue developing as a team.

"Germany will test us against one of Europe's leading teams, while Haiti will provide a different style and perspective. Both will be valuable as we continue to prepare for the FIFA Women's World Cup."

Matildas squad

Alexia Apostolakis, Mackenzie Arnold (GK), Ellie Carpenter, Steph Catley, Alex Chidiac, Caitlin Foord, Mary Fowler, Daniela Galic, Charli Grant, Winonah Heatley, Sam Kerr, Chloe Lincoln (GK), Hana Lowry, Leticia McKenna, Holly McNamara, Alana Murphy, Courtney Nevin, Courtney Newbon (GK), Jamilla Rankin, Hayley Raso, Amy Sayer, Remy Siemsen, Kaitlyn Torpey, Tori Tumeth, Emily van Egmond, Clare Wheeler

World.title: From Kylie to Lachie, everything you need to know for the AFL grand final
World.content:
The 2026 AFL grand final is almost upon us, as the Brisbane Lions look to make history with their second threepeat in 25 years, and the Fremantle Dockers look to win their first flag since joining the league in 1995.

Here's everything you need to know about the game.

When is the 2026 AFL grand final?

The game starts 2.30pm (AEST) on Saturday, September 26 at the MCG.

That's 12.30pm for those watching in Western Australia, and 2pm for South Australia.

Which teams are playing in the grand final?

The Brisbane Lions are facing off with the Fremantle Dockers.

This is Brisbane's fourth grand final in a row, losing to Collingwood in 2023, before beating Sydney and Geelong in the following years.

Should they win, it would be the second threepeat in their history, following 2001-2003, and it would see them join Melbourne (1939-41 and 1955-57) as one of the only two teams to record the feat twice.

Meanwhile, Fremantle is yet to win a premiership after joining the league in 1995. This is the club's second grand final following its loss to Hawthorn in 2013.

Over their past six games against each other, the ledger is tied at 3-3, with the Dockers winning their most recent clash at the Gabba in round 13 this year.

How can you watch watch and listen to the grand final?

The game will be on Channel 7 and 7Plus, but be very aware that it will not be shown on Kayo or Fox Sports. It is the only game of the entire AFL season that is exclusive to Channel 7.

To listen to the grand final, join your local ABC Sport radio team, and follow along with the ABC Sport live blog at abc.net.au.

When will Kylie Minogue be performing?

Australia's pop princess should be on stage from about 1.30pm. Again, be very aware that Minogue's performance is pre-game and is not halftime entertainment. There is no halftime entertainment.

Other performers will be G Flip, musical actor Michael Paynter on the national anthem, and of course Mike Brady doing Up There Cazaly during the retiree motorcade.

The Wiggles will be performing at Friday's grand final parade through Melbourne.

Who will be lining up for the Lions and Dockers?

At this point we don't know.

Teams will be announced about 6pm (AEST) today, but before that we'll have to see if Lions superstar Lachie Neale's tribunal appeal against a one-match ban gets up.

ABC Sport's Andrew McGarry will be live blogging every moment of the appeal, with the case set to get underway at 4pm.

Should Neale miss out, Noah Answerth is the most likely player to come in for the Lions. The injured Brennan Cox is a chance to come in for the Dockers, but it looks odds on that the Dockers will be unchanged from their preliminary final victory over the Swans.

Who will present the cup to the winners?

The Lions have picked Simon Black, a Brownlow medallist and champion midfielder from that first threepeat, while the Dockers have gone with Shaun McManus, who debuted in Fremantle's inaugural season before playing 228 games.

World.title: 'That's why Taliban is scared': Cyclist's incredible journey to silver
World.content:
The easy part for Fariba Hashimi was winning a silver medal in the women's cycling road race at the Asian Games.

The nearly impossible part for the cyclist from Afghanistan was trying to train in her country. To do that, she dressed as a man in a place where women have few rights.

"All the time when I was going to training I was dressing as a guy," she said.

She said she also hid her face to avoid being recognised.

"Because sometimes when they recognised me, they were trying to throw … stone[s] or hitting me," she said.

Hashimi, who is 23, won silver overnight AEST in a time of 2 hours, 50 minutes, 5 seconds, which marked another leg in a journey that began in 2021 when she left Afghanistan, escaping to Italy with the help of former road racing world champion Alessandra Cappellotto.

Hashimi (left) with gold medallist Guo Li of China and bronze medallist Leung Wing Yee of Hong Kong. (Getty Images: Cen Yunpeng/Xinhu)

"In 2021, when the Taliban moved into my country, I escaped my country because I wanted to follow my dream," she said.

"I want to show the Afghanistan women in the world that … we can have an opportunity."

Hashimi talked about having many dreams for women in Afghanistan, dreams for herself and dreams that might take time to be realised.

"I'm really, really happy and I'm full of emotion. I don't know how I can explain it for you," she said.

"I hope one day I come back in my country and ride the streets of Kabul — and riding with the women side-by-side to share the same passion.

"And I hope in the future changing some things.

"I think we are really tired of the situation of our country and I hope the Taliban is watching. I know how much one woman can be powerful, and that's why Taliban is scared [of] women."
