World.title: Football is full of sliding doors moments. Just ask the Fremantle Dockers
World.content:
Football is full of sliding doors moments. Just ask the Fremantle Dockers.

If Lachie Weller hadn't requested a trade to Gold Coast, would Andrew Brayshaw be at the club?

What if Adelaide had taken Hayden Young instead of Fischer McAsey in the 2019 draft?

AFL recruitment, especially at the draft, is an element of good preparation and good luck.

The current Dockers list has been described as "pure" from a recruitment point of view, with no father-son selections, no free agents and no players taken with AFL concessions or free agent compensation picks.

The Fremantle squad that trained this week for a grand final has been carefully put together. (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor)

And it all began in 2016.

"It was pretty clear the list was old, but finishing so high on the ladder in 2015, it's sort of hard to basically finish on top and then enter a rebuild phase," Fremantle's former national recruiting manager Brad Lloyd said.

"We entered [2016] with an old group, which is fine to have an older group, but you need to be getting the results.

"And that wasn't evident through the start of '16."

Grand final fever grips Freo Purple reigns in Fremantle, the home of the Dockers who will play their first AFL grand final in 13 years, with even the public buses running on "Wharfie Time".

The Dockers were winless until round nine that season, after winning 18 games the year before.

"Some decisions were made to reset again, which ended up in some pretty experienced players finishing up and the club going back to the draft," Lloyd said.

Starting over

Lloyd, who joined the Dockers in 2008, was no stranger to building a list — he was part of the recruitment team which put together Fremantle's 2013 grand final side.

In 2008 and 2009, Fremantle used 23 draft picks to bring together the core of the squad that would be competitive across the mid-2010s.

Ross Lyon coached Fremantle to the 2013 grand final and 2015 minor premiership, but the side fell off a cliff in 2016. (AAP Image: Gary Day)

"We'd had a really good crack at it through '13, '14 and '15, and played in a grand final and in preliminary finals, but couldn't quite secure a premiership," Lloyd recalled.

"We had the oldest list and were now struggling on field [in 2016] and decided to sort of enter another build to get going again."

From career crossroad to grand final When Neil Erasmus runs out onto the MCG on Saturday, it will vindicate his decision to stay at Fremantle after almost leaving a year ago.

Lloyd believed a complete rebuild would take between six and eight years, and Fremantle embarked on drafting and trading in players it thought would deliver success.

It's been 10 years since that decision was made and the Dockers have resolutely stuck to the plan, though it hasn't been without some misses along the way.

The recruitment of Jesse Hogan, Shane Kersten and Cameron McCarthy, among others, didn't pan out, while some talented draftees such as Adam Cerra and Lloyd Meek now ply their trade at other clubs.

Jesse Hogan was traded to the Dockers from Melbourne, but struggled in his time in purple. (AAP Image: Richard Wainwright)

But under Lloyd and long-time recruiter David Walls, the club did bring in Luke Ryan, Andrew Brayshaw and Sam Switkowski, as well as Sean Darcy, who became the foundation of the club's list.

The stand-out draft

The Dockers' rebuild was slowly unfolding as the 2010s ended, but the 2019 draft accelerated it considerably.

Fremantle selected Hayden Young, Caleb Serong and Liam Henry with picks seven, eight and nine, before securing Michael Frederick at pick 61.

Hayden Young overcame injury woes to help launch the Dockers into the grand final. (Getty Images: Matt King/AFL Photos)

Mark Micallef was part of the Dockers' recruitment team that year.

"The 2019 draft was something that we pegged in that we thought could really change the platform of the footy club," he said.

Securing Young and Serong attracted much of the media attention at the time, though Micallef believed the selection of Frederick so late in the draft was equally important.

"You're trying to find the diamonds in the rough and you're looking for guys that could have a trait or an ability that not many others can see," he said.

Michael Frederick was a late pick in the 2019 draft, but has become an integral part of the Freo side. (AAP Image: Richard Wainwright)

"We thought Frederick was the right talent. He had a speed skill set that we really, really liked. He had a really good demeanour and a character.

"He had a good talent threshold, but he also had the work ethic and the character to back it up as well. So that's what really makes a back-end pick."

There were several other excellent drafts for Fremantle, including in 2021, which saw Jye Amiss, Matthew Johnson and Neil Erasmus selected, along with defender Karl Worner in that year's Rookie Draft.

Playing the long game

While the players selected by the Dockers in 2019 have become stars of the side, there was another future stud Fremantle wanted but knew they couldn't get in the draft.

Luke Jackson is emblematic of Fremantle's forward planning as they rebuilt an old squad into a flag contender. (AAP: Richard Wainwright)

Luke Jackson was described as a "unicorn" — a ruck who played like a midfielder — but he was slated to go very early in the draft.

Fremantle thought they could lure him back within a few seasons, and laid the groundwork in the build-up to the draft.

"We knew he was going to the top three, but we actually put a lot of groundwork into him that year saying, 'if you ever decide to come back, we want to be the club of your choice,'" Micallef said.

"I think you always look at trades and stuff like that and people think it just happens within that trade period, but there's a lot of time and a lot of work and a lot of resources that goes into that [future planning]."

Shai Bolton's arrival at Fremantle was seen as the cream on the cake after a long rebuild. ( Getty Images: Paul Kane)

Jackson and Shai Bolton both eventually returned to Western Australia as premiership players and are now vital cogs in Justin Longmuir's machine.

A special place

While both Micallef and Lloyd have long since moved on to different things, their time at Fremantle remains dear.

"Fremantle was a very special place. They were very good to me personally. Right from Steve Rosich and Chris Bond, the CEO and footy manager, and Steve Harris, who was the president at the time, to [his successor] Dale Alcock," Lloyd said.

Docker Dudley reflects on improbable AFL rise Plucked from state footy three years after being passed over at the national draft, the shortest player in the AFL, Isaiah Dudley, has become a big part of the Fremantle Dockers.

"It is remote compared to the rest of the AFL, so they don't get a huge amount of turnover of staff.

"When you're watching them celebrate the other day [after the win over Sydney], you just see staff that have been there for decades. It's a very stable club that's operated in their own area.

"You see so many past players in the rooms and they're a very good club at looking after their people.

"I wish them nothing but the best and particularly for the recruiting team that I've worked closely with — David Walls and Dave McMullin and Ed McMullin and that team, wish them well and even their football manager, Joe Brierty."

Lloyd and David Walls (pictured) worked closely together for a decade at the Dockers. (AAP Image: Con Chronis)

Micallef was only at the club for one year, but he's enjoyed watching their success unfold.

"Kudos to the club. They've done an unbelievable job," he said.

"We set a plan and I think they sort of stuck to it, trying to get WA players back, and it worked really well.

"I loved my time at Freo, and Freo has some really special players and people involved in that footy club and even the fans, they just deserve it more than anyone.

"I really hope they get the job done on Saturday."

World.title: V'landys named NRL executive chairman after leaving Racing NSW post
World.content:
Peter V'landys' appointment as NRL executive chairman has been made official after the veteran administrator stepped down as Racing NSW chief executive.

V'landys confirmed this morning that he was ending his 22-year stint at the helm of Racing NSW, following a period of long-service leave that ends in November.

That resignation looms served as the final step in a process of moving into the NRL full time and taking on the most powerful role in rugby league since the Super League war.

"Peter has completely reinvigorated Rugby League during his tenure and the Commission is backing him in to grow the game even further," AR:C commissioner Peter Beattie said.

"Peter inherited a game with limited reserves and no significant assets, one that had needed an advance from its broadcasters just to pay the clubs and players.

"He consistently put the fan first, and the record audiences and the biggest broadcast deal in Australian sport followed."

V'Landys said he was excited to begin his new role and pledged to "take [rugby league] to the world".

Since taking over as ARL Commission chairman in 2019, V'landys has become an increasingly dominant figure in rugby league.

But this move will see his role grow even further, effectively replacing former NRL chief executive Andrew Abdo in his old position while remaining at the head of the commission.

When Abdo announced his resignation in May, V'landys had said only "Superman and Jesus added together" could replace him.

At the time, V'landys refused to speculate whether that figure could be him, but signalled he would take leave from Racing NSW in July to be able to dedicate time to the NRL.

In the months since, the 64-year-old has garnered the support required from both the clubs and the states to allow him to take on the role.

Why Tones And I won't appear at grand final Tones And I has broken her silence after the NRL declared it will forego a grand final tradition of pre-match entertainment.

Fellow commissioners have also approved the move, with the appointment now expected to be made official as early as today.

Since the creation of the independent ARL Commission in 2012, no person has held the role of chairman and executive on a full-time basis.

V'landys had been chief executive of Racing NSW since early 2004, after previously spending 17 years as boss of NSW Harness Racing.

He led the racing industry through the equine influenza outbreak, with the creation of The Everest in 2017 among his other key legacies.

"Naturally, this is a very sad day for me. I have put my heart and soul into racing for 22 years. I have been fortunate to work with outstanding, loyal and hardworking boards of directors and staff," V'landys said.

"As a team, we went from a struggling jurisdiction to a world-leading jurisdiction. I take this opportunity to thank everyone who has been in our team. I will miss them greatly, and I wish the industry every success."

In a statement, Racing NSW said V'landys's "many initiatives" had procured $3.5 billion in new funding.

Racing NSW chair Saranne Cooke said his contribution to racing was without parallel.

"Peter V'landys has been, without doubt, the most effective and successful administrator in the history of Australian sport," Dr Cooke said.

"His contribution cannot simply be measured by the extraordinary growth of racing in NSW during his tenure.

"Peter has fundamentally changed the trajectory of racing in this country and made NSW one of the world's leading racing jurisdictions."

Waterhouse says right time to move on

Horse racing legend Gai Waterhouse said it was the right time for V'landys to move on.

Waterhouse came up against V'Landys amidst his failed attempt to sell Rosehill Racecourse in Sydney to the State Government to build residential housing.

The battle saw the two prominent industry figures disagree about the sport's future, with Waterhouse successfully campaigning among Australian Turf Club members not to sell the track, despite Premier Chris Minns and V'Landys pushing to sell the site.

Australian horse trainer and businesswoman Gai Waterhouse. (ABC News: Abbey Haberecht)

"A lot of money has gone into buying properties that should have been funded back into development of the race tracks and stands," Waterhouse said.

"If we're going to be able to attract people back to the races, they have to be comfortable."

Waterhouse was especially concerned about the state of regional racetracks.

"They've been shockingly neglected over the tenure of Mr V'landys, and they need to have money spent on them," she said.

Waterhouse said his expected move to rugby league from horse racing had come at the right time.

"He's a very strong and very powerful person, but it's time for him to move and he has moved on. So let's move on now," she said.

World.title: Excitement, nerves as Dockers hold final home drill before grand final
World.content:
Thousands of Fremantle Dockers fans have packed out the club's headquarters to watch the team train for the last time in Western Australia before they head to Melbourne for Saturday's AFL grand final.

It has been 13 years since the Dockers last made a grand final, and the open training session in Cockburn saw so much demand that the team ticketed the event.

All 3,000 tickets were sold.

Long-term supporter Katie said the Dockers' success this year had special significance for her and her son Finlay.

Katie wants the Dockers to win for her son Finlay. (ABC News: Mya Kordic)

Finlay was just six weeks old when the 2013 grand final was held. Two years later, he developed cancer, and relapsed a year later.

"It's 10 years now since his relapse," Katie said.

"So it's his year and it's the Dockers' year, and all he wants is the Dockers to win on grand final day … that's his celebration."

Dockers ruckman Mason Cox and his teammates at the open training session. (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor)

Imogen Somerville, who has also supported the Dockers "her entire life", described the event as overwhelming.

Docker Dudley reflects on improbable AFL rise Plucked from state footy three years after being passed over at the national draft, the shortest player in the AFL, Isaiah Dudley, has become a big part of the Fremantle Dockers.

"It was really cool to be able to get down here," she said.

"It was like five bucks to get in, which was awesome, so couldn't miss out on that."

Doing the right thing

Fans cheered the team on the field, then posed for photographs with their football heroes, who signed jerseys, posters and autographs.

Thousands of fans thronged to the event. (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor)

And it was not just the public who were in the stands — past players, the club's chief executive Simon Garlick and Deputy Premier Rita Saffioti also attended the session.

Grand final fever grips Freo Purple reigns in Fremantle, the home of the Dockers who will play their first AFL grand final in 13 years, with even the public buses running on "Wharfie Time".

Lee Spurr, who played in the 2013 grand final, said he felt "nothing but proud" to see his club back in the running for the flag.

"I was pretty nervous watching the prelim, but now that they're there, I feel like I'm almost playing. My phone's been blowing up," he said.

After experiencing the lead-up to the AFL's biggest week, Spurr said it was important for the players to turn off their phones and stick to preparation.

Former Dockers grand finalist Lee Spurr advises the team to lock in ahead of the game. (ABC News: Mya Kordic)

"My advice would be don't get caught up in doing too much, " he said.

" This week's about doing the process, doing what's right and preparing. "

Pure excitement

Superstar ruckman Luke Jackson said he loved having the fans participate in the club's biggest week.

Several Dockers said they loved having their fans take part in the session. (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor)

"Just pure excitement. Can't wait to get over there and can't wait to play on Saturday in front of all these fans. It will be good fun," he said.

Jackson was in his second AFL season when he won his first premiership with the Melbourne Demons in 2021 in Perth.

He said he was looking forward to playing at the Melbourne Cricket Ground, where the Dockers will face the Brisbane Lions.

Dockers defender Jordan Clark (left) talks to coach Justin Longmuir at Fremantle's open training session in Cockburn. (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor)

Defender Jordan Clark was also excited, and grateful, to see the fans.

"They support us through thick and thin, as they have done for the last 30 years," he said.

All the tickets for the training event were sold. (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor)

"So they're pretty happy with this moment and they rightly deserve to be, so it's pretty special when we get this support."

With no chance of making the training session, dozens of Dockers fans 1,600 kilometres away flocked to Broome airport today to catch the only direct flight to Melbourne before Saturday.

David Leslie, who goes by Docker Dave, has followed the team since its inception said his faith had been “restored” after their stellar final performances against Swans and Geelong.

The last direct flight to Melbourne from Broome this week was packed with Dockers fans. (ABC Kimberley: Natasha Clark)

"We are going to flog the lions," he said.

Tech.title: Meta is making a standalone Muse AI gadget
Tech.content:
Meta is building a dedicated hardware device for its new Muse AI agent. The product, called Muse Charm, was briefly shown off by Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg at the end of tonight’s Meta Connect presentation. It looks almost like a chunky smartwatch without the strap — just a big screen, plus a little lanyard for carrying the device around.

The Muse Charm has a fingerprint sensor on the top right corner that you can press to activate and begin speaking to the agent. There appears to be a small camera on the device as well, plus what looks like at least three holes for microphones on the front. Zuckerberg said you don’t have to unlock a phone or open an app to use the Charm, but he didn’t share how it’s actually connecting to Meta’s servers.

Meta plans to ship the Charm “in time for the holidays in December,” but as of now Zuckerberg says the company has “only built a few of these so far.” The company still needs to finalize “the finishing material,” he said. Throughout the keynote, he teased the device and made references to a translucent exterior that would let you see the gadget’s internals. He referred to it as an “elevated hacker aesthetic.”

Zuckerberg promised to share more details “soon.”

Muse is less than a month old, but the AI agent has already become a buzzy new product for Meta. The bot is capable of taking actions on a user’s behalf, and Zuckerberg dedicated part of tonight’s keynote to new capabilities Meta is adding to the agent, including computer use on Macs and control over an email address.

There are a lot of companies racing to win the still-undefined and largely experimental realm of AI hardware. The closest analog to the Muse Charm might be the Rabbit R1, a similarly sized cutesy device that housed an AI agent, which was not nearly capable enough to make the product worth carrying around. Connect is nothing if not a reminder of how badly Meta wants to win the race to whatever that next big hardware platform is — it’s moving quickly to see if Muse as a device is something that can stick.

Tech.title: Meta Connect 2026: The 7 biggest announcements
Tech.content:
is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Meta announced a slate of new wearables during its annual Meta Connect showcase on Wednesday. The star of the event was the new Meta VR Glasses, which pack virtual reality tech into a lightweight smart glasses-style frame with a tethered puck. Meta also announced new pairs of screen-free smart glasses, along with some new AI features and style and frame options.

You can catch up on all the highlights from this year’s Meta Connect below.

Photo by Brett Putman / The Verge

Meta’s latest wearable offers full virtual reality in a smart glasses-style form factor. Unlike a typical VR headset, the VR Glasses don’t have any straps, and Meta says they’re “five times lighter than Meta Quest 3” at just 100g. Similar to Google’s Project Aura, the glasses are tethered to a pocket-sized puck with the compute hardware, battery, and storage, including a Qualcomm Snapdragon Reality Elite, 128GB of storage, and 12GB of RAM. The 5K micro OLED “Infinite Display” has 2412 x 2288 pixels per eye, with a refresh rate of up to 120Hz.

The Meta VR Glasses are launching in spring 2027 for $1,299, pricier than the Meta Ray-Ban Display but less expensive than the Apple Vision Pro, while offering similar features. Users can connect the glasses to a Mac or Windows laptop for use as a virtual external display, with an option for a virtual surface keyboard and touchpad.

The VR Glasses also have access to the full Meta Quest catalog of apps and games and support for Xbox Cloud Gaming. Meta says the glasses are “the first IMAX Enhanced certified VR device ever,” and users will be able to watch “immersive live sports” with them as well as 3D movies. They even have a “hologram” feature that creates a “photorealistic digital version of your face” for using in calls while wearing the glasses, reminiscent of the “personas” on the Apple Vision Pro.

Meta is launching camera-free smart glasses

Image: Meta

The highlight of the Ray-Ban Meta Audio is the feature they don’t have: built-in cameras. You can use them for things like listening to music, taking calls, or chatting with an AI assistant, but they can’t take pictures or record video — features that have sparked privacy and harassment concerns around Meta’s other glasses.

Meta says the new audio-only glasses are also its “lightest, slimmest AI glasses yet,” weighing just 43g. They offer up to 12 hours of battery life per charge, or 48 hours with the charging case. The Ray-Ban Meta Audio will launch on October 13th starting at $349 with 23 different color and lens combinations.

Refreshed Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 arrive with battery and design upgrades

Image: Meta

Meta launched an updated version of its main Ray-Ban Meta glasses, starting at $449. The Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 offer up to nine hours of battery life, one hour more than the Gen 2. They also have “a new customizable action button for instant access to Meta AI” and a new six-mic array that Meta says “cuts more than 90% of background noise.”

The Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 has a slimmer design than the Gen 2 as well, with 27 color and lens combinations, including new Zena and Aviator frame styles. Notably, one thing that hasn’t changed is the built-in LED light that indicates when the glasses are recording, which Meta rolled out a privacy fix for last month.

Budget glasses launch along with new glasses styles

Image: Meta

Alongside its pricier Ray-Ban glasses, Meta also announced some updates to its in-house line of glasses. It’s launching a new lower-cost version of the Meta Adventurer, which will start at $249 for a basic design with black frames and gray lenses, launching October 23rd.

Meta is also introducing a new “Mix & Match” program for customizing its glasses with different frames, lenses, and case colors. Plus, its EssilorLuxottica collection is getting two new styles, Capri and Nova, and the Kylie Jenner Starfire frames are getting a new ivory colorway. Meta’s also launching a new collaboration collection with Lisa of Blackpink.

Meta Glasses are expanding to more countries starting today, too, including Singapore, South Korea, Mexico, and the United Arab Emirates, with availability in Brazil “coming soon.”

Meta Ray-Ban Display is coming to more regions with some new features

Photo by Amelia Holowaty Krales / The Verge

A year after they originally launched, the Meta Ray-Ban Display are coming to more regions. The glasses are on sale in the UK and Canada starting today, and they’ll be available in France, Italy, and Germany starting on October 13th. Meta’s also introducing online ordering for customers in those regions and the US.

Meta’s launching a new Explore app for Display glasses where users will be able to “browse and use a growing selection of experiences built for your glasses.” The Meta Ray-Ban Display is also getting photo editing, an improved calendar, and mirrored phone notifications. Plus, Meta says the “hologram” feature launching on its VR Glasses is rolling out on the Meta Ray-Ban Display “in Early Access on WhatsApp to Meta Ray-Ban Display users in the US later this fall.”

Screenshot: The Verge

After launching its new Muse assistant earlier this month, Meta says it’s “working on” bringing the AI to its smart glasses. When it arrives on the glasses, Muse will be able to do things like guide your workouts, log meals, book appointments, and “help buy products you see.”

Meta also announced some new features for Muse, including video calls with a customizable live avatar of the AI. Plus, Muse agents are getting their own email addresses for completing tasks and communicating with users.

Meta is making an AI ‘charm’

Mark Zuckerberg teased one last device, Muse Charm, a small AI gadget that houses the Muse agent and looks a little bit like a supersized Tamagotchi. More details will be shared “soon,” he said, but the product is supposed to ship in time for the holiday season.

Tech.title: Meta’s next VR device isn’t a headset — it’s glasses
Tech.content:
Meta is launching new VR hardware: a pair of glasses. The new Meta VR Glasses sit on your ears like a typical pair of glasses instead of being strapped over your head, but they still have immersive displays for watching movies, playing games, and getting work done. Imagine a pair of hefty black sunglasses with blacked-out lenses on the outside, but the components of a typical VR headset distributed between the device on your head and a computing puck in your pocket.

The idea is to give you a way to experience VR in a much lighter and more approachable form factor than Vision Pro or Meta Quest-style headsets. I got to try the VR Glasses at Meta’s campus this week, and as Meta walked me through some familiar VR demos like watching content, playing a game, and working from multiple screens, I was impressed by how much lighter the whole experience felt. Some of that was about the literal weight, as the glasses come in at just 100g, far less than the Quest 3’s 515g. But there was also something lighter in a more intangible way: the glasses form factor made the headset seem like something I could easily jump in and out of instead of being a whole cumbersome commitment with big head straps. It felt like a lightweight Vision Pro, and is perhaps a better execution of some of what Apple wanted to do with that device.

The back of the Meta VR Glasses. Photo by Brett Putman / The Verge

To keep things light, the VR Glasses’ display and the sensors are all you actually wear on your face. The separate puck connected with a wire contains the guts powering the headset: a Snapdragon Reality Elite processor, 128GB of storage, 12GB of RAM, and the battery, which Meta says will offer up to three hours of media playback, though you can continue using the glasses even while the puck is being charged.

The display is what Meta calls a 5K MicroOLED “Infinite Display.” It has 2412 x 2288 pixels per eye at 37 pixels per degree and supports a refresh rate of up to 120Hz. On the front of the glasses are two cameras for color passthrough, letting you see through to the world around you. The headset comes in small and large sizes to offer different options for width, though they cost the same.

Here’s the compute puck. It has a solid clip. Photo by Brett Putman / The Verge

You primarily use your eyes and hand gestures to control the glasses. You just look at elements onscreen to navigate, and the OS will highlight what your eyes are looking at using two pairs of eye-tracking cameras. To select something that’s highlighted, you can pinch your thumb and pointer finger together, and to scroll around, you make a fist and move your thumb around the top of your hand. It feels similar to the gestures from the Meta Ray-Ban Display, but those require a neural wristband; the VR Glasses instead use six external cameras to follow your hands.

Based on my demos, I think the VR Glasses will be best for entertainment because of the big virtual screen. Meta showed me a clip from James Cameron’s Billie Eilish concert film, which was impressive on a huge virtual display, and parts of the most recent NBA Finals, which was filmed on a format called VR180 that provided a 180-degree view of the court. I also got to watch some of Avengers: Endgame in what Meta characterized as a “VR Enhanced Cinema” experience made in partnership with Disney and Industrial Light & Magic. In the entire VR environment around the screen showing the film, there were graphics that thematically lined up with what was actually happening onscreen that also changed as the clip went on; when a huge energy beam appeared at a major moment in the film featuring Thor, I saw one shoot out at the top of the VR environment, too. Meta says that VR enhanced versions of Avengers: Infinity War and Star Wars: A New Hope will be available when the VR Glasses launch.

Image: Meta

Gaming remains a major use case, too. Meta showed me a new mode for Beat Saber called Flux that supports playing with hands (though it will work with the Quest’s Touch Plus controllers, too). Instead of waving virtual sabers to hit blocks in time with the music, like in the original, Flux tasked me with moving my hands, which were each surrounded by balls of energy connected by pulsing electricity, to break through flying poles and smash targets. It makes sense when you play it, and the one song I played was really enjoyable. The VR Glasses will have more than 75 games at launch that will support the new hands-first experience (including a VR version of Phoenix Wright: Ace Attorney – Dual Destinies launching in 2027), but they’ll also support the entire current Quest app catalog and can connect to Touch Plus controllers (and Bluetooth controllers).

Meta is also pitching this as a way to browse apps and do some work, and I can see the vision. In one demo, I used the glasses to mirror three windows from a nearby laptop. You’ll be able to connect wirelessly to computers or other devices with a USB-C connection, which could be useful if you want more screen real estate for work. My favorite demo from my whole session was actually one about typing. While using a special version of Instagram made for the VR Glasses, I was prompted to leave a comment on a picture, but I was able to type that comment and navigate the app using a virtual keyboard and trackpad that appeared after I laid my hands flat on the table. To my surprise, the virtual keyboard and trackpad were actually good. Of course, the experience wasn’t as speedy as using a physical keyboard and mouse, but in a pinch for a short message or email, I think it could be quite useful. (I should note it’s not technically new; Meta introduced this for Quest headsets earlier this year, and I haven’t tried it on those devices.)

The glasses cost $1,299.99 and will go on sale in spring 2027. That price puts the VR Glasses between Meta’s $599.99 Quest 3 and a high-end VR headset like Apple’s $3,499 Vision Pro, and I think that’s the right way to think about them. I don’t think they will transform the landscape of VR, especially when Meta itself has been divesting from VR software and largely moving on from the VR version of Horizon Worlds.

Meta is still planning to develop full VR headsets, the company’s VP of product for VR, Angela Chang, tells The Verge. But as tech companies chase the next big hardware category, however, a new form factor is starting to emerge: something that’s more capable than most smart glasses but less overbearing than a full-on VR headset. Google and Xreal are teaming up on XR glasses. Snap’s idea is the augmented reality-focused Specs glasses, and Meta is working on AR glasses too. The VR Glasses represent another fascinating idea of what a computer on your head can be.

Tech.title: Muse is coming to Meta smart glasses
Tech.content:
Just a couple of weeks after launching Muse, Meta announced that it’s “working on” bringing the agent to its smart glasses, including the new glasses it unveiled at Meta Connect. Users will be able to activate Muse from their glasses by saying its name and ask it to handle tasks like guiding a workout, logging meals, or helping them shop for products they’re looking at.

Muse is just one of several major updates coming to Meta’s glasses. They’re also getting some new accessibility features, like a Hearing Enhancement feature Meta says is “FDA-cleared software for adults with perceived mild to moderate hearing loss.” It will be available later this year with a Meta One subscription or as a $149 add-on for compatible glasses. Meta AI will also be able to give “more context-rich answers” when users ask the glasses what they’re looking at, potentially making Meta’s glasses more effective for helping blind and low-vision users interpret their surroundings. A new audio customization feature will also allow users to shift their smart glasses’ volume between their left and right ears, including sending all audio to one side.

Meta’s introducing some new audio and photo features as well, including Dolby Atmos Capture, which will allow users to record videos with 360-degree spatial audio. A new Dynamic Photo feature automatically captures multiple frames when you take a photo with Meta’s glasses, then uses Meta AI to suggest the best frame from each batch.

The Meta Ray-Ban Display glasses are getting the new “Hologram” feature Meta announced for its new VR Glasses, which it says is “a photorealistic digital version of your face for calls from Meta Ray-Ban Display” that “infers” your expression using your voice. The feature’s “rolling out in Early Access on WhatsApp to Meta Ray-Ban Display users in the US later this fall.”

A couple new heads-up navigation features are coming to the Meta Ray-Ban Display as well. Starting later this month, users in the US and Canada will have an option to use their voice to ask for real-time cycling or public transit directions. The Meta Ray-Ban Display will also start using “the world in front of you rather than street signs in turn-by-turn walking directions,” like referencing a house, car, or landmark the glasses detect. A few other new features are on the way for the Display glasses, including an option for editing photos directly on the glasses’ display, a new “Explore” app for finding new apps, an improved calendar, and mirroring for phone notifications.

Tech.title: Meta ditches the camera on its newest smart glasses
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Walking around Meta Connect 2026, everyone’s sporting smart glasses in all sorts of shapes, colors, and sizes. It’s a marked difference here, a tech bubble where “pervert glasses” are not a concern.

Outside Connect, the public backlash against wearable surveillance tech — a catchall term that encompasses not just smart glasses, but also smartwatches and AI pendants — is gaining steam. So it’s incredibly curious timing that this year, the company is launching Ray-Ban Meta Audio Glasses: smart glasses infused with Meta AI, but with no camera for recording others.

To hear Meta tell it, that’s a coincidence. Audio-only glasses have been years in the making.

“Three years ago, it wasn’t clear if AI glasses were going to be a thing. Back then, every other company was backing out of the space,” says Alex Himel, Meta’s vice president of wearables. “Then two years ago, we saw that audio was the top use case, the biggest potential for AI, and that it should work well in a pair of audio glasses.”

There are multiple combinations of colors and lenses across two styles for the audio-only glasses. Clubmaster is in the middle here, sandwiched between two Burbanks. Photo by Brett Putman / The Verge

Himel has a point. Open-ear audio is the least controversial part of the Ray-Bans — and the thing everyone can agree is convenient. Plus, the camera-less glasses are lighter. Himel says that by removing the cameras, Meta could “rearchitect” the glasses. “That allowed us to take a lot of electronics out of the front frame and have a lot more design flexibility.”

The audio-only models start at 43 grams — heavier than normal wire-frame glasses, but noticeably lighter than the roughly 50g Ray-Ban Meta Gen 2 and the 69g Meta Ray-Ban Display. The arms are thinner. They come in two styles: the Mad Men-esque Clubmaster and the more Wayfarer-reminiscent Burbank. The hinges extend for wider faces; the temple arms and nose pads are adjustable. There are 23 color and lens combinations, and they can support the same wider prescription range as the Ray-Ban Meta Optics lineup. Even more so than the standard Meta Ray-Bans, these look and wear like normal glasses. And with a $349 starting price, they’re cheaper too.

Free of a power-hungry camera, the battery lasts an estimated 12 hours on a single charge. The most technical things you can do with them are interact with Meta AI, take phone calls, and listen to podcasts or music. And that’s it.

I think Clubmaster looks fetching on me. But these look like ordinary glasses. Photo by Victoria Song / The Verge

“They don’t record,” Himel says. “The only thing they do, which is the same thing as an Alexa device in your house or some other devices, they’re just listening for a specific wake word. They’re not sending anything … If they hear [the wake word], then they start listening to what you’re saying. When you’re done talking, then it’s processing, and that’s visible to the AI. It gets processed, and that’s kind of it.”

Slipping them on, they’re comfortable and, I think, quite fetching on me. Regardless of how one might feel about Meta, it’s fair to guess most people would feel less like a creeper wearing these.

Meta Glasses and Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3

I feel differently slipping on the new Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3. Partly because the camera is back in play, partly because the pair Meta gives me is the new aviator style with transition lenses. I’m told I can pull it off, but I keep asking my colleague Jay Peters if I’m giving ’80s serial killer vibes. The other new style is called Zena — not the warrior princess — and it’s a bolder, geometric cat-eye frame.

The third-generation glasses feature fairly minor refinements. There’s a sixth microphone, compared to the second generation’s five, for clearer phone calls. Battery life has gotten a slight boost to nine hours, an hour longer than the second gen. The temple arms, like the audio-only glasses, are adjustable for a better fit. All sound will now be captured in Dolby Atmos for spatial audio. Sure! That’s neat if I’m in my quiet hotel room, but it’s harder to appreciate when reviewing footage amid the hustle and bustle of Meta Connect. The new model comes in 27 color and lens combinations, plus three seasonal options.

Along with the hardware changes, the Gen 3 glasses are also getting a price bump. They start at $449, up from $379 for the second-gen models last year.

Teehee, is this 80s serial killer vibes or… Photo by Brett Putman / The Verge

Meta Glasses — the off-brand, more affordable entry-level glasses launched a few months ago — also have more options. There are two new styles, Capri and Nova. Capri is some kind of cat-eye shape, while Nova… honestly, the styles are all starting to blur together. They’re round and remind me of several other Ray-Ban Meta glasses, but slightly different. There’s a new ivory-colored Kylie Jenner pair that costs $399.

But maybe Kylie Jenner isn’t the celebrity collab you’ve been dreaming about. That’s fine. Because Blackpink’s Lisa — a K-pop icon and The White Lotus actress — also has Meta Glasses. They have pink lenses and come with a blind-box-type charm styled after Lisa’s pets. These also start at $399. (Non-celebrity versions of the Meta Glasses start at $249.)

Why the celebrity collabs? Options for more people, including women.

Blackpink (glasses) in your area. Photo by Victoria Song / The Verge

“With the Meta Glasses Starfire with Kylie, we saw a younger, more female audience start to buy the glasses,” says Himel. “Wayfarer is the most popular glasses type in the world, but it tends to be more male — though definitely not exclusively male. The second brand we did was Oakley … but Oakley [also] tends to be a more masculine brand. So I think with Kylie and Lisa, and with more styles, we’re seeing them appeal to more women.”

There are actually more limited-edition versions, styles, colors, and prescription permutations available across the entire existing Ray-Ban Meta lineup at a whole range of price points. I suspect I’d need to make a spreadsheet to list them all. While scuttling about Meta’s campus this week, I’m brought to an entire area where they’re all displayed. It looks like a high-end store for, regular, schmegular glasses. That, I suspect, is the whole point.

AI in your frames

All around the campus, there are life-size cutouts of Meta’s cuddly Muse mascot. That’s because Muse, Meta’s recently released personal AI agent, is coming to the seemingly 4,000 iterations of Meta smart glasses that now exist.

“Muse is gonna be everywhere,” confirms Himel. “Muse is gonna be on every device that we make.”

The pitch for Muse in your glasses is that your AI assistant will better remember your context and do things on your behalf. During a demo, I ask a Muse agent to help me buy snacks that will give me the best protein bang for my calorie buck. It can do it, but fails at adding another snack to my cart. Obviously, this is an early-stage demo, and there are always kinks. I can see the shape of how this could be helpful. I can also see how it’d be a treasure trove of data for Meta.

Less contentious is a demo of a new FDA-cleared hearing assistance feature. I’m asked to wear earplugs to mimic mild hearing loss. Things sound a bit muddled. With the feature turned on, higher voices gain a tinny quality as the AI works to boost conversational tones in a semi-loud environment. After about five minutes, I’ve forgotten I have earplugs in. Adding this capability will cost an extra $149, but I’m told it’s FSA/HSA eligible and designed to be a one-time fee versus an ongoing subscription.

The Nova glasses! Photo by Brett Putman / The Verge

Lastly, there are two minor privacy updates — though neither truly addresses the fears people have been debating this past summer. The first is bringing the same “private processing” pipeline used on WhatsApp to wearables. It’s a server-based system in which a user’s data is inaccessible to Meta or any other third parties when end-to-end encryption isn’t possible or on-device processing isn’t powerful enough.

“It’s so that you know that your data is just yours and you’re the only one who has access to it. Other companies have taken an approach to everything on-device. We do a lot on-device. But the problem with just doing things on-device is that the device is only so powerful and capable. And so if you want to run more capable models and get better functionality, we want to offer the same privacy protections, but with more capabilities. So that’s what private processing is,” says Himel.

Meta will also roll out an update where users can opt out of their visual data being used for AI training. (Audio-only queries are still used for training.)

That’s progress but doesn’t really address people’s primary concerns about the glasses being used to covertly record people in public. Himel also acknowledges that the private processing feature is mostly about protecting the data of the person wearing the glasses.

More is more

Meta’s goal at Connect this year is to bombard everyone with options. By the end of the year, Meta expects to have over 100 versions of its glasses. The more versions of its glasses, the more people they’ll reach. The more AI updates that trickle to each of these iterations, the faster Meta can stake its claim on the next era of mobile computing.

So goes the theory. But providing hardware options isn’t Meta’s problem. Inside the safe bubble of Meta’s campus, everyone wears these glasses. The issue is outside Menlo Park, where a vocal contingent isn’t asking for more. They’re asking for less.

Tech.title: Meta is making Muse more powerful and will let you video chat with it, too
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Meta is quickly iterating on its new Muse AI agent, announcing a bunch of updates today that make the bot more capable and able to chat with you in more ways.

Muse agents are getting their own email addresses that they can use for accomplishing tasks. You’ll also be able to communicate with your Muse agent over the new email addresses, too. In addition, the recently launched Muse Mac app will be getting the ability to use your computer.

Meta is also going to give you another way to chat with its popular AI agent: video calls. Since its recent launch, the primary way to talk with Muse was through a chat interface, but you’ll soon be able to have live video conversations with your Muse avatar. Meta will let you tweak the way your Muse avatar sounds — you can already customize the way it looks — and a new Muse Realtime Avatar model will inform how it moves.

Muse launched earlier this month, and it’s seemingly proving to be a hit, topping the App Store charts and reportedly being downloaded more than ChatGPT on mobile in its first 12 days. Meta appears to be capitalizing on the popularity by quickly introducing the new videocalling features, but that’s not all that’s new for the agent. Meta says it plans to launch Muse on its smart glasses in the coming months, which will let you talk to Muse about what you’re looking at while wearing your glasses.

Tech.title: Meta Connect 2026: The biggest news and announcements
Tech.content: It’s about time for Meta Connect, the company’s annual product launch event. This year, given the company’s major focus on AI and wearables like smart glasses, it seems likely that we’ll see updates from CEO Mark Zuckerberg and his team on those categories. The company has been facing significant scrutiny because of how some users have been covertly recording other people using the glasses, meaning that one of the biggest announcements of the show could be its rumored camera-free pair.

Tech.title: Meta Connect 2026 live blog: On the ground at Mark Zuckerberg’s next big product launch
Tech.content:
It’s time once again for Meta’s annual September product launch event, and The Verge is on the ground in Menlo Park to cover the show live. Meta says that today’s keynote by Mark Zuckerberg will be about how “Meta is building a future for everyone” — something he wrote at length about in a recent essay about AI, smart glasses, and more. That means we can expect more news from Zuckerberg and his team on those topics; perhaps we’ll hear more about Meta’s recently launched Muse AI agent and new glasses hardware.

Whatever Zuckerberg and Meta have to say about smart glasses will be particularly notable. The company is dealing with an outpouring of privacy and harassment concerns stemming from the product line’s built-in camera, which has led to them being derided as “pervert glasses.” Meta has already tried to tackle that reputation with recent privacy fixes and a new marketing campaign, but it could introduce more updates on the Connect stage.

The show is scheduled to begin at 7PM ET / 4PM PT, and you can follow our live updates here.

Tech.title: Everything new coming to Meta’s AI agent Muse
Tech.content:
Meta’s personal AI agent Muse is only a few weeks old, and the social networking giant isn’t wasting any time building out what may be its biggest bet on consumer AI to date.

CEO Mark Zuckerberg kicked off the company’s annual Connect event in Menlo Park on Wednesday with a keynote that made one thing clear: Meta is going all-in on Muse.

The Muse agent (the physical avatar is named Jolly, according to Zuckerberg) is designed to handle everyday tasks by connecting to users’ apps and services, including email and calendars. At Connect, Zuckerberg introduced a slew of new capabilities and integrations to make Muse more useful and more deeply woven into users’ daily lives. Muse will be everywhere, if the user chooses, including on their Meta AI glasses.

Muse, which launched in early September, interacts across a user’s devices and digital accounts. The agent is powered by Muse Spark, Meta’s multimodal AI model built for agentic work. Meta has touted it as a more accessible agent than those offered by competitors — an AI helper that, from the jump, allows users to automate the busy work in their lives.

“The centerpiece of our vision for what we’re building is Muse,” Zuckerberg said as he kicked off a keynote donning khakis and a black T-shirt with the words “Building is My love Language” emblazoned across the front. “In the coming years, I expect that Muse is going to grow into the personal superintelligence that billions of people around the world are going to use to accomplish their goals and improve their lives.”

Zuckerberg also believes that Muse will make money for its users — and of course, eventually for Meta.

“We’re standing behind this by making Muse free for a huge number of tokens, with the expectation that over time we will profit by taking a small fee from transactions,” he said.

Here are the new features and capabilities that got our attention …

Muse gets its own digital avatar

Image Credits:Meta/screenshot /

One of the more fun announcements made Wednesday is that Muse users will soon have the ability to conjure a distinct digital avatar for their particular agent and then video chat with it in real time. A new AI model, Muse Realtime Avatar, has been developed to power the particular feature, the company says.

The idea is that Meta’s previously faceless AI software will be given a face, body, and voice, making them significantly more personable. There’s certainly a hint of Metaverse-ishness to this feature, which was demoed on stage at Connect. Users will be able to have live conversations with this avatar, giving it tasks and asking it questions.

Muse will soon be active in Meta smart glasses

Muse will also be integrated with Meta’s smart glasses line, the company announced. This means that users will be able to communicate with their agent merely by speaking to their glasses. The agent activates via a wake word, the company said, adding that it will be able to guide users through a personalized workout, log meals, book an appointment, and help them buy products they see.

Meta said Muse will work in the background and check back in when it’s done.

It’s not clear exactly when this feature will become available, although Meta says that it should launch sometime in “the coming months.”

Soon, you’ll be able to let Muse run your Mac

Image Credits:Meta/screenshot /

Meta says it is bringing Muse computer work to Mac. The company had previously talked about Muse coming to Mac, and spent more time on Wednesday providing a few new details. This means that users will be able to delegate tasks to the agent, and — much like other popular AI agents from OpenAI and Anthropic — Muse will be able to operate any app on a user’s desktop.

“You can have it help you run your small business, or just get work done for you,” Meta’s chief AI officer Alexandr Wang said Wednesday during the keynote. “You can walk away from your computer and it keeps working for you on all the jobs you lined up.”

Muse will get its own email address

Since Muse will always be working in the background, it will naturally need its own email address. Meta’s Wang announced it is developing that feature and will make it available “soon,” without providing a more precise timeline.

Users will also be able to add Muse to an email thread or forward emails from the agent to handle on their behalf.

Shopping partnerships and connectors galore

Meta has locked in partnerships with companies like Stripe and Shopify, illustrating that the company sees Muse as an important tool for shopping.

Muse can access the entire Shopify product catalog agentically and use Lync and now Shop Pay to buy almost anything on the internet, according to Wang, who noted that Meta has also added more support for payments with PayPal.

The company also announced a string of new partnerships with retailers, including Best Buy, Gap, Sephora, Walmart, and Wayfair. Muse will be able to connect with these retail apps as well as with Expedia and soon, Instacart. Other connectors include GitHub, Granola, and Notion.

Wang noted that the company wants Muse to connect with small business too. Meta recently opened its platform to allow developers to build their own “connectors.” The company received more than 1,500 applications in less than week, he said, adding “I think this could be a generational opportunity to start building for a new platform as it takes off, and the response so far has been really great.”

Tech.title: Meta made a Tamagotchi-like wearable for its Muse AI agent
Tech.content:
The AI amulet has become a bit of a cliché in the tech industry — devices like Friend have turned the idea of physical AI into little more than an exercise in eye-rolling for many consumers.

But that hasn’t stopped Meta from jumping into the arena with its own AI wearable, called Muse Charm, which is designed to give consumers another way to stay connected to its recently launched, and already popular, personal AI agent, Muse.

The device, which CEO Mark Zuckerberg revealed in a “one more thing” moment during the company’s annual Connect event, isn’t ready to ship just yet. Zuckerberg said his team had to “finalize laying out the components” and promised the devices would be “ready to ship in time for the holidays in December.”

The Muse agent, which is now embodied by a cute digital avatar known within the company as Jolly, lives inside the palm-sized totem that users can carry in their pockets or attach to a keychain. The device comes with a tiny screen that displays the avatar representing the agent. Users can talk to the device, which can then presumably carry out tasks on their behalf.

“We packed the whole Muse experience, including the whole real-time voice and avatar stack, into something that fits on a keychain and is always available to talk to,” Zuckerberg said during Wednesday’s keynote. “You just go ahead and tap here in the fingerprint sensor in the corner, and you can start talking without having to unlock a phone or open an app.”

Zuckerberg added: “So if you’re not wearing glasses, this is going to be by far the fastest way to talk to your Muse and to show what’s going on around you.”

Appropriate for what it offers, the gadget has a quasi-Tamagotchi feel to it — a lightweight, personality-filled device designed to keep users always connected to Meta’s software. It also feels like a relatviely low-stakes way for the social media giant to experiment with AI wearables while also offering yet another way to distribute its AI agent to the masses.

Tech.title: Meta is trying VR glasses (again), this time with more IMAX
Tech.content:
Meta is renewing its quest to make virtual reality a thing. At its Connect event on Wednesday, the company announced Meta VR Glasses, its newest entry into the VR market, which will be available next spring starting at $1,299.99.

These glasses actually seem quite promising, thanks to a substantially lighter form factor and a host of new entertainment integrations — including (allegedly) IMAX compatibility.

Moments before unveiling them, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg reminded the audience that the company had decided awhile ago to shift its focus away from the Metaverse and build fewer VR devices until it had real breakthroughs.

“This is a breakthrough,” he exclaimed before showing off the glasses. “A lot of people agree that augmented reality glasses with holograms are clearly going to be part of the future, but we’ve also heard that a lot of people are less interested in wearing a headset. So we have built a new kind of VR device that delivers the same magical feeling of presence and immersion with high-resolution displays and views of the world around you in a form factor that is a pair of glasses for the first time.”

Meta says that the glasses are five times lighter than the Meta Quest 3 — and they look much more like normal eyewear than the bulky headsets the company has released before. The frames are made of magnesium alloy, and the glasses are powered by Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Reality Elite processor. They connect to a computing puck that doubles as a battery, which users can just slip the puck into their pocket to use the glasses on the go.

The glasses are largely built for entertainment. Micro-OLED panels built into the lenses provide what Meta calls a 5K Infinite Display with 37 pixels per degree, along with Dolby Vision and Dolby Atmos audio support. Users will be able to download and watch movies.

Perhaps one of the more unique features of the glasses, however, is that Meta is pitching them as a great way to enjoy IMAX-captured films.

Indeed, the company calls the glasses the “first IMAX-enhanced certified VR device ever” and says they will be one of the few ways to experience the expanded aspect ratio that defines IMAX’s distinct high-resolution viewing experience.

The glasses also support 3D content, including movies that integrate a user’s physical space into their viewing experience. Meta says that it has teamed up with Disney and that in November, Disney+ users will be able to stream specific movies — including certain Marvel movies — in 3D.

Meta says that users will be able to watch specific movies and have their surroundings “transformed with immersive environments, dynamic effects, stunning 3D visuals, and spatial audio” — essentially converting the movie into a VR gaming-type experience.

The glasses will also come with Meta AI — its automated virtual assistant — built in, which means that users will be able to talk to the glasses and automate various tasks via voice command. For instance, Meta says you’ll be able to start a movie just by asking your glasses to do so. Other ways to issue commands include hand gestures.

Tech.title: Meta introduces camera-free AI glasses
Tech.content:
Confirming earlier reports, Meta announced its first pair of camera-free AI glasses, the clunkily named Ray-Ban Meta Audio, at its Connect 2026 conference on Wednesday. Designed to combat criticism around the more malicious use cases for AI glasses, which saw them nicknamed “pervert glasses” by some, the new devices will be audio-only, offering the ability to listen to music and podcasts, take calls, translate speech, and communicate with Meta’s AI assistant, Muse.

The glasses are designed by Meta’s partner in its AI hardware efforts, EssilorLuxottica, and will start at $349.

While Meta today offers a range of AI glasses in a variety of styles, colors, and capabilities, the audio-only glasses could help the brand recover from some of the reputational damage after critics pointed out how people, often men, were using AI glasses to record videos without subjects’ consent. Meta attempted to mitigate this issue with an update that would disable the camera if the LED light that indicated the glasses were recording was ever tampered with. However, the creepiness factor remained.

This latest device could prove to be more popular for that reason, while also providing an answer to something like Apple’s Siri-powered AirPods.

“Once you get used to high quality audio, it’s just a thing that you want all the time, right?” Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said during a keynote Wednesday, adding that the company after working on the idea realized it could design a whole new category of glasses around audio glasses.

Image Credits:Meta/Screenshot /

Because they don’t have to house cameras, the glasses are slimmer than Meta’s other models and weigh only 43 grams. They also have adjustable temple tips, swappable nose pads, overextension hinges, and battery life of up to 12 hours on a single charge, Meta claims. With the included charging case, that battery life extends to up to 48 hours.

They’ll also come in a variety of colors and options — 23 color and lens combinations in total — and in two new styles, a retro-inspired “Clubmaster” Ray-Ban style and “Burbank,” described as more of a “classic, timeless, rectangle shape.” Like other Meta glasses, you can order them with your optical prescription as well, if needed.

The glasses will be available for preorder on October 13, the company noted.

Alongside the glasses, Meta announced its next-generation AI glasses (the ones with cameras), the Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 3). In addition to the Ray-Ban Meta Wayfarer, there will also be two new styles, the Aviator and Zena — the latter offering more of a cat-eye frame shape. These will have a 12 MP camera that supports 3K Ultra HD video, a six-mic array, and up to nine hours of battery life.

The glasses Meta launched with EssilorLuxottica will also see an expanded lineup of styles and colors as well as a new partnership with singer Lisa, which follows the company’s earlier brand partnership with Kylie Jenner. The glasses will also be roll out to more countries globally, Meta said.

All of Meta’s AI glasses will, of course, feature access to its newer personal AI assistant, Muse.

The company also teased other coming updates, including support for Dolby Atmos Capture, a feature that picks the best photo from multiple frames, an option to choose landscape or portrait modes, hearing enhancements for those with hearing loss, more detailed responses, different audio modes, customizable controls, and something called “private processing” that Meta claims will prevent the company from seeing your data.

Tech.title: Vogue sent robots down the runway at Vogue World, and people were not impressed
Tech.content:
Vogue World closed its Milan edition this week with a troupe of robots — perhaps a preview of what’s coming when the event descends on San Francisco next year.

Vogue World is the magazine’s annual traveling spectacle, now in its fifth year: part runway show, part celebrity showcase, part variety hour, part ad-sales opportunity, staged in a different city each time. It has run through New York, London, Paris, and Hollywood. This year’s Milan edition was marketed as a tribute to Italian craftsmanship and “the human touch” in an age of technology, which makes what happened next a little strange.

During the act titled The Age of Intelligence, humanoid robots made by the Chinese firm Unitree walked into the Galleria to Gigi D’Agostino’s “L’Amour Toujours.” They waved their arms in the air, imploring onlookers to clap. One did a lasso. They were not wearing clothes. The pained expression of Alessandro Michele, the creative director of Valentino, quickly went viral.

Vogue World Milano ends (appropriately Europoor-kitschily) with tiny robottini dancing to L’Amour Toujours while Alessandro Michele slowly dies inside pic.twitter.com/xicYWWl6VW — sascha (@SaschaAmato) September 22, 2026

I haven’t seen a single thing about the actual fashion that was presented at Vogue World Milan. Instead, everyone is talking about the robots. (These same robots have been making headlines worldwide for their dance moves, and for falling and breaking.) Similar robots turned up on the runway at London Fashion Week, which is happening now.

Vogue turned heads earlier this year when it announced that the next edition will be in San Francisco, arguably one of the least stylish cities in the United States. The timing isn’t coincidental. Anna Wintour has aligned herself ever more closely with the tech barons of our time, and Vogue World Milan was itself sponsored in part by Meta Glasses, with additional support from OpenAI.

It was one of those moments that reveals how thoroughly tech exists in a bubble, and that not everyone is happy with the rapid adoption of new technology, or by Vogue cozying up to the symbols of the insanely rich — and only getting richer — tech titans during a cost-of-living crisis. That’s before you get to AI, mass surveillance, the displacement of labor, and the energy crisis, all of them overseen by the same titans. For some, a robot on a runway is further proof of what is going wrong in the world right now.

miuccia prada when the fuckass robot walked out during vogue world pic.twitter.com/SebwpV0zkl — noah (@pradachurch) September 22, 2026

We are all Alessandro Michele, sitting front row at Vogue World Milan, having an existential crisis about the absolute state of things while robots awkwardly dance about. Numb to the pain at this point. Madness. — Michael J. Miraflor (@michaelmiraflor) September 23, 2026

just got off the phone with the creative director of Vogue World. First question he asked me. “So you hated the robots?” 🤭

Full interview on Substack tomorrow 👀 https://t.co/FTa3gumPgY — Louis Pisano (@LouisPisano) September 23, 2026

“I’m annoyed by the celebrities cheering the whole thing,” one tech founder wrote me on Instagram. “It’s sick and gloom. People are literally losing jobs and livelihoods because of these things. They need to stop encouraging it. What’s it even modeling? Headphones?”

One fashion reporter friend simply said “No,” when I asked for thoughts on the robots and Vogue World San Francisco. Jason Johnson, founder of Culture Impact Agency, noted that Vogue has been trying to build a relationship with Silicon Valley for at least the past decade, highlighting when Jony Ive co-hosted the Met Gala back in 2015. The dancing robots at Vogue World Milan were inevitable, then, as is Vogue World San Francisco and as was Jeff Bezos and his wife, Lauren Sanchez, getting the splashy Vogue wedding cover and co-hosting the 2026 Met Gala.

“Publications are figuring out new ways to make money and tech has money,” he told me. “Vogue has the cultural influence and access that those tech people want.” Both sides win in the end, he said.

Still, something about the way Vogue is going about this feels unnatural.

The collection I think about every day and what I think should be shown at Vogue World San Francisco. Image Credits:WWD / Contributor / Getty Images

Muna Ikedionwu, founder of MKEDI, a strategy firm for early-stage startups, said what she found most interesting about the robots is that they don’t fully represent the innovation and progress that’s actually happening in the creative technologist space. “I’ve seen such incredible examples of engineering and AI being used to influence fashion, being used to influence design and art,” she told me, adding that robots walking down the runway doesn’t even scratch the surface of what is happening right now at the intersection of fashion and tech.

She points to the artist duo AA Murakami, who created Olympian Eileen Gu’s dress of bubbles at this year’s Met Gala. They are fashion designers but also engineers, Ikedionwu said, noting a presentation she saw them give recently about how to create an “everlasting bubble.” They are helping to pioneer “emphemeral technology,” she said, “this idea of technology and innovation that speaks to the ephemeral nature or the temporariness of art and humanity and the soul.”

Sure, I guess when you compare it to this, the robots did seem quite boring. Whenever I think about the intersection of fashion and technology, I think about that Spring 2024 Schiaparelli collection, which unveiled a robot baby crafted with Swarovski crystals and a dress made with vintage tech like PC microchips. (I once threatened to wear that dress to Disrupt; see image above.)

Ikedionwu wonders whether this robot performance was a way to make the general public more comfortable with technology and fashion overlapping, a merger that has been underway behind the scenes for years. If so, it didn’t work. But maybe Vogue World is saving all the good stuff for San Francisco.

Tech.title: Anthropic says its biology lab has already found something big
Tech.content:
Last week, Anthropic confirmed that it was operating a wet biology lab in the Bay Area where it uses its AI models to run physical experiments. This week, the AI giant announced that this lab has already made what it believes is a big discovery: a new enzyme “system” that has certain “properties reminiscent of CRISPR,” as Anthropic describes it.

CRISPR is a natural immune system used by bacteria to fight off viruses that has become a gene-editing technology widely used by researchers.

Essentially, what Anthropic says it found is a previously unknown enzyme system hidden in the DNA of bacteriophages, which are viruses that infect and replicate within bacteria. Anthropic’s researchers say this system behaves similarly to CRISPR in that it can “perform operations like cutting, copying, and pasting DNA.”

It will be up to the broader research community to validate how big, or new, this discovery actually is. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei acknowledges that the discovery was based on the work of others and that a team from Stanford previously discovered a system “that is in some ways similar to the one Claude found,” he wrote on X.

But Amodei and Anthropic are not just emphasizing the discovery. They are touting it was found “mostly, though not entirely, by Claude,” the CEO wrote.

On the one hand, that is astounding. This lab was only established this spring (though Anthropic declined to be more specific about how many months it has been open). A discovery in just a few short months would be speedy enough work, but the team said it actually only took Claude 21 hours of concerted effort. Claude searched through data using about 950 agents that burned through 210 million tokens.

Still, the revelation that Anthropic has been conducting biology experiments comes right after AI CEOs, including Amodei, publicly admitted that models have become so capable, and so potentially dangerous, that the industry must slow down and develop safety-testing procedures. This after a couple of his employees publicly said earlier this month that there’s a risk AI could kill us all.

Amodei himself has said one of the things he fears most is that AI could be used for bioterrorism. But he also believes AI will “cure most diseases in 5-10 years,” he wrote. So Anthropic has clearly decided the rewards are worth the risks.

Given that, perhaps the biggest reveal in this news isn’t the discovery itself but that the biology lab hasn’t let Claude loose. The physical experiments were done by humans.

“Our lab, located in the Bay Area, looks like a typical molecular biology lab. We do research that involves only the lower-levels of the biosafety risk level (BSL-1 and BSL-2) and we do not handle pathogens that can infect humans. All of the lab work is performed by human scientists.”

It’s also true that AI-powered biological research is hardly unique to Anthropic. Researchers from Stanford just published a paper on the work they are doing with LLMs and CRISPR. Researchers at UC San Francisco used AI to design enzymes from scratch. Google launched its first AI-powered biology research tool, AlphaFold, back in 2020. So AI has clearly arrived in biological research beyond the AI labs pursuing it themselves.

Yet, Amodei hasn’t ruled out a fully automated biology lab in the future. “Eventually it may even be possible for Claude itself to safely perform the experiments by autonomously controlling lab equipment, with appropriate safeguards in place, but we aren’t doing that today,” he said.

.

Tech.title: If Amazon doesn’t know how to eliminate carbon emissions, then who does?
Tech.content:
Amazon’s chief sustainability officer said Tuesday the company doesn’t know how it will achieve its goal of net-zero carbon emissions by 2040.

“We are still striving towards that target,” Kara Hurst said at an Axios event, adding later that she is “not going to sit here and say, ‘We know all the ways that we’re going to do this.’”

The admission was both frank and realistic. It’s also a bit disappointing. If Amazon doesn’t have a plan to decarbonize, then who does?

Amazon is one of the largest companies in the world, with last year’s revenue up 12% to $717 billion — about the size of Ireland’s economy. Its rise is illustrative of how, as UN Secretary General António Guterres has pointed out, power has shifted from governments to a few corporations.

As power moves, responsibility follows. The question is, how much responsibility does Amazon bear?

“This isn’t a question of companies versus governments,” Hurst told TechCrunch in a written reply to questions after the event. “Tackling climate change at the scale it demands takes both, and it takes them working together.” She added, “Where we can lead, we do.”

It’s true that Amazon has not been sitting still. In her talk yesterday, Hurst pointed out that the company is “one of the largest purchasers of clean energy in the world for the last several years running” with 42 gigawatts in its portfolio. She also said that Amazon has reduced its carbon intensity, or how much pollution it generates per dollar of revenue, though that claim depends on the time frame. Last year, carbon intensity rose compared with 2024, even though it stayed below where it was in 2022.

Amazon is a sprawling business, and as a result, its carbon emissions are spread across nearly every sector of the economy, from aviation and AI to agriculture and construction. The company needs suppliers in every sector to achieve its goal. “This is not something we can do alone,” Hurst said at the Axios event.

The company acknowledges that its commitments are its own. “We hold ourselves accountable to The Climate Pledge goal of net-zero carbon by 2040. That commitment hasn’t changed,” Hurst told TechCrunch.

But Amazon has also made choices that undermine its leadership on the issue. Earlier this year, an investigation revealed the company’s plans to build a 7.65 gigawatt natural gas power plant to power an AI data center campus. The project’s 35 turbines could release up to 33 million tons of carbon dioxide annually, making it the largest single source of that pollution in the U.S.

With few exceptions, companies prioritize revenue growth over climate commitments. For a company like Amazon, which operates the largest cloud service in the world, AI is apparently a revenue driver that’s impossible to pass up.

The climate tech world has been hoping that, as clean power gets cheaper, the market would work its magic to lower carbon emissions. There have been a few success stories, but as the AI rush has shown, that approach has its limits. Even Amazon, one of the leaders in the space, bet big on natural gas. In the process, it essentially said that climate change is something for future generations of executives to deal with. Sound familiar?

Tech.title: VC firm Bessemer now has another $5.75B to invest in (what else?) AI
Tech.content:
In Brief

Bessemer Venture Partners announced on Wednesday that it has raised $5.75 billion across two new funds to accelerate its investment across all parts of the AI stack. The firm, which has backed companies such as Anthropic, Cognition, Legora, Perplexity, Ramp, Shopify, and Waymo, dedicated $1.75 billion for seed and early-stage investing and the remaining $4 billion for growth startups.

Bessemer has been well-known as a leading VC in the SaaS era, with a particular knack for picking enterprise winners, like Box, Docusign, and Gainsight. Since 2022, it has invested in more than 260 AI-native companies. So far, the firm has invested $3 billion into AI-related startups, it says, including those focused on compute, infrastructure, foundation models, dev tools, app-layer startups, and agentic tech.

Now, Bessemer positions all things AI as the opportunity of a lifetime — a common sentiment, until the next big trendy tech revolution comes around, of course.

“AI-native companies are scaling faster than any category of technology we’ve backed before,” Bessemer Partner Byron Deeter said in the company’s funding announcement. VC firms also need to keep increasing their war chests, Deeter told Bloomberg, because companies staying private longer has become “a permanent structural shift.”
